#5609. Cisco research: Trust, not technology, is now the speed limit on enterprise AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For several years, the conversation about enterprise artificial intelligence has focused on capability: which model is smartest and which GPU is fastest. That made sense when technology was the constraint.

It isn’t anymore. AI can now do far more than most organizations will allow, and the gap is trust.

That’s the core finding of “Permission to Scale: The Critical Role of Trust in Successful AI Adoption,” new research released today at Cisco Systems Inc.’s Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne. Authored by independent researcher Brad Howarth, the study draws on data from 25 Australian organizations.

At Cisco Live APJC, Cisco hosted a press panel to discuss the report. The panel, moderated by Howarth, featured a number of corporate leaders from companies that participated in the report, including Carl Solder, chief technology officer of Cisco ANZ (far left); Anna Tosky, chief people officer at Elmo Software (second from left); Chris Locke, CTO at Flight Center Travel Group (third from left); Naz Wilson, group culture and enablement manager at Funlab (third from right); and Lucio Ribeiro, chief AI officer at TBWA Australia (second from right).

Though a sample size of 25 is small, the results align with conversations I’ve had with corporate leadership. I appreciated the panel’s mix of technologies, human resources and cultural leadership. I also valued the mix of roles, as the biggest barrier to scaling AI isn’t technical but people-related.

Australia makes an interesting test case. According to University of Melbourne and KPMG research cited in the report, half of Australians use AI regularly, but only 36% trust it, and just 30% believe its benefits outweigh its risks. That’s the lowest among 47 countries surveyed. If you can build trust in AI in Australia, that work will scale globally. In the press release, Stefan Leitl, vice president and general manager of Cisco Australia and New Zealand, discussed the benefits of winning over this region: “It’s a playbook that travels well beyond Australia.”

Solder noted that among the six pillars in Cisco’s AI Readiness Index, chief information officers and CTOs gravitate toward what they know, namely infrastructure and data, and leave culture for others. He described a customer that invested in infrastructure, governance, data and information technology skills but “didn’t focus on the culture. And they found that there was a big pushback from their employees and customers on using the toolsets they’ve invested in.”

This is something I’ve seen repeatedly: Companies spend millions on AI platforms only to see utilization remain tepid. Howarth discussed an adoption “flywheel” in which successful use creates evidence, evidence builds trust and trust enables broader use. Companies sit around waiting for trust before deploying, and the evidence of trust must be something measurable.

Trust in AI needs to be established with realistic parameters. Many people reject AI after a single mistake, even though in most cases the error rate is much lower than that of people. This mirrors what the automotive industry went through when a Tesla accident would trigger a media storm. The reality is that Tesla’s Autopilot system experiences one crash for about every 7 million miles, compared with human drivers, who average about one crash every 1 million miles.

Perfection isn’t a realistic goal, but being faster and more accurate than others is. Users should understand this going into any kind of trial or proof of concept, as the expectation of perfection can erode trust.

Chris Locke offered a great example of an executive leading by example. The company’s 77-year-old founder, Graham “Skroo” Turner, uses AI every day. “He’s a big Anthropic Claude user,” Locke said. “This is also a guy who once said the internet wouldn’t catch on back in 2000. He may have gotten that one wrong, but he’s betting on AI catching on, so I think he gives us permission to play.”

Ribeiro outlined a more structured approach, describing trust as an equation built on four elements: ownership, competence, consistency and transparency. He was matter-of-fact about why asking a nervous workforce whether it wants AI doesn’t yield an accurate answer. “You never ask a barber if you need a haircut, as the answer is always yes.”

His alternative was honesty. Companies can’t promise to protect every job, but they can promise to make employees “the most prepared, trained, trusted person” if AI disrupts their role.

Funlab, where 79% of the workforce is 21 or younger, relies on peer learning. Its “AI Super Squad” convenes representatives from every department every four weeks. Wilson said early sessions simply clarified which tools were safe, because many employees’ real limitation was “just not knowing whether I am allowed to do certain things or not.”

The report’s central concept is calibrated trust. People need to know when to rely on AI, when to verify its outputs, and when a human must decide. Blindly trusting these systems and their outputs is a significant risk.

During the Q&A, I asked how companies protect against over-trust, especially in high-intensity jobs where people just take the answer and move on. Tosky was candid. “The AI slop. It’s real,” she said. “You ask the employee a question, prompt the AI system and then they send a report without looking at it, and it’s completely wrong. It’s 10 pages you now have to read.”

Elmo keeps a human in the loop on nearly everything, and she argued that the fix starts with redesigning the work. “It’s very unsexy, but start with the process itself, instead of just going, ‘OK, let’s throw a bunch of agents at it.'”

The report recommends that IT leaders adopt a specific practice: Stop treating log-ins as a proxy for trust, and track how often people challenge or override AI outputs. Usage shows people are clicking. Override rates show they’re thinking.

I also raised a contact center concern. AI automates the mundane tasks that served as cognitive breaks for agents, leaving them with nonstop, high-intensity work and higher churn. Tosky called it “AI brain fry” and suggested rethinking metrics and breaks. Wilson added that if AI absorbs routine work, employees lose the repetition that builds context and expertise. That’s a talent pipeline problem few companies are considering.

AI that drafts content is one thing; agents that act are another. Locke said Flight Centre now has agents handling a small subset of airline ticketing that was previously outsourced offshore, with security engaged from day one. He used AI to book his Uber to the event, but a return flight to Europe? “Not yet.”

Fewer than half of respondents are very or extremely confident that their foundations are ready for more autonomous AI, and more than half say their infrastructure needs upgrading. Cisco’s 2026 Relentless Defense report found that only 36% of Australian organizations apply consistent controls to AI agents and nonhuman identities. In the report, Lendi Group CTO Devesh Maheshwari described the target as “bounded autonomy, where the agent can act on your behalf but cannot go beyond the boundaries you have established.”

This is where Cisco can help its enterprise customers. Solder argues that trust must be enforced at the network and security layers. “Built into the network and security underneath, control stops being the brake and becomes the permission to move faster,” he said. Cisco is betting that its networking, security and Splunk portfolio will become the trust layer for agentic AI, and the report provides a business rationale for that bet.

As I stated above, the research is qualitative and aligns with what I hear from CIOs globally. My advice for IT leaders:

The AI winners won’t necessarily have the best models. They’ll have employees, boards and customers who trust the systems enough to let them do more. As Solder put it, “The leaders in our research aren’t scaling AI first. They’re scaling trust.”

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5607. ‘Home Is Where You Spend’: How Your Neighborhood Shapes Your Buying Habits

Your home isn't just where you live; it's also where you spend the majority of your money, a new study from financial technology platform Bilt has found.

Bilt partnered with 451 Research and S&P Global on the 2026 State of the Neighborhood survey, aimed at exploring consumer spending habits as it doubles down on American business with the launch of Bilt Neighborhood OS and the expansion of its membership platform.

Bilt Neighborhood OS is an AI operating system and commerce network designed to unlock America's $6.6 trillion neighborhood commerce opportunity to help businesses grow without replacing their existing systems, the company says.

In the consumer spending survey, around two-thirds of the 6,951 survey participants conducted at least 80% of their "everyday spending" within 15 miles of their homes, and 92% of those surveyed planned on spending the same or more at local businesses in the coming months.

That's not surprising, given the results of a recent Re/Max survey, which found that 29% of prospective homeowners valued proximity to grocery stores and shopping, while 20% said they valued having restaurants and cafes nearby.

More than half of all survey respondents said future neighborhood development, including new housing or retail development, was "very important" to how they chose where to buy a home.

The results of the Bilt survey spell good news for small businesses in popular residential areas, suggesting that physical stores close to dense residential neighborhoods may continue to thrive in the age of online shopping.

"The disconnect between what people talk about versus where people actually spend is quite significant," Ankur Jain, founder and CEO of Bilt, tells Realtor.com®. "When you you look at the stats, all online shopping in the U.S. is $1.3 trillion a year. But offline, small- and medium-business local retail and food spending is $6.6 trillion."

On a quarterly basis, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, that broke down to $340.2 billion in online spending in the second quarter, making up 17.1% of total consumer spending.

Bilt's study found that 70% of food and grocery spending is still made in person.

Consumers spent an average of $375 on in-person grocery shopping each month. They spent an additional $175 on in-person dining and takeout and another $175 on in-person general shopping. Study participants reported spending an average of $50 each on entertainment and recreation; health and personal care; and transportation.

Sixty-six percent of survey respondents said they were were actively looking to support local businesses over big-box and online retailers and were willing to spend more to support them.

A recent report on consumer spending habits around the holidays from research firm Epsilon found that Gen Z in particular values in-store options for gift shopping. And while online shopping is still, overall, the preferred method for gift shopping, the study found that consumers across all generatios are doing the majority of their food and decoration shopping in person. Furthermore, they spent about an equal amount of their holiday clothing budgets online and in store.

One possible reason for the continued primacy of in-person shopping is consumers' paradoxical relationship with artificial intelligence marketing.

Research from McKinsey found that AI continues to drive sales and that AI usage in completing purchases climbed 70% year over year. However, younger, more tech-native shoppers "tend to be more skeptical of AI on average," the report found. (Sixty-seven percent of American Gen Z AI users trust AI chat and search tools versus the global average of 73%.)

The study was conducted in advance of Bilt launching its new offerings. Alongside Bilt Neighborhood OS, the Bilt Membership Platform is an expansion of the company's existing membership and loyalty technology. The company says it will enable organizations to launch their own branded membership programs via white-labeling or extend existing loyalty programs into the neighborhood.

"We are betting pretty big on the neighborhood versus online commerce," Jain says. "There is a huge gap between what the media and the Silicon Valley world talk about versus how real Americans are living. People talk about AI as 'How are we going to do online commerce AI and replace coding and jobs and all this stuff.'

"The truth is, the biggest beneficiaries of AI can be the local mom and pop businesses who don't have the ability to hire 2,000 people to go compete with, like, a Walmart or Amazon online.

"Everything is tied together. The more you can invest in the neighborhood, the more value you create in the housing. The more housing you have, the more you can invest in the neighborhood," he adds.

Bilt also announced a coalition of partners spanning payments, point-of-sale technology, reservations, and commerce platforms. Partners include Altamarea Group, AM Parking, Bungalow Hospitality Management, ByNext, FlyBox, Lettuce Entertain You, Lowe’s, Prince Street Hospitality Group, The Dinex Group, Thumbtack, among others.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5606. Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC Connect Florida and Indiana Property Data Through RPR View

Business professional using laptop with connected digital document icons, representing document management, data sharing, cloud workflow, file organization, and business automation.

Realtors Property Resource (RPR) has announced that Realtors serving clients with real estate interests in both Florida and Indiana will have access to additional property information through a new data-sharing collaboration between Stellar MLS and MIBOR Broker Listing Cooperative (BLC).

According to a release, using RPR View, the MLS data-sharing capability from RPR, eligible customers in both markets will be able to access approved off-market listings, including historical listing data, across MLS boundaries.

RPR says the collaboration reflects a natural connection between Indiana and Florida, where seasonal residents, relocating homeowners and buyers often have real estate interests in both markets. Expanded access to listing history gives Realtors additional context to research properties, understand past market activity and help clients make informed decisions.

“Buyers and sellers deserve informed guidance wherever their real estate goals take them,” said Shayne Fairley, CEO of Stellar MLS. “Often, they don’t stop at market boundaries, and neither should access to trusted listing information for the real estate professionals who serve them. With strong ties between Florida and Indiana, especially among seasonal residents, our collaboration with MIBOR BLC and RPR will provide greater access to property information across both markets, so the professionals who guide their clients can do so with greater confidence.”

He added: “We’re pleased to bring this expanded access to our collective customers, and we look forward to creating similar opportunities with other MLSs and associations.”

A practical approach to cross-market data sharing

Beyond the benefits to Realtors, the release says the collaboration demonstrates how MLS organizations can expand property data access using technology already available through RPR.

With RPR View, participating MLSs determine which listing information to share and which markets can access it. This gives organizations flexibility to expand access while maintaining control over their data-sharing permissions.

For Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC, the arrangement enables reciprocal access to approved off-market listing information, including historical listing data, through an established platform, without developing a separate data-sharing system.

“MLS organizations create the greatest value when we look beyond traditional market boundaries and focus on how real estate professionals actually do business. Our partnership with Stellar MLS reflects that philosophy,” said Shelley Specchio, CEO and President of the MIBOR Broker Listing Cooperative in Indiana. “By connecting the Indiana and Florida marketplaces through RPR, we are reducing friction for professionals working in both states and demonstrating what is possible when MLSs collaborate around the needs of brokers, agents and consumers.”

Building connections through existing infrastructure

The release notes that as of October 31, 341 of the nation’s 487 MLSs (70%) participate in RPR View data sharing, representing more than 1 million Realtors. The Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC collaboration demonstrates how this existing infrastructure can support cross-market access while allowing each organization to maintain control over its shared data, RPR says.

“One of the advantages of RPR View is that MLSs can expand data access without having to build a new solution,” said Liz Gunski, vice president of Industry Relations at RPR. “Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC are showing how existing infrastructure can support collaboration while keeping participating organizations in control of their data.”

The expanded data access is scheduled to become available to eligible customers in both markets beginning Nov. 4.

#5604. Alphabet’s Wing to invest $125M in new delivery drone factory

Wing Aviation LLC today announced plans to spend $125 million on the construction of a new delivery drone factory.

The initiative is part of a broader investment that also encompasses the Alphabet Inc. unit’s research and development teams in California. Additionally, Wing stated that it plans to invest in the communities where it operates. It currently offers deliveries in five U.S. cities and intends to bring its service to 14 more markets soon.

Wing is building its factory in Fort Worth, Texas. The 15,000-square-foot facility is expected to create up to 100 jobs. Wing says it will have capacity to make tens of thousands of delivery drones per year, which should significantly speed up its market expansion efforts.

The Alphabet unit’s drones reportedly have a wingspan of about 4.9 feet. They’re based on a frame made of styrofoam, a foam that mostly consists of trapped air, and carbon fibers. Styrofoam is lightweight and repels water, which comes handy when a drone is navigating challenging weather. The frame’s carbon fibers, in turn, boost its sturdiness.

The drone frame is equipped with 16 electric rotors that enable it to reach speeds of up to 60 miles per hour. Workers at stores that use Wing’s delivery service attach merchandise to its drones via a tether. After a drone takes off, it reels in the tether until the package comes into physical contact with its frame. When it reaches the customer’s house, the drone descends to an altitude of 20 feet and lowers the parcel.

Wing has built a software stack that automates much of the work involved in coordinating deliveries. It picks the most suitable drone for a given delivery run, plans its flight path and ensures that it won’t interfere with other drones. Human safety teams monitor for weather and air traffic changes that may make it necessary to adjust flight plans.

The unit plans to make its delivery service available to more than 40 million Americans by 2027. It’s pursuing the growth initiative in partnership with retailers such as Walmart Inc., which uses its drones to process e-commerce purchases. Last month, the latter company announced plans to make Wing deliveries available at more than 270 stores.

The Alphabet unit also intends to offer its service in Japan. Last month, it teamed up with Tokyo-based internet provider KDDI Corp. to make drone deliveries available to local consumers in 2027.

Although the drone delivery market is in an early stage, Wing already faces a significant amount of competition. In August, Amazon.com Inc. announced plans to make its Prime Air service available in nearly 500 U.S. markets by year’s end. More recently, drone delivery startup Zipline International Inc. raised $1.5 billion in funding at a $21.5 billion valuation.

#5603. California Voters Reject ‘Billionaires Tax’ Amid Fears of an Exodus of Wealth From the State

California voters have rejected a proposed wealth tax, which could have meant a one-time influx of billions for the state but threatened to trigger an exodus of billionaires in the state.

The ballot measure, one of several housing issues Californians considered, is projected by the Associated Press to narrowly fail, with 53% voting against the measure with most votes counted a week after Election Day. Proposition 40 would have created a one-time 5% wealth tax on individuals with a net worth above $1 billion.

The Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the measure, said it could have offset federal funding cuts. It estimated the one time tax could have brought in $100 billion in one-time revenue.

But the measure could have affected about 200 people, and billionaires in the state have put significant money toward fighting it. The California Budget & Policy Center estimates they hold a combined $2 trillion in wealth. Proposition 40 excludes real property holdings from determining an individual's net worth.

State leaders say tax could trigger some of those wealthy people to flee the state and take their spending with them. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation estimates California could collect $40 billion from the tax. But it could lose $25 billion in other taxes if wealthy people leave.

Governor Gavin Newsom opposed the measure. "This will be defeated, there's no question in my mind," Newsom told the New York Times, as it reported that several wealthy people had begun moving assets out of the state.

Palantir and PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin all have reportedly moved some assets to Florida. Voters in that state approved a measure on Tuesday that would reform its property tax system, potentially setting it up to be yet more attractive.

However, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had pledged to remain in California, where he has spent more than $112 million assembling a megacompound in Palo Alto. Earlier this year, Zuckerberg reached an agreement with Meta board to remain in California regardless of the outcome of Prop 40. He would have faced a potential tax bill of some $12.5 billion if the measure had passed.

Taxes raised by Prop 40 would have gone to health care, education, or food assistance. But the state legislature would have had discretion to determine how those funds are used.

The California Association of Realtors President Tamara Suminski said at an elections forum last month that it opposed the measure. CAR is concerned about the potential loss of tax revenue and the state's economic competitiveness, she said.

"Prop 40 is just a bad idea," Jennifer Barrera, President & CEO, California Chamber of Commerce, said at the event. "Billionaires are the individuals who have the ability to move quickly, they have the ability to live outside the state, they don't have to be in California. And yet they pay a tremendous amount of revenue to our general fund if they're living here."

Two other items on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42 both aim to block or counter Proposition 40, but their language could have much broader implications, Barrera said.

But even if Proposition 40 were to pass, it would invite years of litigation, said Joe Bishop‐​Henchman, executive vice president at National Taxpayers Union Foundation. Prop 40 applies to all of a California-domiciled billionaire's holdings across the globe, inviting Constitutional challenges.

And then there's the matter of actually calculating net worth. Wealthy individuals hold assets that can be hard to value, such as patents, artwork, and stakes in private companies. So, would likely take years of expensive legal process to determine how much to tax them.

"The Franchise Tax Board currently has no infrastructure for valuing these types of assets," Bishop‐​Henchman said. "Valuing these kinds of assets will entail years of costly litigation on both ends and establishment of an extensive and costly administrative apparatus for an ostensibly 'one-time' tax."

Californians meanwhile also voted on a set of other measures. Voters passed Proposition 1 to authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing affordability programs. Co-chairs of its organizing campaign Chione Flegal and Ray Pearl called the win "a resounding show of support for affordable housing."

Voters also approved Proposition 37, which creates a $25 billion loan program for middle-income buyers to purchase new homes. Realtor.com economist Joel Berner said this could be a boon for new home sales. But he cautioned it might not touch the more expensive parts of the state.

"The complicating factor here is that the major California metro areas are short on newly built homes below $1.5 million, and the ballot measure does nothing to address the supply of these homes, only bolstering demand for them," Berner said.

"Proposition 37 has the potential to help prospective California homebuyers, but only if they can find new homes to buy," he said.

The California Association of Realtors, a major supporter of Proposition 37, cheered the result.

“This measure will help create more housing, provide low-cost down payment options and give teachers, nurses, firefighters and other hardworking Californians a better opportunity to own a home in the communities they serve," Suminski said. "We look forward to working with stakeholders to bring Proposition 37 to life and deliver on its promise for California families.”

But, voters rejected the controversial Proposition 45. It would have set timelines on environmental reviews for some projects under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA.

California earned an F grade on the Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card. It tracks how effectively each state balances affordability and new construction.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5602. Inflation Remains Hot in October and Strengthens Case for Another Fed Rate Hike

Inflation accelerated faster than anticipated in October, driven by surging costs for housing and food, which will bolster the case for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike next month.

On a monthly basis, overall prices rose 0.4% from September, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Tuesday. That's down from the 0.6% monthly increase recorded in September but higher than the 0.2% gain forecasted by economists.

CPI measures the average costs consumers pay for a range of goods, including food, energy, commodities, and services.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy categories, rose 0.3%, also exceeding the anticipated 0.2% gain.

The BLS did not publish an official annual inflation rate because last year's government shutdown prevented the agency from collecting survey data for October 2025.

October saw the index for shelter jump 0.3%, accounting for over 30% of the monthly all-items increase. Meanwhile, the food index increased 0.5%, and the energy index rose 0.7%, coming on the heels of a 5.2% surge in September.

Prices for a wide range of goods and services, including recreation, transportation, medical care, vehicle insurance, education, airfare, and tariff-sensitive categories like furniture and apparel all increased in October.

"These figures hardly qualify as a shock to markets or the outlook, but the details of the report show inflation remains broad-based," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel.

The October CPI print, coupled with the better-than-expected jobs number released last week, signals for the Federal Reserve that it must continue focusing its efforts on combating inflation.

At last month's meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), policymakers voted 10-2 to keep the overnight rate at its current 3.75%-4% range.

However, a December hike now looks all but certain, with odds of a 25-basis-point increase climbing to 99% Tuesday morning, before settling back down to 85%, according to CME FedWatch.

Krimmel says that market reaction is both due to the warmer-than-anticipated CPI print and Fed Gov. Christopher Waller’s latest comments.

Speaking before the inflation report release, Waller put a 50-basis-point move on the table for December and stressed the need to follow through on market expectations for rate increases.

"When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out," said Waller.

Additional hikes in early 2027 look more in play as well, with the 10-year Treasury going up 9 basis points just 25 minutes after the CPI release.

For housing in the near term, Krimmel says the rising yields and growing speculation about future interest rate increases could put upward pressure on mortgage rates again, reversing a recent downward trend that saw the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans drifting to 7.18% last week.

October’s spike to 7.4% showed how quickly higher rates hurt demand, with contract signings and new listings each falling about 10% from September as buyers and sellers pulled back from the market.

And while rate swings grab the headlines and matter for the marginal buyer, the real wage squeeze is a longer-run, underexplored headwind for demand.

Real average hourly earnings were flat in October as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation, leaving annual real wage growth negative for buyers already facing mortgage rates above 7%.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5601. Only a Quarter of U.S. Households Have Children at Home

Household composition is a fundamental driver of housing demand, influencing everything from floor plans and bedroom counts to community amenities and long-term land strategies. Understanding how household composition is changing can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to serve different types of buyers.

As of 2024, 25.4% of U.S. households had children under age 18 living at home, according to Zonda’s analysis of U.S. Census data. Put another way, nearly three out of every four households did not have children at home.

The finding is consistent with trends visible among home buyers: the 2025 Home Buyers and Sellers Generational Trends Report from NAR showed that only 24% of buyers had children under 18, a historic low.

Several structural demographic forces help explain this shift, including fertility rates below replacement levels, later family formation, and an aging population that has contributed to more empty nesters, retirees, and older adults living independently. At the same time, households without children, including DINKS (dual income, no kids), represent an important part of housing demand.

These shifts highlight the changing composition of household types shaping housing demand and reinforce the importance of segmentation over assumptions. The traditional family household remains an important customer, but understanding the needs of other household types can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to reach a broader range of buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5600. IBM builds on hybrid cloud and governance to advance its enterprise AI operating model

Enterprises are moving beyond AI pilots, putting greater emphasis on governance, production readiness and measurable business outcomes.

Research from Deloitte highlights a significant gap between enterprise AI ambition and execution: 54% of organizations plan to move at least 40% of their AI initiatives into production within six months. Yet only 25% have done so today. IBM is betting on its strengths — mainframe hardware, hybrid computing assets and a legacy of strong governance — to gain a leg up on the rest of the market, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante.

“In our opinion, IBM has found a differentiated path in enterprise AI by productizing workflow-level outcomes across a stack that, while sometimes confusing, customers generally trust,” he said. “Client Zero proof, a workload-first hybrid design, durable platforms reimagined for agents and a pragmatic quantum roadmap create a credible basis for sustained advantage.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of how enterprise AI has moved beyond the race for model supremacy, with major technology players now focused on enabling governed enterprise AI that delivers trust, reliability and predictable business outcomes. (* Disclosure below.)

IBM already has a substantial book of business around generative AI, with AI-related software sales and consulting engagements totaling more than $12.5 billion as of Q4 2025, up from $9.5 billion the previous quarter.

Through a series of investments, acquisitions and product launches, IBM is gathering assets for an enterprise AI operating model with four pillars: agent orchestration, trusted data, intelligent operations and governance.

Many of these capabilities were rolled out as part of a steady drumbeat of announcements leading up to IBM Think 2026 in May. In February, the company announced a partnership with Deepgram Inc. to integrate voice capabilities into watsonx Orchestrate, its enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing agents. Two months later, it made IBM Bob — an AI-assisted coding tool that helps developers plan, write, test, modernize and deploy code —  globally available.

In May 2026, IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent, the data streaming platform, to enhance watsonx.data. By integrating streaming and real-time data, IBM aims to make watsonx.data the trusted data foundation, providing AI agents with continuously updated context.

At Think 2026, the company repositioned Concert from a point product into an agentic IT operations platform designed to unify observability, optimization, security and automation across hybrid environments. The move positions Concert as the intelligent operations layer of IBM’s broader enterprise AI strategy.

The IBM Sovereign Core platform announced at Think 2026 is designed to address the final pillar: governance. It helps enterprises build and operate AI-ready sovereign environments by embedding governance, compliance and operational control directly into the underlying infrastructure.

June brought more AI-related announcements: IBM joined OpenAI’s Daybreak Cyber Partner Program, which aims to identify AI-driven cybersecurity threats. IBM has partnered with Google Cloud to help IBM consultants design, build and govern enterprise-grade agents on Google Cloud.

All these announcements paint a picture: IBM wants to be the one-stop shop for enterprise AI, and to do so, it is investing significantly in new capabilities while leaning on its reputation for trusted enterprise security and governance, according to theCUBE Research’s John Furrier.

“While others chase frontier models, IBM is betting on something harder: trusted AI in production,” he told theCUBE. “The question coming out of Think is simple — are they becoming the system of record for enterprise AI or just another layer in the stack?”

In a media briefing ahead of Think 2026, IBM Chief Executive Arvind Krishna pointed out that over 70% of all enterprise data remains locked up in on-premises systems. That makes hybrid cloud a critical component of IBM’s enterprise AI operating model, allowing enterprises to use corporate data for AI workloads without abandoning existing infrastructure.

Recent earnings reports appear to reinforce IBM’s bet on hybrid cloud in the AI era. Red Hat Inc., whose OpenShift Kubernetes platform underpins IBM’s hybrid cloud software portfolio, saw revenue increase 13% year over year. Meanwhile, revenue from IBM Z, the company’s mainframe platform, saw revenues grow 51% year over year, underscoring the continued importance of mainframes in IBM’s infrastructure business.

IBM is embedding AI technology directly into IBM Z mainframes to support demanding AI workloads, according to Ric Lewis, senior vice president of the Infrastructure Division at IBM.  This strategy has resonated with clients and led to 20%-30% program-to-program growth for almost a decade. Z mainframes, a key priority for enterprises looking to deploy AI while maintaining control over their data and systems, are also a pillar of IBM’s sovereignty strategy.

“Sovereignty is our home court. We do 70% of the world’s financial transactions,” Lewis told theCUBE. “The most important data that travels around the world is in our Z systems. Those are sovereign systems. They’re on-prem, they’re in environments, they’re in banks, they’re in financial institutions, they’re in insurance. Sovereign is our home court, and we know this space extremely well.”

IBM’s view of sovereignty centers on customer control: keeping critical data and AI workloads in environments customers own and govern, rather than depending entirely on third-party infrastructure. Javier Olaizola, global managing partner for hybrid cloud and data at IBM Consulting, explained that the topic is coming up earlier in client engagements.

“Sovereignty and exposure was coming in on slide 40 in a PowerPoint pitch,” he told theCUBE. “Now it’s coming up front: ‘How much is my exposure?’ That is coming up with a new set of conversations that we are having with clients.”

Sovereign Core is the company’s answer to those questions, according to Sripriya Srinivasan, general manager for Core and ALM software products at IBM. Its goal is to help companies maintain operational consistency even as AI regulations and geopolitics constantly shift. It also helps companies contend with massive AI agent sprawl.

“The proliferation of agents is real in enterprises. Everybody is starting to build agents,” Srinivasan told theCUBE. “How do you, as a [chief information officer], make sure that there’s a level of standardization, consistency, governance, orchestration? All of these are internal fears, not necessarily coming, just based on regulations.”

How does this all translate to real-world results? It’s useful to look back at Krishna’s comments from Think 2026, where he presented IBM’s point of view on what makes a successful enterprise AI strategy.

“The enterprises pulling ahead are not deploying more AI; they’re redesigning how their business operates,” Krishna said during a media briefing.

IBM sets its own example by viewing itself as Client Zero for its enterprise AI strategy, according to James Kavanaugh, senior vice president and chief financial officer of IBM.

“AI is now embedded across our business, from how we deliver services to our software portfolio to the capabilities we are adding to our infrastructure platforms and how we drive our own productivity,” he said.

IBM reports that more than 80,000 of its employees use IBM Bob, with users reporting more than a 45 percent increase in productivity. Additionally, IBM Consulting has deployed more than 4,000 digital workers across 450 active projects, including agents from watsonx, Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC.

To keep this digital workforce under control, the company relies on a management philosophy that treats AI agents like human workers, an idea that Krishna himself suggested, explained Mohamad Ali, senior vice president and head of IBM Consulting.

“Arvind called me, and we had a conversation about three years ago, and he said, ‘I want you to come over, and I want you to be a consulting business,’” he said in an interview with theCUBE. “‘What is digital labor? It’s a whole bunch of bits of software. I need you to come in, and I need you to build this set of software and do it in a way that it could be managed. You could think of this as HR management … but now you have to HR manage human workers and digital workers.’”

IBM customers are also putting elements of the enterprise AI operating model into practice. Global bank BNP Paribas SA has nearly 1,000 AI use cases underway across its operations, using a group-level framework with governance distributed across business units and functions.

“The strategy is to use AI, not to become AI — to use AI to better serve our customers and to give more value to them,” Jean-Michel Garcia, group chief technology officer at BNP Paribas, told theCUBE. “But also internally, for employees, to give them more capabilities to focus on the right set of tasks and to make them more efficient and more focused on what they do.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the IBM Think event. Neither IBM, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5599. Century Communities Promotes Jim Francescon to President

As part of its long-term succession planning process, Century Communities has promoted Jim Francescon to president, effective January 1, 2027. Francescon currently serves as executive vice president, corporate operations.

“Today’s announcement reflects the implementation of a succession plan that our board, Rob, and I have been planning and executing over the past two years,” says Dale Francescon, executive chairman of Century Communities. “We have been very thoughtful in how we have approached succession, with the goal of best positioning Century for long-term alignment with shareholders, success, and growth.”

Dale Francescon will continue to serve as executive chairman and Rob Francescon, who currently serves as CEO and president, will solely serve as CEO. As president, Jim will oversee the company’s home building operations, land, and related corporate functions and will help drive the company’s strategy and growth.

“Jim has played an integral role in shaping our strategic direction and our growth into one of the largest home builders in the country, including leading our recent acquisitions that have deepened our footprint and strengthened our platform,” says Rob. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with Jim and our entire executive team as we position Century for continued success.”

Before serving as executive vice president, Jim was president of Century Living, the company’s multifamily platform, and prior to that served as corporate vice president. Jim also serves as a trustee of the University of Denver, Children’s Hospital Colorado Foundation, and ACE Scholarships Colorado.

“I am honored to take on this role and grateful to our board, Dale, and Rob for their confidence,” adds Jim. “We have built a strong operating platform and a talented team, and I am excited about the opportunities ahead as we continue to grow and deliver on our promise of “A Home for Every Dream.””

The new market is the latest of several victories for the brokerage this year, which has expanded into Massachusetts, California, Texas, Colorado, and Illinois in 2026 alone.

With the addition of Utah, SERHANT. is operating in 21 states.

“There’s an established luxury market in Salt Lake City and Park City, which is in line with what we do,” Serhant tells Realtor.com®. “It’s a natural connection point for the business that we’ve been building nationally because a prospective buyer in this marketplace is oftentimes already a client of ours in New York, Miami, Dallas, L.A., etc., so we can bring those relationships together.”

Salt Lake City is among the fastest growing cities in the country, with the downtown population increasing 63% since 2019, according to the Downtown SLC Alliance. As the area continues to develop and grow, an opportunity presents itself to entrepreneurs like Serhant.

“Utah will be one of our larger individual market launches, considering that Park City alone did about $5 billion in residential sales over the past 12 months,” says Serhant. “So it’s a good market to go in. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is now at the center of a growing Chinese espionage scandal. The latest crypto selloff follows a dramatic reversal across US technology markets. Bitcoin erased its post-election rally, falling below $75,000. Ethereum dropped more than 7%, while XRP and Solana also suffered heavy losses.

The Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.5% during the same session. The Nasdaq 100 lost 6.4%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index crashed 12%. Nvidia and AMD were among the biggest casualties.

This selloff has been DEVASTATING.The AI stocks have erased $13.2 TRILLION in market value from stocks’ 2026 highs.Only U.S and China have an annual GDP larger than that loss.Market value erased at six AI giants:– Alphabet: $1.62 trillion lost (−32%)– Nvidia: $1.49… pic.twitter.com/i065m2W4b4

More than $2.5 trillion in Nasdaq market cap disappeared during October. Investors are increasingly questioning if massive AI infrastructure investments will deliver sufficient returns. Major technology companies continue pouring billions into chips, data centers, and computing infrastructure.

Then add political uncertainty, which is adding another headache. Democrats secured control of both congressional chambers during the US midterm elections. Investors now fear greater opposition to data center expansion and potentially tougher regulatory scrutiny.

The resulting selloff has exposed how closely crypto trades with speculative technology investments. Bitcoin increasingly moves alongside high-growth equities when institutional investors adjust their risk exposure.

The damage has also spread into derivatives markets. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions disappeared during Thursday’s selloff. Most liquidations involved traders betting on higher prices.

That forced selling can quickly turn an ordinary correction into something considerably uglier. As Bitcoin falls, liquidations push prices lower and expose leveraged altcoin positions to further losses.

Nvidia’s problems have suddenly become considerably more personal. The company’s board announced an independent investigation yesterday. It wants to examine reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The controversy involves Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. US authorities reportedly suspected her of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

Megaspeed has also faced scrutiny over allegations involving access to advanced Nvidia chips restricted from export to China. Republican lawmakers have requested a briefing from Huang regarding the allegations.

Separately, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife. He apologized to his family and colleagues, accepting responsibility for his actions.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang sends a company-wide email regarding his recently reported relationship with a Chinese spy. pic.twitter.com/NTdoSgaxoy

The combination creates an uncomfortable situation for Nvidia shareholders. Huang is not simply another corporate executive. He remains the public face of the AI revolution and one of its most influential decision-makers.

A prolonged investigation could introduce uncertainty around Nvidia’s leadership, relationships with international customers, and exposure to geopolitical tensions.

Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. However, the investigation could keep the controversy alive while investors are already questioning AI valuations.

The biggest concern for crypto is what happens if the AI selloff spreads. Nvidia has become a central pillar of the global technology investment cycle. Its chips power the infrastructure behind many of the world’s largest AI projects.

If investors begin questioning the sustainability of that investment cycle, semiconductor stocks, data center operators, and technology companies could face another round of selling.

Bitcoin is particularly exposed because institutional investors increasingly treat it as part of their risk portfolios. When confidence disappears from technology markets, crypto often loses buyers alongside speculative equities.

The Binance security incident has added another source of pressure. The exchange’s clients withdrew approximately $6.1 billion following the exchange’s recent security breach.

That creates an uncomfortable combination of falling institutional confidence, weaker market liquidity, and leveraged positions being forced out. Bitcoin now needs a recovery in risk appetite to regain momentum. Otherwise, another wave of technology stock selling could drag crypto prices lower.

So why is crypto down? The AI market has a new problem to deal with, and Bitcoin is discovering that Nvidia’s troubles can become its troubles too.

#5596. Andersen Partnership Helps Build Accessible Homes for Wounded Veterans

Since 2018, Andersen has worked with Jared Allen's Homes for Wounded Warriors, a nonprofit organization that builds injury-specific, accessible mortgage-free accessible homes for veterans who sustained severe injuries during their military service.

Since 2018, Andersen has partnered with Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors to help provide accessible, mortgage-free homes designed around the individual needs of severely injured military veterans.

Through the partnership, Andersen has donated windows and doors to 12 veteran families and home projects across the country. The manufacturer also supports the nonprofit through financial contributions and company matches of employee donations.

Most recently, Andersen contributed to a custom home for Marine Lance Corporal Josh Wege in Fond du Lac County, Wisconsin. Josh Wege, who sustained life-changing injuries while serving in Afghanistan, received the keys to the mortgage-free home alongside his family.

The residence was designed around Wege’s accessibility and mobility requirements, with the broader goal of providing greater independence, comfort, and quality of life.

“Building a home that meets the needs of a critically wounded veteran and their family takes a team of people who believe in our mission,” says Jared Allen, founder of Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors since 2009. “Andersen is an important part of that team, and we’re grateful for their support and commitment to the veterans we serve.”

Jared Allen, a Pro Football Hall of Famer and former Minnesota Vikings defensive end, added that the partnership helps create homes “where veterans can live more independently, and families can make memories together for years to come.”

For Andersen, the partnership also provides an opportunity to apply product selection and design considerations to the specific mobility needs of each homeowner. Depending on the project, those considerations can include wider openings, low- or zero-threshold transitions, accessible hardware placement, and patio door configurations intended to make movement easier between indoor and outdoor spaces.

Charlie Jackson, an account sales manager at Andersen, has helped project teams identify window and door solutions based on individual veterans’ accessibility requirements.

“My father was a World War II Marine, so supporting veterans has always been personally meaningful to me,” Jackson shares. “These projects bring Andersen’s work into focus because you can see how thoughtful product choices and accessible design come together to make everyday life easier for a veteran and their family.”

“As a 10-year Andersen employee, I’m proud to contribute my experience to help identify the products and solutions that best support each homeowner’s accessibility, comfort, and long-term needs,” he adds.

The homes are completed through collaboration among Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors, manufacturers such as Andersen, local businesses, tradespeople, and other supporters.

#5595. Inside Josh Allen and Hailee Steinfeld’s Multimillion-Dollar Real Estate Portfolio

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen's football career continues to go from strength to strength, with him most recently leading the New York-based team to victory against the Minnesota Vikings.

The 30-year-old athlete, who has been with the Bills since being selected in the first round of the 2018 NFL Draft, previously added an overtime win to his resume, marking a significant personal achievement for the football star.

Now, he has once again showed off his skills in the Bills vs Vikings game, which saw the Bills leading 23-6 on Nov. 9.

The victory is another highlight in Allen's impressive career, which has seen him become one of the NFL's most recognizable quarterbacks.

However, while Allen continues to make headlines for his accomplishments on the field, his life away from football is equally impressive—particularly when it comes to the multimillion-dollar real estate portfolio he shares with his actress wife, Hailee Steinfeld.

Allen and Steinfeld, 29, tied the knot on May 31, 2025, during a romantic ceremony at San Ysidro Ranch in Montecito, CA, nearly two years after their relationship first became public.

The couple welcomed their first child, a baby girl, in April 2026, adding another milestone to what has already been an eventful period in their personal lives.

Although Allen, who was born in Firebaugh, CA, spends the majority of the season in Buffalo, he has maintained a close connection to the Golden State, snapping up a $7.2 million property in Dana Point back in 2023.

The four-bedroom, three-bathroom dwelling is located inside a "prestigious" guard-gated community that features its own private beach club—and offers proximity to a host of nearby five-star resorts, including the Ritz Carlton.

It's understood that Allen spends much of the offseason at his California abode, soaking up the warm weather after a traditionally frosty Buffalo winter.

However, the sporting sensation also boasts another very sizable dwelling much closer to the Buffalo Bills' training ground and stadium: a custom-built megamansion that he had erected on a plot of land he snapped up in 2021 for the relatively low price of $500,000.

Records show that he purchased the 31-acre plot via an LLC, with Google Maps indicating that he has had quite the impressive property built on it.

Located in the tony community of Orchard Park, approximately eight minutes away from Highmark Stadium, the home features a stunning swimming pool, pool house, and a private sports court that can be used for both basketball and tennis.

Additionally, there is a private lake on the land, which has been outfitted with a small dock as well as a waterfront seating area that can be accessed via steps that lead down to the water from the pool.

Ironically, the property appears tailor-made for summertime activities, despite the fact that the football season takes place largely during the colder months.

Still, it provides the perfect place for Allen to lap up the last of the warm weather when he returns to Buffalo for preseason training camp, which kicks off on July 24.

However, thanks to his fiancée, the NFL pro also has his pick of properties over on the West Coast—where Steinfeld also owns a dazzling abode, which she picked up for $8 million back in 2021.

Located in Encino, CA, more than an hour away from Allen's Dana Point dwelling, the home was previously owned by rocker John Fogerty, who sold it to Steinfeld for $7.98 million—more than $3 million more than he had paid for it in 2018.

The actress' property spans an impressive 9,000 square feet and features six bedrooms and eight bathrooms. Much like her beau's abode in Buffalo, it has a sizable private pool, which can be accessed via a motorized window wall that opens up from the main living area into the backyard.

Upstairs, the primary suite features its own sitting room as well as two fireplaces, two walk-in closets, and two bathrooms—perfect for the couple that prefers to have their own space to get ready in the morning.

Cozy date nights can be enjoyed in the home's private movie theater, while the couple can host plenty of guests in the property's lounge, bar, or great room that has a custom "floor-to-ceiling entertainment wall."

And while the backyard has ample space for entertaining—and even includes an outdoor kitchen—that is not the only place where the pair can kick back and enjoy the open air.

In addition to the yard, there is also a roof deck on the property, which provides an additional outdoor space for relaxation or sunbathing.

However, if the pair are hoping to invest in property together, they may look elsewhere in California, specifically Malibu, which is where Allen popped the question to Steinfeld on Nov. 22, 2024.

The actress opened up about the proposal during a February interview with Who What Wear, telling the publication that Malibu serves as her "happy place" and adding that she couldn't have been happier with how the proposal happened.

"I'm so grateful that he did it the way he did so that I looked good, and we have these photos that we'll have and cherish for the rest of our lives that I'm not looking at being like, 'What was I wearing?'" she said. "We were in Malibu, which is my happy place, and it was magical."

"When you realize that so much is already out there in every other aspect of your life, you really learn to cherish the little that isn't. It just makes things extra special, and it's just for you," she explained.

#5594. Invitation Homes Invests in HBI Training for Veterans

The Home Builders Institute (HBI) and Invitation Homes have launched a partnership aimed at helping transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families build careers in construction, property maintenance, and the skilled trades.

The partnership will expand Invitation Homes’ existing Invitation to SkillUp initiative through an investment in HBI’s Military Services program, which provides hands-on, instructor-led skilled trades training, industry-recognized certifications, and job placement assistance.

Through the partnership, HBI and Invitation Homes will connect HBI-trained veterans, military spouses, and family members with career opportunities in the build-to-rent and single-family rental sectors. The organizations also plan to expand recruitment at HBI Military Services locations, including Fort Stewart, Georgia, and Jacksonville, Florida.

Invitation Homes’ Veteran Employee Resource Group will participate in mentorship and career guidance efforts.

“Veterans and their families have dedicated themselves to serving our country, and we are proud to support them as they transition into rewarding civilian careers,” Invitation Homes president and CEO Dallas Tanner says. “Through our Invitation to SkillUp initiative, we are investing in talented individuals whose dedication and service strengthen our communities, while helping create meaningful opportunities in the skilled trades.”

HBI has spent a decade training, certifying, and placing transitioning service members, veterans, and their families in skilled trades careers. According to HBI president and CEO Ed Brady, nearly 90% of graduates from the organization’s military program find jobs, earning an average of more than three times the federal minimum wage.

“We know this model works, and with this important investment from Invitation Homes, we can help more veterans enter the skilled trades every year because the people who served this country deserve a career as strong as their service,” Brady said.

Invitation to SkillUp is Invitation Homes’ national skilled trades development initiative, which works with trade schools and organizations to expand trades education and increase awareness of career opportunities.

Invitation Homes joins other companies supporting HBI’s military programs. The Home Depot Foundation and DEWALT were early supporters, while Google recently provided a $1 million contribution to the effort.

The partnership comes as the housing industry continues to look for ways to strengthen its skilled labor pipeline. For transitioning service members and military families, the effort offers a pathway from military service into construction and housing careers while providing the industry with another source of trained workers.

#5593. Trump stands by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang despite spy scandal, but FBI is investigating

The revelations this weekend that Nvidia Corp. boss Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman who has been accused of working for Chinese intelligence have now ensnared U.S. President Donald Trump, raising further questions about national security.

At the same time, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said it’s looking into the affair, meaning it’s likely to get continuing attention in coming weeks or longer.

Nvidia said it has launched an investigation into Chief Executive Huang’s actions after he admitted to cheating on his wife with a woman known as Alice Huang (no relation), who serves as the CEO of a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.

U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang has been feeding information about Huang and the chipmaker’s plans to the Chinese government. And though Trump was informed of the possible infiltration, he has continued working with Nvidia and Huang on domestic policy issues related to technology and artificial intelligence, which have become of vital importance to the U.S. economy.

Huang has spent the last two years cultivating a close relationship with Trump, gaining extraordinary access to America’s top decision-maker and influence over the country’s AI strategy. He has gone from being virtually unknown to the president to being a key member of a cadre of technology industry executives accompanying him on trips aboard Air Force One, including a visit to China in May.

He has come to be seen as a major ally of Trump, attending numerous White House events while repeatedly praising his policies. Notably, his company made a $25 million donation to the president’s gaudy ballroom project, becoming its top corporate contributor alongside Apple Inc.

Those efforts seem to have gone a long way toward getting Huang into the president’s good graces, and it seems to have paid off for the company. Last year, after months of lobbying from Huang and Nvidia, the Trump administration agreed that it could sell more advanced chips to China that were previously banned from being exported to the country.

Though that decision was widely known, it seems that the Trump administration has intervened in other ways to protect Nvidia’s interests. Earlier today, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling banned chips into China, was abruptly canceled after receiving an email from Nvidia’s general counsel. Commerce official Jeff Kessler, who was nominated for the role by Trump, reportedly gave Nvidia permission to contact the investigation team and mention his name, which goes against standard protocol.

Investigators had grown suspicious that Megaspeed was essentially just a front for smuggling embargoed Nvidia chips into China, but the correspondence from Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter kicked off a kerfuffle that ultimately led to the investigation being transferred to the Department of Justice.

But Trump defended Huang late on Sunday, stating that the Nvidia boss is an “honorable guy” who has not committed any wrongdoing. The president had been briefed about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation as far back as October 2025, but decided not to do anything, according to the Times. “I haven’t heard that he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody, but, you know, so does everybody else.”

Trump continued to defend Huang on Monday when quizzed about the situation again, before revealing that the Federal Bureau of Investigation is also looking into his relationship with the suspected spy. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” he said at a White House briefing.

Despite the apparent protection afforded by Trump, Huang appears to be taking no chances. A report in Wired said today that the Nvidia boss has hired the services of a public relations firm called Heller that specializes in handling public scandals. Rise Heller, the firm’s founder, has developed a reputation for helping powerful men sidestep allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies. She previously represented clients including the former Congressman Anthony Weiner, the writer Jeffrey Toobin and the chef Mario Batali, Wired reported.

Tech industry personalities have also leapt to Huang’s defense. Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital said in a post on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” and stressed that although he did something “incredibly dumb,” he believes there was “no bad intention.” Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk later shared Maguire’s post, saying he agrees with all of it.

However, no intervention has managed to protect Nvidia’s stock, which slid more than 4% on Monday, wiping around $190 billion off of the company’s valuation.

Nvidia is scheduled to hold its next financial earnings call on Nov. 17, in which Huang is likely to face some very difficult questions — if he is on the call as has been customary.

#5591. Lennar, Operation Finally Home Surprise Two Military Families With New Homes

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier with their families.

Two military veterans and their families received life-changing news ahead of Veterans Day when Lennar and Operation Finally Home surprised them with the gift of new homes.

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier were surprised with the announcement during the inaugural Operation Finally Home Golf Classic reception in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 9.

Neither family knew about the plans beforehand and attended the event as guests of Operation Finally Home.

The announcement followed a live performance by country music artist and Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan. Operation Finally Home founder Dan Wallrath and Lennar San Antonio division president Brian Barron then revealed that each family would receive a new Lennar home.

The partnership builds on Operation Finally Home’s mission of providing mortgage-free homes and home modifications to wounded, ill, and injured veterans, first responders, and their families.

Gallmeier served in the Marine Corps from 2005 to 2015 after being motivated to enlist by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. During his service, he deployed twice to Iraq in support of combat operations and later deployed to Okinawa, Japan, as part of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit.

Gallmeier sustained a traumatic brain injury following a grenade blast during combat operations in Iraq. He also developed post-traumatic stress disorder and continues to manage PTSD, amongst other conditions, according to Operation Finally Home.

Following his military career, Gallmeier earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in divinity from Biola University and became a pastor. He currently lives in California with Tatiana Zaragoza and their three children, Alyssa, Caspian, and Everett.

A formal groundbreaking for the family’s new Lennar home is scheduled for Nov. 10 in the Freedom Crossing community in Killeen, Texas.

Taylor enlisted in the U.S. Army in August 2004 shortly after graduating from high school in Washington state. He served as an infantryman and filled roles including Squad Automatic Weapon gunner, driver, and team leader.

From June 2006 to September 2007, Taylor deployed to Baghdad in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom. His unit lost 21 soldiers during the deployment.

After completing his military service in December 2007, Taylor continued serving his community as a firefighter and emergency medical technician.

A serious back injury in January 2024, combined with the lasting physical and emotional effects of his military service, ultimately forced Taylor to medically retire from firefighting in March 2025.

Following the injury, Taylor and his wife, Aylynn, and their four children faced financial uncertainty and eventually sold their home and moved in with relatives. The family’s new Lennar home will provide a fresh start. A groundbreaking for the Taylor residence is slated in December.

#5590. NAR Board Approves 2027 Budget, Installs New Leadership

At its Nov. 9 meeting during NAR NXT in New Orleans, the National Association of Realtors®’ (NAR) board of directors approved a 2027 budget and installed new leadership.

The board approved an operating budget projecting approximately $280 million in revenue and $247 million in expenses. Under the new approach, NAR departments were required to evaluate expenditures from the ground up rather than simply carry forward previous spending levels, prioritizing initiatives and identifying measures of success.

NAR Treasurer Craig Sanford described the approach as a significant step in the association’s financial modernization efforts. The board approved the budget by an overwhelming majority.

Directors also approved the following financial recommendations:

In his final board of directors meeting as NAR president, Kevin Brown highlighted progress on initiatives aimed at protecting members’ business interests, expanding housing opportunities and helping members adapt to a changing industry.

He also highlighted progress on MLS collaboration, including outreach to nearly 500 MLS executives and the formation of a work group to address emerging challenges and modernize policies. That work helped inform four policy recommendations approved by NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee during NAR NXT, aimed at strengthening copyright protections for listing content, giving MLSs greater flexibility in setting local data feed requirements and clarifying permitted uses of MLS data.

For Realtor® members, the changes address business concerns, including protecting the time and money invested in marketing properties, preserving access to their own listing information and establishing clearer rules for how listing data can be used and shared.

Brown also pointed to NAR’s advocacy surrounding the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a housing package aimed at increasing supply, improving affordability and expanding homeownership opportunities. NAR’s attention is now turning toward implementation, including working with federal agencies and supporting state and local associations.

Other initiatives highlighted during the meeting included six “modernized” Center for REALTOR® Development courses scheduled to launch Dec. 1, more broker summits (on track for 85-plus by the end of the year) and continued advocacy, including for the bipartisan More Homes on the Market Act, which would increase the capital gains tax exclusion for homeowners selling their primary residences (something the Trump administration previously floated as well).

New NAR President Christine E. Hansen’s priorities include advancing NAR’s three-year strategic plan, improving awareness of member tools and resources, and restoring pride in the Realtor® brand.

The association’s 13 regional vice presidents were also installed.

“It’s so easy to be manipulated, especially if you have a brain that is still forming, and who pays the price? Not us, not our generation, who, maybe at 25, learned how a BlackBerry worked. It’s a cruel experiment on children, on teenagers," Cruz said.

#5588. Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with science, coding upgrades

Anthropic PBC today pulled back the curtains on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, its two most capable large language models to date.

The LLMs are identical as far as their core capabilities are concerned. The difference is that Fable 5.2 blocks certain biology and cybersecurity use cases, while Mythos 5.2 includes more relaxed guardrails. The latter model is only available to trusted researchers through a pair of limited-access programs.

Anthropic tested Fable 5.2 against its predecessor across 14 artificial intelligence benchmarks. The model beat Fable 5.1’s score by more than 10% across most of the tests. It’s particularly adept at scientific research: Fable 5.2 scored 74.6% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a 22% improvement over Fable 5.1.

Earlier this year, Anthropic used an unreleased LLM to generate a computer-verifiable version of a famous mathematical proof. The project took 11 days. According to Anthropic, Fable 5.2 reduced the workflow to 30 hours by spinning up 1,000 agents to parallelize calculations. In a separate project, it answered two open questions about a theoretical physics concept related to black holes.

The company also tested Mythos 5.2, the invite-only version of Fable 5.2. It asked the model to study the protective shells of harmless viruses called AAVs. AAV shells, or capsids as they’re known in scientific parlance, are used by some therapies to deliver drugs.

Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled the structure of 28 out of the 34 AAV capsids it studied. The result is notable because capsids comprise dozens of different proteins. Other cutting-edge models that are optimized for biology research, notably Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold2, can only model the structure of individual proteins. The creators of the latter model won one half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry.

Fable 5.2 includes guardrails that block most research biology questions and many cybersecurity-related prompts. If users enter a request that falls into either of those categories, the model sends it to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 is 55% less likely to erroneously block safe prompts than Fable 5.1.

The model outperforms its predecessor by more than 13% across two coding benchmarks called FrontierCode 2.0 FrontierSWE 2.0. According to Anthropic, one of its engineers put the model’s programming capabilities to the test by asking it to build an operating system. Fable 5.2 spun up up 1,000 agents that completed the task in about eight days. The operating system they created can run on a laptop, offers network access and features a Claude sidebar.

Anthropic sees customers using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 to speed up highly complicated, open-ended technical tasks. The company says more day-to-day workflows can be automated more efficiently using Opus 5.5, an LLM it introduced in July. Users can also combine the models by having Opus 5.5 ask Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 for advise when it encounters a bottleneck.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. That makes them 20% more affordable than Anthropic’s previous-generation models. Both LLMs offer a high-performance mode that generates prompt responses 2.5 times faster than the standard tier for double the price.
