#5538. A $35 Million Home Just Hit San Francisco’s Market, Marking the Most Expensive Listing of the Year

San Francisco’s most expensive home of the year just hit the market and is expected to draw interest from potential buyers flush with cash from the AI boom.

The home at 2770 Broadway officially went on the market on Monday with a nearly $35 million price tag.

The seven-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom home is already drawing inquiries, listing agent Neil Ward of Compass told SFGate.

Located in the exclusive Gold Coast neighborhood, the home sits on a 50-foot-wide, double-width lot, with breathtaking views of the San Francisco Bay, Golden Gate Bridge, Palace of Fine Arts, and other famed landmarks, according to the listing.

The home was designed in 1894 by Reid & Reid, the same architectural firm responsible for the iconic Fairmont Hotel. While many Gold Coast homes of this age, most of which are generational properties, need complete renovations after being sold, Ward told SFGate that the potential buyer of 2770 Broadway can “walk in with their toothbrush and their furniture.”

A 2007 renovation by architect Jim Jennings and Van Acker Construction brought together the home’s original turn-of-the-century grandeur with the functionality needed for modern family living.

The home’s 9,000 square feet are spread across four floors, where prospective buyers will find herringbone-patterned floors, arched openings, and fine millwork, all evidence of the home’s architectural greatness.

The property also features a two-car garage, wine cellar, and sport court in the rear of the house.

The home was purchased by San Francisco business executive David Chamberlain in 1989, according to SFGate. He was CEO of companies such as Shaklee, Stride Rite, and Genesco, but also had a deep connection with his city, serving as president of the San Francisco Opera and the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce.

After his death earlier this year, Chamberlain’s two daughters decided to sell the home.

Ward told SFGate that he thinks the property will sell for its $35 million asking price, which would make it the most expensive home sold on the multiple listing service in San Francisco this year.

“It is a really, really rare product that does not hit the market,” Ward said.

Between the home’s turnkey condition and the city’s competitive ultraluxury home market, Ward thinks the home’s time on the market will be brief.

“I’ve done this for over 35 years. I was here for the dot-com boom and everything in between. Nothing comes close to what’s taking place right now,” Ward said.

San Francisco is experiencing what some real estate brokerages are calling a “mansion shortage,” according to NPR. The AI boom, much of which is concentrated in San Francisco, has caused demand for luxury single-family homes in the area to skyrocket, while the supply remains stagnant.

Home to major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, the San Francisco market had a median of just 37 days on the market, according to Realtor.com data, two weeks less than the national median of 61 days.

Some listings have had over 50 offers, and 44 homes were sold for at least $1 million over asking in June alone, according to a report from NPR.

In October, the sale of a home in San Francisco’s Presidio neighborhood broke the record for the highest sale above asking. The 1966 midcentury home was listed for $18.5 million and sold for $28.5 million, an eye-watering $10 million premium.

#5537. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5536. Hedra’s new Model Factory cranks up the production volume for physical AI model training

Autonomous artificial intelligence agents have been a massive hit in the digital realm, and now a startup called Hedra Inc. is hoping to take the next step with physical AI systems that can automate tasks in the real world too.

The company today announced the Hedra Model Factory, a new post-training and inference platform that enables the recursive self-improvement of AI models, or RSI for short, designed specifically to power autonomous robots and other machines.

Hedra says that physical AI requires a very different and more specialized form of intelligence that can enable robots and other real-world hardware systems to perform very specific tasks, such as packing irregular-shaped parcels onto palettes. One of the main challenges of physical AI is that each robot and each task it performs requires a different model.

But training all of those models is not feasible, given the vast amounts of data required to create them. That’s why Hedra wants to use RSI to adapt existing models to new tasks.

RSI is a relatively new technique in AI that describes systems that can autonomously evaluate, train and then improve their own architectures. There has been a lot of research into these systems in frontier AI labs, but until now no one has managed to apply that continuous loop to the physical world.

The challenge is that physical AI models require massive volumes of multimodal data inputs, from sources such as high-resolution video, sensor feeds and 3D simulations. Running RSI against such enormous data environments simply is not practical given the staggering compute costs such an operation would incur.

Hedra says its Model Factory changes that. It’s an autonomous training pipeline offered as a service that’s designed for robotics, manufacturing, biology and defense workloads, pairing Hedra’s in-house research teams with AI agents that orchestrate the training runs, curate the data and iterate autonomously according to the customer’s specifications.

Hedra founder and Chief Executive Michael Lingelbach (pictured) told SiliconANGLE that RSI has already had a major impact on the way frontier models are developed. He believes that the next big frontier is physical AI, where the data primarily comes from video feeds, sensor readings and simulations. “Hedra Model Factory gives robotics, manufacturing, biology and defense teams the infrastructure to post-train, deploy and keep improving their own models,” he promised.

Lingelbach, a former reinforcement learning researcher for visual and physical systems at Stanford University and Nvidia Corp., said what his company has developed is basically an end-to-end production platform for physical AI models. The customer provides the base model, uploads their proprietary simulation and video data, which is then provisioned within a flexible graphics processing unit sandbox environment powered by its proprietary inference engine.

The RSI process then begins, with Hedra’s researchers keeping close tabs on its progress. Lingelbach said they use vision-language models to score data and provide live reinforcement learning feedback in order to continuously optimize the model to perform the task specified by the customer. Once done, customers can then deploy the model on-premises in their own systems, or with one of Hedra’s cloud data center partners.

The models can also be distilled to run on edge systems for lower-latency workloads. Once they’re up and running, they feed data back into the customer’s sandboxed environment, creating an autonomous flywheel that continuously optimizes the model, making it better over time.

Hedra has worked hard to validate the system. For instance, it retrained MiniMax Group Inc.’s open-weight H3 video model to enhance its physical consistency, creating a distilled version that bumped up its score on the Physics-IQ benchmark from 30.3 to 34.9. In another training run, the startup was able to distill the Krea 3 2K image generation model from 30 sampling steps to just 14 while reducing latency from 22 seconds to just 3.6 seconds, a sixfold speed boost that took just one week to achieve.

Lingelbach said Hedra’s ultimate goal is to help create the thousands of bespoke, cost-effective models needed to usher in the physical AI revolution by optimizing training as much as possible. With RSI, sometimes it’s possible to bypass the retraining process altogether. In one example, Hedra demonstrated that it was able to swap out a robot’s gripper with a new one and restore its task success rate to 100% without any additional training, simply by mapping the new hardware’s reach and grasp metrics to the robot’s wrist camera view.

The Hedra Model Factory service is available today, giving enterprises the option to bypass compute-intensive training and quickly develop the specialized autonomous systems needed to bring intelligence into real-world environments.

#5535. Ripple Insider Sold 2.5M XRP, But Still Thinks Its Price Could Flip Bitcoin

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

David Schwartz sold 2.5 million XRP in 2025, but the Ripple veteran isn’t giving up on the coin at this price. The former CTO recently revealed a $1.7 million capital gains tax bill while defending himself against accusations of dumping. His latest comments also revived an ambitious XRP Price debate about whether the token could eventually overtake Bitcoin.

The $1.7 million I paid in capital gains tax says otherwise.

Schwartz confirmed the sale after critics questioned his commitment to XRP. He said nearly all the tokens came from bonuses received for his work in 2020 and 2023. Rather than quietly dismissing the accusations, he shared evidence of the taxes paid on those transactions.

But selling millions of tokens hasn’t stopped Schwartz from entertaining an even stronger possibility. During an X Spaces discussion, he agreed that XRP could eventually surpass Bitcoin in market cap.

Schwartz’s selling history stretches much further back than the 2025 transactions. The XRP Ledger co-creator previously revealed that his holdings peaked at 26 million XRP.

By August 2026, that balance had fallen to around 2 million tokens. He acknowledged selling most of his holdings, although some also went toward gifts and transfers. That represents a substantial reduction from his previous position.

His earliest sales began when XRP traded around $0.10. Schwartz admitted he never expected the coin to break $0.25. He also regretted selling 40,000 ETH for just $1.05 apiece.

The developer explained that he dislikes taking excessive financial risks. He and his wife followed a strategy of selling portions whenever their investments reached new all-time highs. The approach helped them reduce exposure and sleep better at night.

That strategy explains why Schwartz could sell millions of XRP without necessarily abandoning its long-term potential. He has also disclosed that much of his remaining financial exposure shifted toward Ripple equity.

His September comments offer another important clue about his conviction. Asked whether XRP could eventually overtake Bitcoin, Schwartz answered affirmatively. He clarified that XRP would need to grow faster rather than Bitcoin necessarily losing value.

He described the outcome as probably more likely than not, although he offered no timeline. Schwartz also stopped short of providing a specific XRP Price target.

For perspective, September’s market-cap comparison put XRP near $90 billion and Bitcoin around $1.57 trillion. XRP would have needed approximately $25 to match Bitcoin’s valuation at those market levels. That calculation is illustrative.

Bitcoin’s position as crypto’s leading asset comes from something deeper than its market capitalization. Satoshi Nakamoto introduced Bitcoin in October 2008 as a peer-to-peer electronic cash system.

The original whitepaper challenged the need for financial institutions to control digital payments. Banks and central authorities had become trusted intermediaries, despite their ability to freeze accounts and influence monetary supply.

Bitcoin offered a different arrangement through cryptographic verification and a distributed network. Its creator even embedded a newspaper headline about bank bailouts into the January 2009 genesis block.

That message remains central to Bitcoin’s appeal. Investors increasingly view BTC as an alternative to traditional monetary systems, where governments can expand money supplies and financial institutions control access.

XRP approaches the problem differently. The XRP Ledger uses a validator-based consensus mechanism, while Ripple remains a major commercial force behind its ecosystem. Its payment infrastructure prioritizes transaction speed and institutional settlement.

Bitcoin’s permissionless monetary foundation offers a different proposition. This gap also explains interest in projects attempting to expand Bitcoin’s functionality without replacing its underlying network.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 using the Solana Virtual Machine. Its proposed architecture combines faster transactions, decentralized applications, staking, and DeFi functionality with settlement commitments to Bitcoin’s Layer 1.

The project is a bridge that verifies Bitcoin block headers and transaction proofs before representing BTC on its Layer 2. It also plans to use zero-knowledge proofs to validate transactions and periodically commit network state to Bitcoin.

The presale has recently raised more than $33.2 million raised, with a token price of $0.0136 and staking rewards of 35%. Its development updates also identify November 26 as an important milestone, giving prospective participants a limited window before the next announced stage.

That timeline adds urgency to the developing Bitcoin Layer 2 narrative. Comparing XRP with Bitcoin-based alternatives, the gap is increasingly important. XRP offers an established payments network, while Bitcoin represents a monetary system designed around independence from centralized financial intermediaries.

Schwartz may have sold millions of XRP to reduce personal risk. Yet his willingness to entertain a future where XRP overtakes Bitcoin shows that he hasn’t dismissed its potential.

Whether that vision becomes reality will depend on adoption, liquidity, and actual network usage. For now, the XRP Price debate has another unlikely participant: one of the people who helped build the ledger.

#5533. Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce Get Neighbor’s Support for 8-Foot Privacy Wall at $5.35 Million Ohio Estate

The Kansas City Chiefs tight end, 36, snapped up the eight-bedroom lakefront mansion in March for $5.35 million.

Since then, Kelce and Swift have reportedly taken steps to keep prying eyes away from the historical residence, including introducing plans to construct an 8-foot wall around the property—which were rejected in September.

Speaking anonymously to Page Six ahead of the board’s next meeting, the neighbor pushed back on the idea that the proposal had angered residents.

“I think they’re excited. I think it’s great. I don’t think people are angry,” the neighbor told the outlet.

The Bratenahl Architectural Review Board previously considered the proposal on Aug. 11 and Sept. 8 and is scheduled to take it up again on Nov. 10.

The proposed wall appears to conflict with local regulations, which state that solid fences and walls—as well as fences with less than 75% openness—cannot exceed 30 inches in height.

According to TMZ, a new proposal has since been submitted, although it remains unclear what changes have been made to the original plans.

The setback came after the couple implemented other stringent security measures at the property.

Page Six previously reported that the residence is equipped with a sophisticated security system capable of issuing verbal warnings to anyone who ventures too close.

“A neighbor approached the house and got a voice warning about not passing onto the property after getting too close to the house,” a nearby resident told the outlet.

Built in 1895, the residence spans more than 21,000 square feet and sits on approximately 3.5 acres along Lake Erie.

The mansion boasts eight bedrooms and 11 bathrooms, as well as multiple fireplaces, a home theater, game room, wine cellar, fitness center, sauna, and heated pool overlooking the lake.

The estate is located near Cleveland and is also close to a private airport, according to the outlet—offering the star athlete a convenient launching point for trips with his wife, 36.

Kelce purchased the dwelling from Figurati Construction Group, which is owned by Gary Pellegrino. The company acquired the property for $1.95 million in 2023.

The home was subsequently listed for $6.99 million in 2024 before its price was reduced to $5.99 million in May 2025. Kelce ultimately secured the estate for $5.35 million.

Located in Bratenahl, OH, the property sits just a few miles from Cleveland Heights, where Kelce grew up alongside his older brother, Jason Kelce.

The tiny village is nestled along the southern shore of Lake Erie and offers a mix of multimillion-dollar estates and more modest residences. Homes currently on the market in the area range in price from roughly $250,000 to $2.4 million, according to Realtor.com® data.

The transaction was represented by David Ayers and Nick Zawitz of The Agency Cleveland.

“We’re thrilled for the new owners and so excited for Cleveland,” Ayers and Zawitz said in a statement.

News of their purchase came just one day after it was confirmed that Kelce and Swift added a fluffy white dog to their family.

He introduced the couple's adorable white pup to the world while starring in Tommy Hilfiger's fall 2026 ad campaign.

The sweet cameo confirmed months of speculation that Kelce and Swift had quietly expanded their family with a Samoyed in 2025.

Just days after Kelce and Swift wed, it was revealed that the pup had become such a key part of their lives that it even played a role in their wedding celebrations.

The "Lover" singer is known to have a very soft spot for her own pets: three cats, named Meredith Grey, Olivia Benson, and Benjamin Button.

It's not yet known how the felines have responded to the family's newest member.

However, the dog playing such a key role in Swift and Kelce's wedding ceremony indicates what a big part of their lives it has become—with a framed photo of the pup taking center stage in one of the few glimpses of the venue leaked since the wedding.

A spokesperson for the couple did later confirm reports that the ceremony was officiated by Adam Sandler, while also sharing details about the couple's wedding-day looks.

According to the official release, both the bride and groom sported Christian Dior Haute Couture, Christian Louboutin shoes, and Cartier jewelry—and neither had a bridal party. Instead, they relied on their siblings to be by their side during the ceremony.

“Taylor and Travis did not have bridesmaids or groomsmen. Austin Swift served as Taylor’s Man of Honor, Jason Kelce was Travis’ Best Man," the statement read.

According to People, the singer walked down the aisle to an acoustic version of her hit "Love Story."

The A-list couple joined a long line of celebrities who have wed in New York City, where Swift has owned property for more than a decade.

#5532. Inside Tommy Lee Jones’ 6,000-Acre Texas Ranch Complete With 2 Polo Fields

Texas native Tommy Lee Jones moved to New York City to pursue an acting career back in 1969, but he knew he had found real success when he realized he could head back to the Lone Star State.

“There was a time when I became aware that I could live anywhere I want to,” “The Fugitive” star told The New York Times in a profile. “So, in my wisdom, I went home.”

These days, “home” for the 80-year-old actor is a sprawling ranch in San Saba, TX. Jones resides on the 6,000-square-foot property with his wife, Dawn Laurel-Jones, 62, who is from San Antonio.

In addition to a two-story limestone residence that was built as a fort in 1856, the massive plot of land is a full-fledged retreat. There is not one, but two polo fields, and an array of animals from horses to dogs to feral pigs.

The property is a fully operable ranch, and in 2006, Jones told Texas Monthly all about what a typical day is like.

"In the summers, we'll work cattle, and then at about 7 o'clock at night, we'll start playing polo," he said. "We'll play until about 9, and then when we're done, we put the meat on the fire and watch the dark come. It's a good life. Everyone is happy."

Although Jones is famously private and has not shared imagery of the home, he did share a quote that piques interest.

“I didn’t want any fences around the house,” he said while telling the Times of the feral hogs that dig up his yard. “As you can see, the house has an architectural statement to make.”

Inside, the abode is just as fascinating. The publication reported that the living room is furnished with two Frank Lloyd Wright slate-top tables and a Gustav Stickley sofa that is more than a century old.

Antiques and collected art pieces can be found throughout the home, as well as other finds from the property itself, such as flint arrowheads, shed antlers, and small animal skulls.

Jones has ridden horses for most of his life and took an interest in polo in the 1970s. He regularly hosts polo matches at his ranch, which is home to 25 horses.

According to Social Life Magazine, Jones has been expanding his cattle ranch for decades after first acquiring it in the 1980s. He has built onto the property with additional parcels of working ranchland over time.

The couple’s passion for polo has made an impression on more than one of their homes. In 2019, Jones offloaded his Florida equestrian estate for $11.5 million. The 55-acre property, known as “San Saba,” the same name as his hometown, is 72 miles north of Miami in a town called Wellington.

While that residence was considerably smaller than the Texas ranch he lives in today, its polo facilities are remarkable.

Bradley A. Scherer, the listing agent who handled the sale, told Mansion Global that the estate was “one of the only, if not the only, property listed during 2019 that was a true, full-service polo facility with existing polo fields.”

Jones had purchased the Florida estate in 2002 for $2.95 million, then acquired a secondary parcel for $550,000 in 2012. With an additional third parcel, the land was all sold in a single transaction, after it lingered on the market for eight years.

The original asking price was $26.75 million.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5530. SUSE points Rancher Prime’s AI agents at virtual machines and updates its enterprise Linux

Open-source enterprise software company SUSE S.A. today extended the artificial intelligence troubleshooting agents in its SUSE Rancher Prime platform from Kubernetes clusters to virtual machines.

The company released version 16.1 of its SUSE Linux Enterprise Server operating system at the same time. The updates are pitched at enterprises trying to run AI workloads next to existing applications in hybrid environments.

Research sponsored by SUSE found that information technology leaders rank Kubernetes management as their top investment priority, with AI second, and 24% named AI-assisted troubleshooting as one way to make Kubernetes easier to manage.

Thomas Di Giacomo, SUSE’s chief technology and product officer, said companies moving from AI experiments to deployment at scale need infrastructure that can take on the new workloads alongside the applications they already run. He said SUSE’s commitment to open infrastructure lets organizations adopt AI “on their terms, without being locked into a single technology stack or vendor.”

The troubleshooting agents report to Liz, the Rancher Prime assistant SUSE first shipped as a tech preview in November 2025. Virtual machines come within their reach through a new integration with SUSE Virtualization. Peter Smails, SUSE’s general manager of cloud native, told theCUBE in March that customers could also bring agents of their own to Liz. SUSE said nothing the agents propose gets carried out until someone approves it.

New OAuth2 support lets Liz connect to Model Context Protocol servers. SUSE has also introduced an AI-first version of the Rancher command-line interface, and operators can use its server-side dry run to see what a command would change before it takes effect.

Further down the stack, SUSE Rancher Prime Virtual Clusters gains a hosted control plane mode so platform teams can offer Kubernetes as a service on SUSE’s RKE2 distribution. Stateful workloads run up to 10 times faster on the v2 data engine in SUSE Storage, according to the company.

Version 16.1 of SUSE Linux Enterprise Server pulls in deployments that previously needed separate SUSE products. Customers on the immutable SUSE Linux Enterprise Micro or on SUSE Linux Enterprise Real Time can migrate to it, according to the release notes, and keep everything on one support lifecycle.

The release also carries an on-box MCP framework for AI-assisted diagnostics. Support for accelerated infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. is included, as are expanded live patching and preparation for post-quantum cryptography.

The security updates run from the components AI applications are built on through to the workloads in production. SUSE Application Collection now holds more than 1,000 Python libraries built from verified sources, each shipped with a software bill of materials and provenance information that developers can use to assess dependencies.

The upcoming SUSE Security 6.0 release will add SUSE Security Vulnerability Scanner to find and rank flaws in deployed workloads and cluster nodes. Its Runtime Enforcer component will detect anomalous workload behavior and block it.

SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1 is available now, with its MCP framework in tech preview. The AI-first Rancher command-line interface and the hosted control plane mode for Virtual Clusters are in open beta, and the remaining Rancher Prime features will ship on their own release schedules.

#5529. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5528. Staera launches with $4.6M to develop an optical interconnect for chiplets

Staera Semiconductor Inc., a startup that develops technology for linking together chiplets, launched today with $4.6 million in pre-seed funding.

Singaporean fund Openspace Capital led the investment. It was joined by SGInnovate, Black Kite Capital, 28 Holdings, In Group and financial software company Decimus Technologies.

High-end artificial intelligence accelerators comprise multiple chiplets, silicon dies that each perform a narrow set of tasks. They’re linked together by a kind of miniature network that also functions as the host accelerator’s base layer.

That miniature network takes the form of an interposer, an advanced device that sometimes includes computing circuits, or a bridge. A bridge is essentially a small interposer that costs less to make.

Interposers and bridges both use tiny copper wires to move data between the chiplets they connect. San Francisco-based Staera hopes to replace those copper wires with optical links. According to the company, optical technology is faster and uses less power. It can also transmit data over longer distances without slowing down, which enables chipmakers to build bigger accelerators.

“Copper performance plummets over the millimeter-to-meter distances that matter most in AI accelerators, and bolt-on optics add power and complexity.” said Chief Executive Officer Andrew Kim. “We build the light into the chip, the entire optical link inside a chip, so the connection gets smaller, cooler and faster with each generation.”

Staera’s first product is called Lightwire. It transmits data over optical links, or waveguides, made of a transparent material known as silicon nitride. Light beams can only travel through a transparent material if their wavelengths fall within a specific range. Silicon nitride supports a larger range of wavelengths than many alternatives and causes less light loss, which boosts connection speeds.

The light beams into which Lightwire encodes data traffic are produced by miniature LEDs. Those devices are made of gallium nitride, a compound that is widely used in optical systems because it has a direct bandgap.

The electrons that orbit an atomic nucleus have different energy levels known as bands. Light is produced when an electron jumps from one band to one another and then collides with a quasiparticle called an electron hole.

Usually, the process also involves a second quasiparticle known as a phonon. Direct bandgap materials such as gallium nitride don’t require a phonon, which makes the light generation process more efficient.

Staera says Lightwire transmits data between an AI accelerator’s chiplets at a rate of up to 8 gigabits per second. The technology can provide more than 600 optical links per square millimeter. In practice, that means a Lightwire-powered HBM4 memory stack can move up to 24 terabits of data per second instead of the 2.8 terabits supported by current technologies.

Staera’s funding round will advance its commercialization efforts. It will enhance Lightwire, grow its U.S. team and build out a manufacturing supply chain. The company hopes to begin commercial shipments in 2030.

#5527. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5526. 3 AI agents value a home similarly, could they be wrong?

Three AI valuation systems can produce similar home values while relying on the same market definition and comparable selection assumptions. Agreement does not validate accuracy if the competitive market area is misidentified.  AI Summary

The similarities in the estimations made by three independent systems might be perceived as confirmation of accuracy. However, when AI-powered systems operate under the same assumptions regarding a property’s competitive market, the agreement might bring no additional assurance.

Imagine three different AI agents estimating the value of your house. The first system offers a $1.59 million valuation. The second – $1.61 million. And the third – $1.60 million.

It looks like three independent systems agree on the price. This information can be quite reassuring for the homeowner who plans to sell. Moreover, the similarity in the numbers can be influential for the asking price.

However, this question comes to mind: Have three different systems produced the same number because they analyzed the data independently, or is the result just similar due to the same initial assumptions?

Let’s talk about this case in more details and figure out whether agreement can increase the probability of a mistaken valuation.

The issue can arise long before any of the numbers is calculated by the systems.

The real estate sector accumulates huge volumes of property data. Closed transactions, MLS records, active listings, public records and other sources provide rich information about the prices, property features and market activity.

Modern valuation models use highly advanced statistical techniques and machine learning algorithms to make sense of this information. AI agents can extract and analyze property records, use third-party valuations or generate an accurate price explanation based on the market data.

However, the three independent systems can be based on the same underlying sources, analytical methods or similar understanding of the competitive market. And, in case the initial assumptions are incorrect, the similarity of results cannot provide any additional assurance.

Let’s imagine a condominium in Miami on the 24th floor of a high-rise building.

AI generates valuation based on the recent transactions of condominiums with the same square footage, number of bedrooms and geographical proximity. It uses the information to make calculations and produce a detailed valuation.

Everything looks good. Properties exist. Transaction histories are true. Property characteristics match the search criteria. The calculations are accurate. But do these properties compete in the same market?

In dense residential markets like Miami, geographical proximity and similar property characteristics can hide significant differences in competitive positioning.

Two condominiums may have the same number of bedrooms, the same square footage, and even be located right across the street from each other. But one may be located in the entry-level residential community while another – in the waterfront development.

They may have identical property types, but different price ranges, ownership costs, amenities, views, and other characteristics that are relevant for the market analysis.

On paper, the properties look comparable. But in reality, they may attract different buyers and be in competition with different properties.

This concept is well understood by established organizations like Fannie Mae. According to the Appraiser Update of December 2024, two properties that are located side by side can be in the same neighborhood, but occupy different market areas since they appeal to different buyers.

According to the guidelines on the comparable sales, the comparable properties should compete for the same buyers as the subject property.

This is an important difference between searching similar property records and identifying relevant market evidence.

Competitive market area may begin with the condominium building where the subject property is located, include similar units within the same development, or some competing residential communities in the area. Price range classification and property characteristics can help with the organization of this analysis, but they cannot substitute the process itself.

The market area should be defined with the help of buyer alternatives, not the geographical proximity.

I have worked with residential property data and analyzed the range of automated valuation models and AI-generated valuations, and the distinction between preparing property records and organizing the market analysis keeps coming back.

Property records can contain accurate addresses, standardized property types, verified square footage, complete transaction history, and precise geographic coordinates. All of the duplicate records are deleted, inconsistencies are corrected, and missing information is added.

These are important steps in data preparation. But clean data does not tell anything about the competition between the residential communities, the price range segments they occupy, and the relevant properties for the market analysis.

This requires one more step: organizing residential communities, analyzing their characteristics, establishing the relations between the properties, and validating those relations on the market evidence.

These processes can be automated with the help of machine learning. But the underlying definitions and inferences require testing and maintenance as well. It does not mean that current valuation models are based on radius searches. Many of them use the much more complicated methods and can find the complex relationships between property characteristics, locations, and market activity.

The challenge here is more fundamental: can we make sure that the information used to support the valuation is the appropriate representation of the competitive market area of the subject property?

Larger dataset, more advanced model, or a better explanation of the results cannot guarantee this. More property data does not mean more market evidence automatically.

Defining market areas has its consequences not only for comparable sales, but for the statistics describing the supply, demand, and the current competitive conditions as well.

Inventory, speed of selling, days on market and months of supply depend on which properties are included in the calculation. Let’s take a simplified, hypothetical example.

Imagine a competitive market area that consists of a group of competing condominium communities with 12 active listings. This market area has been experiencing three sales per month. So, the inventory represents four months of supply.

Now, let’s imagine an AI system combining these properties with another residential area with 48 active listings and three sales per month.

Combined market area will include 60 active listings and six monthly sales, resulting in 10 months of supply.

Both calculations are mathematically correct. But the second number describes a different set of properties, not necessarily the competitive environment of the first market area.

For the homeowner, the difference is important. Four months of supply and 10 months of supply can indicate very different competitive conditions. Depending on the way of interpretation, this statistic may have impact on the pricing expectations and the decision whether to change the asking price.

Of course, the actual market analysis requires consistency of the measurement periods, sufficient transaction activity, and the consideration of changing conditions. Small samples can lead to uncertainties, even in case of correct market definition.

But the example shows an important point. Calculation can be mathematically correct, but the population of properties that is included in the calculation can be wrong for the particular decision.

The same concerns median prices, selling speed, and other market indicators. If the dataset includes communities from different competitive segments, its summary statistics may cover the completely irrelevant competitive conditions.

That is why market definition and maintenance of relevant residential communities is not just an improvement of comparable selection. This is an essential part of market analysis.

Research in other industries provides one more argument to be skeptical about the opinion agreement of several AI systems.

The 2025 study Correlated Errors in Large Language Models published at the International Conference on Machine Learning has examined more than 350 language models and has found out substantial correlations in their mistakes.

On one benchmark, when both models produced a mistake, they chose the same wrong answer in 60% of cases. Correlations were also found between models of different architecture and provided by different organizations.

However, the study was not concerned about the home valuations, and its results do not prove that AI pricing agents routinely make the same mistakes. But it reveals an important limitation of apparent model independence: different models can make correlated mistakes.

In case of property valuations, the risk of correlated mistakes is associated with shared assumptions.

If several AI systems analyze overlapping market information, use similar property-selection criteria, or rely on the same initial valuation source, their conclusions may be less independent than they seem.

And when the underlying market is improperly defined, these systems can reinforce misleading interpretation without generating a single false record.

It is important to remember that this situation differs from the usual problem of AI hallucinations. Hallucination provides some unsupported or invented information. Market definition mistake can produce misleading conclusion on the basis of the correct data.

Verifying the existence of transactions is necessary. But it does not guarantee that these transactions are really relevant for the analysis.

The most valuable AI pricing advice should do more than producing a number. It should help homeowners to understand the market evidence behind the number, assumptions and uncertainties associated with it.

First of all, it is the market itself. Which residential communities and competing properties have been considered as relevant, and why? Does the analysis distinguish between the properties that are geographically close and actually compete with the same buyers?

Then it is the evidence itself. Which closed transactions serve as the base for the recommended price? How the characteristics of the subject property compare to these sales? Which active listings show the current competition? Were the relevant transactions excluded, or less comparable properties were included just due to the geographical proximity?

Understanding of the limitations of the system is also important.

Model can have limited transaction activity in the subject’s competitive market. The particular unit may have some unique characteristics. Comparable properties may require adjustments, or the market conditions have already changed after the closing of the most relevant transactions.

In these circumstances, admitting the uncertainty is more valuable than producing an artificial precise conclusion.

Also, homeowners should be able to distinguish between explanation and validation. System can provide a good explanation of its estimation, but this fact does not confirm the predictive accuracy of the method.

Where possible, evidence of how a valuation method performs against actual sales prices for comparable properties and market segments can be more valuable than the agreement of several AI-generated estimates.

Not every automated valuation model operates with a conventional list of comparable sales, and not every proprietary system allows checking its inner workings. This is the reason why transparency of available evidence, limitations, and performance metrics is especially important.

For the homeowner receiving three similar estimates, the next step should be to check whether they are based on the different market evidence or they just reflect the same initial data.

Agreement may be reassuring. Understanding of the reasons for it is more valuable.

As AI becomes more and more accessible, the ability to retrieve property records, calculate statistics, and generate the polished price explanations will become commonplace.

The meaningful differentiation will consist in the quality of the market intelligence. It includes reliable property data, well-organized residential communities, relevant relations between the competing properties, consistent market definitions, and methods that can be validated.

Neither proprietary dataset nor publicly available records are superior. What matters is how this information is organized, validated, maintained, and applied to solve the particular problem.

Technological sophistication of models will continue to grow, but it should not be mistaken for independent verification.

For the homeowners preparing to sell, the consequences are practical. Pricing decision can impact the way of entering the market, the competition of the property with alternatives, its listing period, and the negotiating position of the seller.

The purpose is not replacing the professional judgment with the impressive number. It is providing homeowners and real estate professionals with the better evidence and the more precise market context.

Three AI agents valuing your home similarly sound convincing. However, before trusting their conclusion, one more question is important to ask.

Is the market they are analyzing the right one?

Jake Miakota is the CEO of Subdivisions.com, a residential community-based real estate market intelligence platform.

#5525. What 1,000 U.S. real estate ads reveal about lead generation

Reviewing 1,000 active U.S. residential Meta ads found pricing mentioned in 38% of ads, while explicit qualification cues appeared in 7.7%. The findings suggest lead handling and follow up should differ by offer type and destination.  AI Summary

In Texas, a homebuilder advertised new homes starting around $240,000 and sent visitors to its community website. A property search service offered free listing alerts through a Meta Instant Form. Both wanted buyer inquiries, yet the buyers were signing up for different experiences. I would hesitate to hand those contacts to an agent as if they meant the same thing.

I reviewed 1,000 active residential real estate ads across 20 U.S. regions, collected from Meta’s public Ad Library on October 15, 2026. Buyer-focused ads accounted for 73% of the sample. The sharpest divide was between property-search and lead-generation pages, which used Instant Forms in 66% of their ads, and homebuilders, where that figure was 4%. It is a striking difference for businesses competing for many of the same people.

The sample excluded rentals, commercial properties, mortgage services and unrelated promotions. I capped the number of ads from each Facebook page so large advertisers would not overwhelm the results, then classified the intended audience, advertiser type, offer, written price information, qualification cues and click destination. The data went through additional checks before the figures were calculated.

Individual listings made up 29% of the sample, new construction 27.5%, and broader home-search offers roughly 17%. An inquiry on a specific listing gives an agent an immediate subject for a conversation. Someone requesting alerts for an entire neighborhood may have no property in mind and could be months from making a decision.

When I look at a lead-generation campaign, that difference shapes my advice more than the choice between a form and a website. I want to know whether the sales team is set up for property inquiries or for a longer search relationship. Those are different workloads, even if both begin with a name and a phone number.

Seller advertising offered another contrast. It accounted for 19% of the ads, with agents and teams responsible for 41% of that group and cash homebuyers for 27%. One Utah cash buyer cited a $420,000 sale completed in 33 days, a claim I could not independently verify. Its offer emphasized selling without repairs or a traditional listing. An agent replying with a generic home-valuation ad would be competing against a much more specific promise.

Price or monthly-payment information appeared in the written copy of 38% of ads. For individual listings it was 60%; for new-construction offers, 53%. Among broad buyer campaigns, it fell to 22%. Only 9% of seller-focused ads mentioned a price-related figure.

I was more interested in what the copy left unsaid. Just 7.7% of ads included an explicit qualifying cue, such as budget, financing readiness or purchase timing. For ads using Meta Instant Forms, the figure was about 10%. We did not inspect the questions inside those forms, so I would not claim advertisers skipped qualification altogether.

Still, an agent cannot respond intelligently to every inquiry in the same way. If a campaign advertises homes within a defined price range, I would rather see that range stated clearly than leave the salesperson to discover a basic mismatch on the first call. With monthly-payment offers, financing assumptions deserve equal attention.

Overall, 51% of ads led to websites or landing pages, 30% used Meta Instant Forms, and about 5% invited conversations through Messenger, Instagram or WhatsApp. Among builders, 88% sent traffic to their websites. A development page can explain a property before anyone speaks to sales; an instant form can capture interest sooner.

Neither choice tells us how well a campaign performs. But it does affect the work that follows. A search service can use saved listings and alerts to keep a buyer engaged. If a small brokerage has no process for staying in touch, borrowing that same offer may fill its CRM with people it will never properly serve.

My first check would happen after the click. I would submit the form myself, open the resulting CRM record and see what the agent actually receives. Does it identify the property that attracted the buyer? Could someone on the team call back without asking the prospect to repeat the entire inquiry? If the answer is no, I would fix that before buying more traffic.

For listing ads, I would test putting a realistic price range in the written copy, then listen to the conversations it produces. The point is to find out whether prospects arrive with clearer expectations. A higher cost per inquiry could be acceptable if more of those conversations lead to relevant showings.

For a broad search offer, I would make sure the team has a reason to contact people again. Asking about purchase timing may be helpful if an agent uses the answer to plan follow-up. Adding five questions to a form that nobody reads solves nothing.

I also would not copy a large search platform’s campaign simply because its ads are everywhere. It may have an entire operation built around people who are still browsing. A brokerage with a handful of agents needs a funnel suited to the people it can actually help. That is the decision I would make before choosing the ad format.

Oleh Odukalets is a performance marketer with seven years of experience in paid acquisition and more than $1 million in real estate ad spend managed across international markets.
