#5511. Resideo Announces Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Updates 2026 Outlook

SCOTTSDALE, Ariz., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Resideo Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: REZI), a leading global developer and manufacturer of critical control and sensing solutions for residential markets, today announced financial results for the third fiscal quarter ended October 3, 2026.

"Resideo delivered top and bottom line third quarter results that were near the high end of our outlook ranges in our first quarter following the separation of ADI, underscoring our team's continued strong execution. We achieved 3% revenue growth year-over-year across all sales channels and 6% growth year-over-year excluding OEM Security, driven by customer demand for our differentiated, non-discretionary products. We also reduced our debt by $1.1 billion, using the $900 million dividend received from ADI and $200 million of cash on hand," said Tom Surran, Resideo's President and CEO.

"We remain focused on creating value for our customers with our differentiated products and services. That includes new AI-powered capabilities on our next-generation FORTIQ software platform, which delivers actionable intelligence that enhances customer productivity and optimizes the end-user's experience. We are executing on our strategic priorities with discipline and consistency, creating positive momentum in a soft housing market and a dynamic macro environment."

Total revenue of $727 million was up 3% compared to $703 million in the third quarter of 2025, and includes an unfavorable impact of approximately 50 basis points from foreign currency exchange. Total revenue was near the high-end of the provided outlook range for the third quarter of 2026.

Revenue excluding OEM Security of $694 million, was up 6% compared to $653 million in the third quarter of 2025, and grew year-over-year across all of our sales channels and product categories due to volume, driven by customer demand for our products, and pricing. OEM Security revenue of $33 million was down 34% compared to $50 million in the third quarter of 2025, and declined as expected due to reduced volumes from a large OEM Security customer.

Gross margin of 40.4%, marking the 14th consecutive quarter of year-over-year gross margin expansion. Gains from price increases, operational efficiencies, and tariff refunds were partially offset by unfavorable product sales mix and inflationary input costs.

Research and development expenses increased $4 million from the third quarter of 2025 driven by investments in new product launches to drive future growth. Selling, general and administrative expenses increased $24 million from the third quarter of 2025, driven primarily by $30 million of non-recurring business separation expenses associated with the ADI Spin-Off. Restructuring, impairment and extinguishment expenses increased $17 million from the third quarter of 2025 due to continued manufacturing operations optimization and higher debt extinguishment charges.

GAAP income from continuing operations, net of taxes, of $31 million was down 66% compared to $90 million in the third quarter 2025. Standalone Adjusted EBITDA(1) of $154 million was up 5% compared to $146 million in the third quarter of 2025, primarily due to higher gross profit dollars and controlled growth in operating expenses. Standalone Adjusted EBITDA was near the high-end of the provided outlook range for the third quarter of 2026.

Net cash provided by operating activities of continuing operations was $33 million in the third quarter 2026 compared to net cash used by operating activities of continuing operations of $1.59 billion in the third quarter of 2025. The increase in cash provided by operations was primarily due to the $1.59 billion payment made in the third quarter of 2025 to Honeywell to terminate the Indemnification Agreement.

In connection with the ADI Spin-Off, Resideo received a $900 million cash dividend from ADI as partial consideration for the assets transferred in the ADI Spin-Off. We used this dividend, along with $200 million of cash on hand to repay $1.1 billion of gross debt during the third quarter. We also made a $20 million payment to ADI as part of the post-separation adjustment mechanism to true up cash. At October 3, 2026, Resideo had cash and cash equivalents of $229 million and total outstanding gross debt of $2.1 billion.

In connection with the completion of the ADI Spin-Off, Resideo's outstanding Series A Cumulative Convertible Participating Preferred Stock ("Preferred Stock") was reduced by 150,000 shares, leaving 350,000 shares outstanding, with a proportional adjustment to the conversion price and an ongoing smaller quarterly dividend payable on Resideo's Preferred Stock.

On August 3, 2026, Resideo completed the separation of its former ADI Global Distribution segment by distributing to Resideo common shareholders on a pro rata basis all of the issued and outstanding common stock of ADI Global Distribution Inc., the entity incorporated to hold the ADI business (the "ADI Spin-Off"). As a result of the ADI Spin-Off, we present the historical results of the ADI business as discontinued operations in our financial statements.

Its comfort and protection solutions can be found in more than 150 million residential and commercial spaces globally, with tens of millions of new devices sold annually. #5510. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5509. AMD brings Zen 6 architecture muscle to embedded systems with new EPYC 9006 series chips

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. is delivering a massive compute upgrade to the specialized embedded systems used to validate semiconductor technologies with the launch of its 6th Gen AMD EPYC Embedded 9006 Series SP7 processors.

Announced today, the new chips are designed to bring superior performance to semiconductor automated test equipment or ATE, enterprise storage systems and high-end network firewalls, the company said.

AMD is targeting what it says is mounting friction in the semiconductor hardware supply chain with its new processors. As the data demands of artificial intelligence workloads increase, the systems used to validate, secure and move that data are reaching their limits.

Semiconductor ATE workloads in particular are showing signs of strain. They’re performed by automated testing rigs that act as high-speed quality control during chip manufacturing operations, running continuous electrical parametric tests, functional stress tests and signal validation across dozens of silicon dies simultaneously.

The goal of these tests is to identify any defects or performance issues with new silicon chips before they reach mass production, but as their performance capabilities increase, existing ATE controllers are unable to provide the massive parallel compute power required to orchestrate them.

AMD’s EPYC Embedded 9006 family is designed to eliminate this bottleneck. It’s based on the company’s high-performance Zen 6 core architecture and it packs up to 256 cores and 512 threads into a single socket. It’s an extremely dense computing footprint that delivers 1.8 times more throughput, 1.5 times greater networking bandwidth and 2.7 times higher memory bandwidth than the company’s previous 5th Generation 9005 series embedded chips.

They can also facilitate much more rapid data movement with up to 96 lanes of PCIe Gen 6 running at 64 gigatransfers per second, with flexible CXL 3.1 expansion and 16 DDR5 memory channels that support multiplexed rank dual inline memory module speeds of up to 12,800 megatransfers per second. That last number refers to the chip’s effective data transfer rate between the memory controller and the memory module, and represents a significant jump from the standard 6,400 to 8,000 MT/s of standard, high-end server DDR5 random-access memory chips.

AMD said EPYC Embedded 9006 series chips can also provide more control plane muscle for 400G and 800G network firewalls. that enables them to process expanding security policies better, as well as faster compression and redundant array of independent disks in storage workloads.

Salil Raje, senior vice president and general manager of AMD’s Adaptive and Embedded Computing Group, said the industry urgently needs this increased computing heft at the embedded layer if it’s to maintain the momentum of its current development cadence. “The systems that test semiconductors, secure networks and manage enterprise data must keep pace or risk becoming bottlenecks to progress,” he said. “With AMD EPYC Embedded 9006 SP7 processors, we’re extending AMD CPU leadership by bringing data center-class compute to embedded systems and by helping customers increase capacity and do more within their power budgets.”

When it comes to testing advanced semiconductor designs, security is of paramount importance, and that’s why AMD introduced a number of innovations on that front. For instance, the EPYC Embedded 9006 chips incorporate the company’s Root of Trust or ART technology to establish an immutable boot chain, secured by post-quantum cryptography, to safeguard firmware signing against potential threats from quantum computers in the future.

There’s also a new AMD Security Processor or ASP that handles runtime trust execution, virtual machine encryption and authorized diagnostic debugging. The chips further integrate Caliptra, which is an open-source and vendor-agnostic silicon root of trust technology that supports remote attestation to mathematically verify device identities and prevent firmware tampering.

With mass volume production already underway, the 6th Gen AMD EPYC Embedded 9006 Series SP7 processors are expected to be shipped to customers later this month, the company said. Customers will be able to choose from configurations ranging from 64 to 256 cores, with the first 128-core offering launching on Nov. 15.

#5508. RealPlus brings HouseCanary Google Listings to NYC clients

RealPlus is partnering with My State MLS to offer HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program to NYC residential brokerages. Active listings can appear in Google mobile search with photos, pricing, and click-to-contact links to the listing agent.   AI Summary

RealPlus is partnering with My State MLS to make HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program available to its New York City residential brokerage clients, giving brokers and agents a new channel to surface listings directly in Google mobile search results.

The integration allows active listings to appear in mobile search with property photos, pricing and agent contact information, according to the company announcement. The placements appear above traditional sponsored real estate ads and include a click-to-contact feature that connects prospective buyers directly with the listing agent.

For brokerages, the offering effectively functions as an additional digital listing distribution channel, alongside portals and IDX, but inside Google’s search environment where most buyers begin home searches. In a tight lead-conversion market with rising online advertising costs, direct search visibility and agent-connected lead flows can help firms diversify away from solely portal-driven leads.

“We are always looking for ways to expand the value and capabilities we bring to our clients,” Jennifer Boucher, the chief product officer at RealPlus and a HousingWire Insider, said in a statement. “This partnership is a great addition to our offerings, giving brokers and agents another way to put their listings in front of prospective buyers and generate direct connections.”

The HouseCanary Google Listings Program will be available to RealPlus clients later in November and will be offered at no cost to participating listing brokers and agents, the company said.

RealPlus said the move aligns with its broader strategy of building listing and data infrastructure tailored to New York City residential brokerages at a time when firms are reassessing tech stacks, lead sources and marketing spend. For listing agents, a no-cost path to higher placement in search results could support listing presentations and seller expectations around online exposure.

The Google Listings Program is powered by HouseCanary, which negotiates agreements with multiple listing services to send their brokerage members’ listings to Google. Participating MLSs include  Arizona Regional MLS, Bright MLS, California Regional MLS, IRES MLS, Permian Basin Board of Realtors, REcolorado and San Diego MLS.

HouseCanary said it also works directly with brokerages, like the three announced Wednesday, to ensure their listings flow into the program via a participating MLS. Brokerages that want their listings included need either to belong to an MLS that is in the program or to encourage their local MLS to opt in.

Over the past few weeks, HouseCanary has announced that real estate brokerages REMAX Advantage, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Florida Properties Group, ENRG Realty, Side and The Keyes Company and Illustrated Properties, all RealTrends Verified firms, have signed on to the program, sharing its listings with HouseCanary via My State MLS.

These announcements also comes as HouseCanary continues to work through its Chapter 11 restructuring. Under the firm’s proposed plan, which remains subject to court approval, HouseCanary is targeting emergence from bankruptcy before year-end, with full recovery for all approved creditors. Management has positioned initiatives such as the Google Listings Program and the AI platform as core to its go-forward strategy while it continues to serve existing customers.

Launched in early 2026 and slated to expand to all eligible U.S. markets this fall, the program is one of several industry experiments that put MLS and brokerage listings in front of consumers in new contexts, potentially changing how buyers first encounter a property and which party — portal, brokerage or platform — captures the initial inquiry.

#5507. HawkEye 360 Appoints Former CIA Director Ambassador William J. Burns to Board of Directors

Distinguished national security and diplomatic leader brings decades of intelligence, foreign policy, and global affairs expertise to HawkEye 360

HERNDON, Va., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HawkEye 360 (NYSE: HAWK), the global leader in signals intelligence data and analytics, today announced the appointment of Ambassador William J. Burns, former Director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), to its Board of Directors. Ambassador Burns brings more than three decades of distinguished leadership across U.S. intelligence, diplomacy, and national security, providing valuable strategic insight as HawkEye 360 continues to expand its capabilities and support for U.S. and allied defense and intelligence missions.

"Ambassador Burns brings an extraordinary depth of experience in intelligence, national security, and global affairs, along with a firsthand understanding of the challenges facing the United States and our allies," said John Serafini, CEO of HawkEye 360. "His expertise and leadership will be invaluable as we continue advancing our capabilities, integrating our data and analytics into operational workflows, and delivering trusted intelligence directly to the Warfighter. His guidance will help us remain focused on what matters most: supporting our customers' missions, strengthening operational decision-making, and helping protect those who serve."

Ambassador Burns served as Director of the CIA from 2021 to January 2025, becoming the first career diplomat to lead the agency. Prior to his appointment, he spent more than three decades in U.S. diplomatic service, holding senior leadership positions including Deputy Secretary of State, Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, and U.S. Ambassador to Russia and Jordan. Throughout his career, he played a central role in advancing U.S. national security interests, strengthening international partnerships, and navigating complex geopolitical challenges.

Ambassador Burns currently serves as Senior Advisor for Global Affairs at Evercore, a position he assumed in June 2025. Previously, he served as President of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace from 2015 to 2021. He holds a bachelor's degree in history from La Salle University and master's and doctoral degrees in International Relations from Oxford University, and is the author of the bestselling book, The Back Channel: A Memoir of American Diplomacy and the Case for its Renewal.

"I greatly admire the work of Hawkeye 360," said Ambassador Burns, "I am delighted to have the chance to serve on their board."

Ambassador Burns joins HawkEye 360's Board as the company continues expanding its space-based collection capabilities, advancing signals intelligence analytics, and strengthening partnerships across the global defense and intelligence community. His appointment reinforces HawkEye 360's commitment to delivering trusted, operationally relevant intelligence that supports the evolving mission priorities of U.S. and allied defense and security partners.

HawkEye 360, headquartered in Herndon, Virginia, is a signals intelligence company delivering mission-critical intelligence data and analytics to strengthen national and global security. By detecting, characterizing, and geolocating RF signals, HawkEye 360 equips defense, intelligence, and commercial partners with critical information to make informed decisions, respond quickly, and enhance operational effectiveness. Leveraging advanced AI-supported analytics, HawkEye 360 delivers early warning indicators, enhances situational awareness, and informs strategic and operational decision-makingâensuring allied forces and security partners maintain a decisive advantage in complex and contested environments.

Tomorrow’s US Consumer Price Index report for October 2026, due at 8:30 a.m. ET on November 10, arrives at a delicate moment for risk assets. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts what the upcoming CPI data drop could look like and how the market may react.

After September’s hotter-than-expected print (headline +0.6% month-over-month and 3.7% year-over-year), markets are braced for another reading that will shape December Federal Reserve rate expectations.

Consensus currently clusters around a headline rise of +0.2% to +0.3% MoM and a core increase of roughly +0.2% MoM, with the annual headline rate expected near 3.7%.

My base-case prediction is a mild downside surprise relative to the more hawkish end of expectations: headline CPI at +0.2% month-over-month and core CPI also at +0.2%. Energy prices appear to have stabilized after September’s sharp gasoline spike, while shelter and services inflation show early signs of moderation.

If those assumptions hold, the report would mark a clear deceleration from the prior month without signaling a sudden collapse in price pressures. Year-over-year figures, if published, would likely remain sticky near 3.6–3.7% for the headline and around 2.5% for core.

Such a print would not eliminate the possibility of further Fed tightening, but it would reduce the urgency for an aggressive December hike and ease upward pressure on Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar.

Right now, analysts and prediction markets price the odds of a December rate hike at 75% to 80%, but if the Meta AI CPI data prediction plays out, that number could drop sharply.

#5505. Third spaces perform a star turn in this new Florida master plan

Wyld Oaks, a 215-acre mixed-use project in Apopka near Orlando, is underway with 325 apartments starting. The plan totals 6,000 multifamily units, 300,000 SF retail, and major nonresidential uses after a nearly 2-year delay tied to financing constraints.  AI Summary

In a crowded, competitive and bumpy market, residential developers and builders do their best to stand out in a sea of sameness. Some bet that they’ll seize a competitive edge by leaning into walkable communities with “third spaces,” ones where residents can easily connect with one another and feel a sense of belonging.

Wyld Oaks, an upcoming mixed-use community near Orlando, Florida, where construction is now underway, will put that thesis to the test. In October, Hathaway Development became the first developer to begin horizontal construction at Wyld Oaks, where it is building 325 apartment units.

That’s for starters. Once fully built out, the community is expected to have 6,000 multifamily units and a small adjoining single-family portion with fewer than 100 homes.

Residential, mind you, is only part of the plan. Wyld Oaks is designed around a walkable main street anchored by a large park and 300,000 square feet of retail space. Elsewhere in the community, the master plan calls for two hotels, a medical campus, 1.5 million square feet of industrial and distribution space, multiple other parks, an outdoor concert venue and a gas station.

For Wyld Oaks master developer Joseph Beninati, the goal is to create a walkable, mixed-use community that functions like a complete neighborhood, with daily needs all within walking or biking distance.

“Could you take your car? Of course you can,” Beninati said in an interview with HousingWire TBD. “But the option to walk is going to be there.”

With walkability at its core, Wyld Oaks stands apart from the overwhelming majority of new suburban development in the region, which is largely car-centric.

Getting the project off the ground has been difficult, however. The original multifamily development, which only just broke ground, was slated to begin in late 2024 or early 2025. The delay resulted from a challenging local multifamily capital environment that has plagued many other Sun Belt markets.

The 215-acre Wyld Oaks community is located in Apopka, a high-growth suburb of Orlando that saw its population grow by roughly 20% between 2020 and 2025. Despite this growth, and the rapid growth of adjacent communities, there remain relatively few walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods for residents and visitors alike.

This need in the market was among the top considerations for Wyld Oaks, which was designed with walkability, livability and community in mind.

“It all starts with density, and trail systems and parks, and having everything closer to one another as opposed to further apart. We have multifamily, and we’re working on retail, food and beverage, coffee stores and grocery stores, all within walking distance,” Beninati said. “Run the list. [Residents] need fitness. They need healthcare. They need a convenience store and daily conveniences, dry cleaning, hair salons and barber shops.”

All of the commercial uses designed within easy walking distances in the community will work together to keep residents in the neighborhood, bring in employees to work at the industrial park and various businesses and draw in visitors to enjoy the local shops, restaurants and parks. Once fully built out, Beninati expects, or at least hopes, that Wyld Oaks will become a top-tier regional destination.

“Economic activity begets economic activity. If you’re bringing your kids to the dentist, that allows you to also maybe do a little grocery shopping. Or if you’re going to work out and you’re with some friends, maybe you’re going to go out and have a drink or supper together. When everything is in one place, it allows that to happen,” Beninati explained.

Beninati envisions a neighborhood where residents can get outdoors and meet one another, whether at local parks, restaurants, the community’s future farmers market or other events. For visitors, he wants a community that is memorable and draws people back in.

“For me, some of the softer things would be, are prom pictures getting taken and wedding pictures getting taken there? Or is it a meaningful place that the community rallies around? Is there a Christmas tree, and is there going to be a Halloween event for the kids? Things like that are what make a community something that is memorable,” he said.

Although Wyld Oaks is primarily multifamily and non-residential, homebuilders could potentially learn lessons from it. The community’s emphasis on third spaces – places that bridge work, home and school – where residents can connect and feel a sense of belonging, could apply just as well to many single-family neighborhoods.

Central Florida, like many other high-growth Sun Belt markets, experienced a post-COVID multifamily building boom. A surge in new construction following the pandemic led to a coinciding surge in new deliveries.

In 2021 and 2022, developers delivered about 8,500 to 8,800 new multifamily units in the Orlando MSA, according to data from Cushman & Wakefield. In 2023 and 2024, the number of deliveries rose to about 12,500 and 13,000, while 2025 saw about 11,000 new units completed.

Like many other Sun Belt markets, this surge in completions oversupplied the market and pressured rents to soften. As a result, financing new multifamily projects in Central Florida became quite challenging by 2024, the reason the first multifamily community at Wyld Oaks was delayed by nearly two years.

According to Beninati, the biggest challenge in the multifamily financing environment in the Orlando market over the past couple of years hasn’t been securing construction loans so much as finding equity investors to fund projects. Investors have grown more discriminating, directing available capital toward established developers with strong track records and projects in desirable locations.

In Wyld Oaks’ case, the developer’s reputation and the project’s location and desirable master plan helped it secure an equity partner, despite the challenging environment.

However, Beninati believes local financing conditions may be starting to improve. A slowdown in new multifamily development over the past couple of years means that the market has become more balanced, and rent power has begun to stabilize. That dynamic could help other multifamily projects become more financially viable.

For Beninati, breaking ground on the community’s first phase was a major milestone, especially after a delay of nearly two years. But it is only a small piece of a much larger vision, and bringing the full community to life will take years, with market conditions shifting along the way. Weathering those changes, Beninati said, comes down to one thing.

“I think it’s just patience. This is a business where you need to be incredibly, incredibly patient,” he said. “It doesn’t just happen overnight. That’s the nature of the real estate business.”

#5504. Mamdani gives nonprofits first dibs on buying apartment buildings

Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed COPA, requiring owners to notify the city and qualified nonprofits before selling covered buildings. The law takes effect in 1 year, as a 38 building portfolio with 850 mostly rent stabilized units heads to foreclosure auctions.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed legislation Tuesday giving vetted nonprofits a first shot at buying troubled city apartment buildings.

The new measure arrived too late to spare hundreds of rent-stabilized units from foreclosure, a second loss in Mamdani’s bid to protect such units.

Mamdani ran for office and won on creating and protecting affordable housing. National attention has since focused on his efforts to build more housing and cut red tape. His political inspiration and influence have spread to other parts of the country.

Nithya Raman is a prime example. Under a similar affordability theme, the Los Angeles City Council member, also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, ousted an incumbent to become L.A. mayor.

The Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, known as COPA, requires owners of covered buildings to notify the city and qualified nonprofits before selling. Those groups then get time to make an offer and a right to match a later one. The law takes effect one year after enactment, after the Department of Housing Preservation and Development writes rules.

“This law will give New Yorkers a tool to keep their homes out of the hands of predatory investors seeking to make a quick and easy buck,” Mamdani said at a signing event Tuesday.

He also won in court last week. A Brooklyn appellate panel ruled Nov. 4 that the administration can resume collecting its pied-à-terre tax on high-end second homes, reversing a Staten Island judge who found the rollout flawed. Mamdani says the tax could raise $500 million a year. Other legal challenges remain.

But his administration could not stop the sale of a 38-building portfolio with 850 mostly rent-stabilized apartments. Spatial Equity, an affordable housing developer with City Hall’s backing, failed to close a deal to buy the portfolio before an East Harlem auction began Tuesday afternoon.

The 38 buildings belonged to bankrupt Emerald Equities Group. Banks and other institutions that control about $250 million in mortgage loans will foreclose on each building over three auction days.

Lenders rejected Spatial Equity’s initial $68 million bid, according to a City Limits report. They also turned down a $110 million offer last month, tenant leader Cara Polte told Gothamist.

Polte said tenants will keep pushing for a buyer committed to fixing the buildings. Tenants had hoped to turn her building and four others on the block into a community land trust.

A trust managed by several banks and by Sabal Investment Holdings controls the loans. Freddie Mac partially insured them. Sabal has yet to respond to media requests.

Cea Weaver, director of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants, said the sale does not end the city’s effort to force owners to improve conditions.

This setback follows Mamdani’s first loss on this front. On Jan. 1, he stood in a Pinnacle-owned building and vowed to take on bad landlords. He then sought a 30-day delay of the bankruptcy auction of Pinnacle’s rent-regulated portfolio, hoping to find a buyer other than Summit Properties USA.

A judge allowed the sale to proceed. Summit won about 5,100 mostly rent-stabilized units from Pinnacle, which had filed for Chapter 11 after Flagstar Bank foreclosed.

Emerald bought the 38 buildings for $350 million in 2016 and began raising rents on stabilized apartments. It took out another $180 million loan in December 2018, six months before state lawmakers passed tenant protections that outlawed many of those tactics.

Lenders foreclosed in 2024. Emerald filed for bankruptcy a year later.

A state investigation found Emerald had illegally removed 21 apartments from rent stabilization. The buildings had more than 2,300 housing code violations in April. A retaining wall behind buildings on East 103rd Street collapsed earlier this year, days before Mamdani and Weaver visited in March.

About 1,600 rent-stabilized buildings face financial distress, according to Rent Guidelines Board data. Landlord groups blame rent restrictions, including the board’s two-year rent freeze. Tenant advocates say owners like Emerald borrowed heavily expecting rent increases that later law barred.

In June, Mamdani won a rent freeze through the Rent Guidelines Board for the city’s roughly 1 million stabilized apartments.

Landlords sued to reverse the freeze. The case began in Staten Island, but Justice Ralph Porzio moved it to Manhattan in August, handing Mamdani a partial win. In September, the judge ordered City Hall to turn over communications with the board and signaled he would likely not rule by Oct. 1.

Oct. 1 came and went without a ruling, and the freeze took effect for new and renewing leases.

Meanwhile, a federal lawsuit remains pending over a 2019 state law that limits rents on stabilized units. Small property owners sued in November 2025, arguing the law unconstitutionally keeps stabilized apartments vacant.

COPA’s path was uneven until Mamdani took office. The City Council passed an earlier version in December 2025, but then-Mayor Eric Adams vetoed it, and the Council did not override him. A revised, narrower version passed Oct. 22.

“Progress … is something that we celebrate, and also, we know that it is not inevitable,” Mamdani said. “It has to be won.”

#5502. AI’s future starts to look surprisingly old-school: theCUBE’s KubeCon day one keynote analysis

The cloud-native community that turned Kubernetes into an enterprise standard is now being asked to carry artificial intelligence into production. As the underlying technology looks more alike from one company to the next, the hunt for domain-specific AI value is spotlighting how AI is put to work – and how to do so safely.

That shift is on display this week in Salt Lake City, where the Cloud Native Computing Foundation has added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track to its flagship conference. The plumbing built for microservices is proving to be the substrate for AI factories and agents, along with a renewed focus on tried-and-tested security and business principles, according to John Furrier (pictured, left), co-founder and executive analyst of theCUBE Research.

“The AI-native world that we’ve been covering and following and living — AI factories, the rise of agentic, which involves coding and now tasks — are all based fundamentally on the substrate of cloud-native technologies,” Furrier said. “This community is the heart and soul for the AI generation.”

Furrier spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight (right) as a part of a keynote analysis at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can secure and govern AI agents while turning proprietary knowledge and workflows into measurable business value rather than simply maximizing token consumption. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes has matured from a niche orchestration project into the reference platform for major clouds and neoclouds, and enterprises are now standardizing on it. That maturity is what makes it useful for AI, which needs the same control planes, scalable data layers and telemetry the community already worked out for microservices, according to Furrier.

“Kubernetes got boring, which means it’s working,” Furrier said. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world.”

Those lessons now apply to a pressing question: how much freedom enterprises will give AI agents inside real systems. Agents that cause trouble are usually poorly instructed rather than malicious, and the answer lies in context, identity and guardrails, according to Furrier. Perimeter-style security thinking is expected to make a comeback, along with a move away from token consumption as a measure of value and toward tangible business outcomes.

“We’re gonna get back to an era of, ‘Build something, show me what you built, present it for value,'” Furrier said. “If it’s worth something, there’s an exchange for value.”

Stay tuned for the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA.

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 event. Sponsors of theCUBE’s event coverage do not have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. Join theCUBE’s Alumni Trust Network, where technology leaders connect, share intelligence and create opportunities.

Founded by tech visionaries John Furrier and Dave Vellante, SiliconANGLE Media has built a dynamic ecosystem of industry-leading digital media brands that reach 15+ million elite tech professionals. Our new proprietary theCUBE AI Video Cloud is breaking ground in audience interaction, leveraging theCUBEai.com neural network to help technology companies make data-driven decisions and stay at the forefront of industry conversations.

Presented by the Office of Collaborative Learning and Educational Engagement, the webinar is designed for higher education leaders, employers, nonprofit organizations, University of Phoenix faculty, staff, students, alumni and community members. Why experience still matters in an AI-driven workplace

#5499. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5497. Non-deterministic agents break the rules traditional software security was built on

AI agent security has become the critical gating factor for enterprises that want autonomous software doing real work.

Unlike chatbots that answer questions, agents take actions, and every tool or credential they touch widens the potential damage. To that end, Red Hat Inc. has spent the past year building guardrails for that shift, including a sandbox for OpenClaw agents. The complexity lies in the fact that agents break the assumptions traditional software security was built on, according to Joe Fernandes (pictured, right), vice president and general manager of Red Hat AI at Red Hat.

“For forever, we’ve been building software, but that software is deterministic. It does what we program it to do,” Fernandes said. “Agents are different. They’re non-deterministic; you’re giving them a goal. You don’t know what actions they’re going to take to get to that goal.”

Fernandes and Jessica Forrester (left), senior distinguished engineer and chief architect of Red Hat AI at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Red Hat is building layered security for autonomous AI agents through sandboxing, identity management, access controls and enterprise-scale agent management. (* Disclosure below.)

Red Hat learned lessons through its own engineering teams. When it first built an agentic software development life cycle, it handed agents prefetched data and let them touch nothing else, Forrester explained. OpenShell, the open-source agent runtime Nvidia Corp. launched in March with Red Hat as a founding member, let the company loosen that grip safely. The two companies have since expanded their partnership around securing autonomous agents. One approach from Red Hat involves giving agents access to the tools they need while keeping sensitive credentials out of reach.

“With OpenShell, your agent doesn’t ever get any real keys to anything. It gets masked on the way in and then swapped on the way out,” Forrester said. “If something convinces it to give away its keys, it’s not actually giving any real keys away. That really helps you have a little bit more faith in what’s happening inside that agent box.”

OpenShell can also run agents in Kata Containers with their own kernels, inside full virtual machines on OpenShift Virtualization and behind network egress controls, Forrester noted. Red Hat has also detailed kernel-level agent isolation in its platform. Identity comes next, with every agent assigned its own identity and the narrowest set of permissions, Fernandes added.

“It’ll integrate with different identity systems to basically allow you to assign agent identity,” he said. “Then you can authorize what that agent can do — and more importantly, what it can’t.”

Red Hat is now looking beyond individual agents. It is working with OpenAI Group PBC on OpenClaw Enterprise, a project for managing thousands of personal agents at scale, while OpenShell is available in preview in Red Hat AI. For enterprises still weighing AI agent security, the project’s maturity is the moment to watch, Fernandes explained.

“We’re really now approaching that stable milestone,” Fernandes said. “That’s when we feel like, ‘Okay, we’re comfortable enough. We can actually rely on this for enterprise production.'”

Stay tuned for the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA.

(* Disclosure: Red Hat sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Neither Red Hat nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5493. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5492. 10 lawmakers who set records for tenure and age in Congress

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A selection of the longest-serving members of Congress and its oldest record holders, from John Dingell's more than 59 years in the House to Strom Thurmond's Senate exit at 100

John Dingell spent more than 59 years in the House of Representatives. Strom Thurmond was still a senator at age 100. Those two careers sit at the far edges of two different records. Together they mark the outer limits of tenure and age on Capitol Hill.

Length of service and age in office are separate measures. Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, holds the record for the longest service in Congress. He entered the House in December 1955 and left in January 2015. Robert Byrd of West Virginia holds the Senate record, with more than 51 years in that chamber. Thurmond, who represented South Carolina, holds a record of a different kind. He was the oldest person ever to serve in the Senate. Ralph Hall of Texas holds the same distinction in the House. He was 91 when he lost his 2014 primary.

Long tenure matters in Congress because seniority shapes power. Committee chairmanships have traditionally gone to members with the most years on a panel. Jamie Whitten of Mississippi, who served in the House for about 53 years, chaired the House Appropriations Committee. That committee writes the bills that fund the federal government. In the Senate, the post of president pro tempore customarily goes to the longest-serving senator in the majority party. Byrd held that office. So did Daniel Inouye of Hawaii, a Medal of Honor recipient who was president pro tempore when he died in 2012.

Dianne Feinstein of California holds a narrower age distinction. She was the oldest sitting senator when she died in office in September 2023 at 90. She had served in the Senate for about 30 years.

The 10 lawmakers below are a selection of the longest-serving members of Congress and its oldest record holders, not a ranking or a complete list. Some hold records outright. Others are included for the length or shape of their careers. Carl Hayden represented Arizona for more than 56 years in the House and Senate, starting in 1912, the year Arizona became a state. Ted Kennedy held a Massachusetts Senate seat for nearly 47 years. Chuck Grassley of Iowa served in the House from 1975 to 1981 before entering the Senate in January 1981. Each slide covers one career: how it began, how it ended and the record or role that defined it.

John Dingell holds the record for the longest service in the history of Congress. The Michigan Democrat served in the House from December 1955 to January 2015, a span of more than 59 years.

His path to Washington began with a family loss. His father, John Dingell Sr., also served in the House and died in office. The younger Dingell won the seat after his father's death. The seat that carried him to the record had first belonged to his father.

House members face voters every two years. Senators serve six-year terms. Dingell's record rested on winning reelection again and again rather than holding a few long terms. Each of those House races could have ended his career.

The record for congressional service counts total time in Congress, including years in both chambers. Dingell spent his entire congressional career in the House. That sets him apart from Robert Byrd, the West Virginia Democrat whose total he overtook. Byrd's total combined his years in the House with his longer run in the Senate. Dingell surpassed that combined figure while serving in one chamber alone.

Dingell passed Byrd's total in 2013. He stayed in the House after setting the new mark. Each term he served after that point extended a record no other member of Congress had reached.

His tenure also carried him past the record for service in the House alone. Jamie Whitten of Mississippi had held that distinction until Dingell surpassed him. That left Dingell holding two marks at once: the longest service in the House and the longest service in Congress overall.

Dingell left the House in January 2015. He died in February 2019.

Robert Byrd of West Virginia holds the record for the longest service in the history of the U.S. Senate. The Democrat took his Senate seat in January 1959 and held it for more than 51 years, until his death on June 28, 2010, at age 92.

Byrd's congressional career started in the other chamber. He won a seat in the House of Representatives and served there from 1953 to 1959. He represented West Virginia in both chambers. He moved directly to the Senate in 1959, the year his House tenure ended.

Those six House years count toward a second kind of record: total time in Congress across both chambers. The longest-serving senator and the longest-serving member of Congress are separate titles. One lawmaker does not always hold both.

For decades, the benchmark for combined congressional service belonged to Carl Hayden of Arizona, who sat in the House and then the Senate. Byrd's House and Senate years together eventually passed Hayden's total, giving the West Virginian the combined record as well.

That combined mark did not last. John Dingell, a Michigan Democrat who served only in the House, passed Byrd's total in 2013. Dingell's record rests on House service alone. It did not affect Byrd's Senate record. The two records measure different things.

Byrd also served as president pro tempore of the Senate. Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution creates the office. The president pro tempore presides over the chamber when the vice president is absent. The officeholder is third in the line of presidential succession, after the vice president and the speaker of the House. The Presidential Succession Act of 1947 sets that order.

Byrd's Senate career did not end with a retirement or an election defeat. He was still a sitting senator when he died. His Senate record therefore covers one continuous tenure that began in 1959 and ended in 2010.

Strom Thurmond of South Carolina is the oldest person ever to serve in the U.S. Senate. He retired from the chamber in January 2003 at age 100.

Thurmond was born on December 5, 1902. He was born in the first years of the 20th century, and his Senate service continued into the 21st.

He took an unusual route into the Senate. He first won the seat in 1954 through a write-in campaign. A write-in candidate's name does not appear on the printed ballot. Voters who want to back that candidate must write the name in themselves. Thurmond won the seat that way.

His first stint in the chamber was brief. Thurmond resigned his seat in 1956. He then ran for the same seat in a special election. A special election fills a vacancy outside the regular election calendar. Thurmond won that race and returned to the Senate.

After that return, Thurmond held the South Carolina seat for the rest of his career. His tenure ran through the second half of the 20th century and ended with his retirement in January 2003.

Thurmond's record measures age in office, not length of service. It rests on how old he was while he held the seat, not on how many years he spent in the chamber. That makes it a separate distinction from the tenure records held by other members of Congress.

Thurmond died in June 2003, the same year he left the Senate.

Jamie Whitten, a Mississippi Democrat, held the record for the longest service in the history of the House of Representatives until John Dingell surpassed him. Whitten entered the House in 1941 and left in January 1995. His tenure lasted about 53 years.

His House career began in the same year the U.S. entered World War II. It ended in January 1995, when the 104th Congress convened. That Congress gave Republicans a House majority for the first time since the 1950s. Whitten spent the entire span in a single chamber.

Franklin D. Roosevelt was in the White House when Whitten arrived. Bill Clinton held the office when he left.

Every House seat goes before voters every two years. Holding the seat that long meant winning his Mississippi district again and again over more than half a century.

Whitten chaired the House Appropriations Committee. The panel writes the annual spending bills that keep federal agencies and programs running. Its power traces to Article I, Section 9 of the Constitution. That clause bars any money from being drawn from the Treasury except through appropriations made by law.

The House traditionally handed committee gavels to the members with the longest continuous service on each panel. Whitten's decades on Appropriations put him at the front of that line.

Whitten's mark counted years in the lower chamber alone. Some lawmakers built longer careers by serving in both the House and the Senate. Carl Hayden of Arizona sat in the House from 1912 to 1927 and in the Senate from 1927 to 1969. His combined service exceeded Whitten's House tenure. Robert Byrd also served in both chambers, moving from the House to the Senate in 1959.

Whitten's House record eventually passed to John Dingell, a Michigan Democrat who entered the chamber in December 1955. Dingell moved past Whitten's total while still in office and became the longest-serving House member in history.

Carl Hayden represented Arizona in Congress for more than 56 years, serving first in the House and then in the Senate. The Arizona Democrat held the record for the longest congressional service in U.S. history until Robert Byrd passed him.

Hayden's congressional career began in 1912, the year Arizona became a state. Arizona entered the Union on February 14, 1912, as the 48th state. Hayden became the new state's first member of the House of Representatives.

He served in the House from 1912 until 1927. House members face voters every two years. Holding the seat for that long meant winning one election after another.

In 1927, Hayden moved across the Capitol to the Senate. He won the seat in the 1926 election. He held it until 1969. Senators serve six-year terms. After the switch, he faced Arizona voters far less often than he had as a House member.

His Senate career came after a major change in how senators were chosen. The 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, gave voters the power to elect senators directly. Before that, the Constitution left the choice to state legislatures. Every Senate term Hayden served fell under the newer system of popular election.

Hayden's exit from Congress came by choice. He did not seek reelection in 1968. He left the Senate when his final term ended in January 1969.

His combined total in both chambers came to more than 56 years. That figure stood as the benchmark for congressional longevity until Byrd's service in the House and Senate went past it.

Hayden's record depended on time in both chambers rather than either one alone. Byrd, who later took the record, followed the same route. He served in the House from 1953 to 1959 before moving to the Senate. Daniel Inouye of Hawaii also started in the House, in 1959, and moved to the Senate in 1963.

Daniel Inouye represented Hawaii in Congress from 1959 until his death on December 17, 2012, first in the House and then in the Senate. A World War II Medal of Honor recipient, he was serving as president pro tempore of the Senate when he died.

Inouye entered the House in 1959, the year Hawaii became the 50th U.S. state. He was the first Japanese American to serve in Congress. He stayed in the House until 1963, when he moved to the Senate.

He held the Senate seat for the rest of his life. Senators serve six-year terms, compared with two-year terms for House members. Inouye was still in office when he died in December 2012.

His military record came before his political career. During World War II, Inouye fought with the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. That U.S. Army unit was made up largely of Japanese American soldiers. He lost his right arm in combat in Italy in April 1945.

The Army first awarded him the Distinguished Service Cross for those actions. In 2000, President Bill Clinton upgraded the award to the Medal of Honor. Inouye was one of 22 Asian American veterans honored at that White House ceremony. The Medal of Honor is the highest U.S. military decoration for valor in combat.

In the Senate, Inouye sat on the select committee that investigated the Watergate scandal in 1973. He chaired the Senate select committee on the Iran-Contra affair in 1987. From 2009 until his death, he chaired the Senate Appropriations Committee, which handles that chamber's spending bills.

The president pro tempore is a Senate office created by the U.S. Constitution. Its holder can preside over the chamber when the vice president is absent. The office ranks third in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president and the speaker of the House. Inouye took the post in 2010, after Robert Byrd died, and held it until his death.

In 2013, President Barack Obama awarded Inouye the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously.

Ted Kennedy held a U.S. Senate seat from Massachusetts for nearly 47 years. The Democrat entered the Senate in 1962 and kept the seat until he died on August 25, 2009.

Senators serve six-year terms. Holding one seat for nearly 47 years meant Kennedy had to win reelection from Massachusetts voters repeatedly over the course of his career.

Kennedy's Senate service ended with his death in office. He did not retire from the seat.

He was the brother of John F. Kennedy and Robert F. Kennedy.

Dianne Feinstein was the oldest sitting senator when she died in office on September 29, 2023, at age 90. The California Democrat had served in the Senate for about 30 years.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933. She joined the Senate in November 1992.

Her age distinction was relative, not all-time. It compared her with the senators serving alongside her when she died. It did not compare her with every senator in the chamber's history.

She held the seat until her death. Her Senate career did not end through retirement or an election defeat.

Her place among these lawmakers rests on age in office rather than on length of service. Her Senate tenure was shorter than the multi-decade records held by several other members of Congress.

Ralph Hall of Texas is the oldest person ever to serve in the U.S. House of Representatives. Born on May 3, 1923, he lost his 2014 primary at age 91.

Hall's House career began in 1981. He took his seat as a Democrat representing a Texas district.

He did not stay in that party. Later in his House tenure, Hall switched his affiliation and became a Republican. As a result, he served his Texas constituents under two different party labels.

His age record rests on how the Constitution treats House service. Article I sets a minimum age of 25 for representatives but no maximum age. A representative must also have been a U.S. citizen for at least seven years and must live in the state he or she represents. Article I also sets two-year terms. Every member must face voters again at each election to keep the seat.

Congress has no term limits either. In 1995, the Supreme Court ruled in U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton that states cannot impose term limits on their members of Congress. A representative who stays in office into old age has done so by winning one election after another.

Hall's run ended in 2014. A primary is the contest in which a party's voters choose its nominee for the general election. Losing his meant Hall would not appear on the November ballot as his party's candidate for the seat.

He served out the rest of his term. His tenure ended in January 2015, when the new Congress convened and his successor was sworn in. The 20th Amendment sets noon on January 3 as the start of each new Congress, unless lawmakers pass a law choosing a different day.

Hall's mark is a record for age, not for length of service. John Dingell of Michigan holds the record for the longest House tenure. Hall's record also applies to the House alone. The Senate keeps its own separate mark for the oldest person to serve in that chamber.

Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican, served in the U.S. House from 1975 to 1981 and entered the Senate in January 1981. His time in Congress spans both chambers.

Grassley was born on September 17, 1933. That is the same year Dianne Feinstein of California was born.

He began representing Iowa in the House of Representatives in 1975. His House tenure ran through 1981.

The switch to the Senate came at the start of that year. Grassley took his Senate seat in January 1981.

His path from the House to the Senate matches the careers of Robert Byrd, Carl Hayden and Daniel Inouye. Each of them also served in both chambers.

#5490. AI operations expand to Kubernetes upgrades as IT teams do more with less

AI operations are moving out of the slide deck and into the platform itself. Hiring freezes and smaller teams are colliding with growing workloads, so enterprises now expect the infrastructure layer to investigate, plan and help fix problems.

Kubernetes platforms are among the first places that shift is landing. Red Hat Inc. launched OpenShift 5 this week, the platform’s first major version in seven years, with Model Context Protocol servers, guardrails and agent skills built into the stack. Customers’ expectations of the platform have changed enough to justify a new version number, according to Mike Barrett (pictured, left), vice president and general manager of hybrid platforms at Red Hat.

“We started putting in guardrails. We started putting in agent skills, and now you can really have an agentic experience with the platform,” Barrett said. “The platform itself can actually do things for you. It can notice what’s running.”

Barrett and Ju Lim (pictured, right), senior manager of product management at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how OpenShift 5 builds AI into upgrades, troubleshooting and day-to-day operations. (* Disclosure below.)

On paper, upgrades look like routine, predictable work. In practice, a single cluster can run hundreds of applications, each with its own dependencies, release notes and Kubernetes version requirements. OpenShift 5 uses AI to sort through all of that and produce an upgrade plan, Barrett explained.

“We have customers that sometimes plan this out in weeks and months,” Lim said. “Now, through what Mike was just saying, we have a way where, through a single click, you can actually generate an AI plan that actually does all that risk analysis and assessment for you.”

Troubleshooting gets the same treatment. OpenShift 5 pulls in telemetry, logs and Kubernetes resource metadata to investigate problems and suggest fixes, according to Lim. Every action is opt-in, and a human operator stays in control. Fully autonomous troubleshooting and agentic updates remain in technology preview, according to Virtualization Review. Red Hat’s own site reliability engineering team offers an early test case.

“We run OpenShift as a managed service, and they’re seeing anywhere between an 8x and 10x time improvement to find the root cause of issues,” Barrett said.

Security is adding urgency. A surge of software vulnerabilities and exploits has cut the time between disclosure and attack from days to hours, according to Barrett. Customers want help moving older applications faster, and running existing virtual machines in Kubernetes clusters is part of Red Hat’s answer.

“We felt that really emphasized a number change,” Barrett said. “How people want to work with the platform is completely different now, and so we needed a major number.”

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA:
