#5481. The debt ceiling explained: 10 things to know about the U.S. borrowing limit

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The debt ceiling explained in 10 parts, from its 1917 origins and extraordinary measures to the X-date, credit downgrades and proposed workarounds

The U.S. government puts a legal cap on its own borrowing, even though Congress has already passed the spending and tax laws that make the borrowing necessary. That cap is the debt ceiling. The gap between what lawmakers have committed the country to pay and what the Treasury Department may borrow is the source of recurring fiscal standoffs in Congress.

The debt ceiling is also called the debt limit. It is a dollar figure set in federal law. Once total federal debt reaches it, the Treasury cannot borrow more until Congress raises or suspends the cap. Tax revenue keeps arriving, and obligations under existing programs keep coming due. What disappears is the ability to cover the difference by borrowing.

The stakes reach well beyond Congress. The central question in every standoff is what happens if the U.S. defaults, meaning it cannot pay all of its obligations on time. Treasury securities are held by investors, banks and governments around the world. Each deadline draws attention far outside the U.S.

The U.S. credit rating has also changed in recent years. All three major rating agencies have lowered the country from their top grade: Standard & Poor's in 2011, Fitch Ratings in 2023 and Moody's $MCO in 2025. The first two downgrades followed debt limit fights. Fitch listed repeated standoffs among its governance concerns.

This is the debt ceiling explained from the ground up. The first slides cover what the cap is, what it does not do and how it grew out of a World War I-era borrowing law. A fourth slide looks at which kinds of federal debt count against the limit. Two more explain the extraordinary measures Treasury uses to buy time and the X $TWTR-date, when that time would run out.

The rest of the piece traces three recent turning points: the 2011 Budget Control Act, the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act and the 2025 increase under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. It closes with proposed alternatives, from a legal argument built on the 14th Amendment to a platinum coin to abolishing the limit outright. None of those ideas has been tested.

The debt ceiling is a cap, written into federal law by Congress, on the total amount of money the Treasury Department may borrow. Only a new law, passed by both chambers of Congress and signed by the president, can change that figure.

The statute sits in Title 31 of the U.S. Code, at section 3101. It sets a single dollar figure for the government's borrowing as a whole. It does not set separate caps for individual programs or agencies.

Borrowing fills the gap between what the federal government collects and what it pays out. Treasury raises that money by selling securities to investors. In any year the government runs a deficit, it has to borrow to cover the difference.

The debt limit runs on a separate track from the budget. Congress decides how much agencies can spend through appropriations bills, which fund the government one fiscal year at a time. Programs such as Social Security and Medicare pay benefits under permanent law and do not need yearly approval. Tax law determines how much revenue comes in. The debt ceiling is a separate vote on whether Treasury may borrow to cover the result of those decisions.

The House has at times tried to link the two tracks. Under a procedural rule known as the Gephardt rule, adopting a budget resolution automatically produced a matching debt limit measure in the House. The chamber has dropped and restored that rule several times.

Changing the limit takes ordinary legislation. A debt limit bill can move on its own or inside a larger package. In the Senate, a standalone bill can face a filibuster, which takes 60 votes to end. A budget reconciliation bill can pass the Senate with a simple majority.

Congress has two main ways to change the cap. It can raise it, replacing the old dollar figure with a higher one. Or it can suspend it, setting the limit aside until a fixed date. Either way, the new room to borrow lasts only until debt catches up with the higher figure or the suspension period ends.

Raising the debt ceiling does not approve a single dollar of new federal spending. The obligations it covers come from spending and tax laws Congress has already passed. The limit decides only whether Treasury may borrow to pay for them.

The distinction comes from the order in which Congress makes its decisions. Spending choices are made elsewhere in the legislative process. Congress passes annual appropriations bills that fund agencies such as the Defense Department. It also keeps permanent laws on the books that set benefits for programs including Social Security and Medicare. Those programs pay out without a yearly vote.

Revenue is set the same way. Tax laws determine how much money flows into Treasury from income, payroll and corporate taxes. When those laws together call for more spending than taxes bring in, the government runs a deficit. Treasury covers that gap by selling securities to investors.

The debt limit enters only at that final step. It does not change how much an agency may spend or how large a benefit payment is. It governs whether Treasury can raise the cash to honor commitments already written into law.

A common comparison is a household credit card. Raising the debt limit resembles paying off charges already made on the card, not approving new purchases. The analogy has limits. A household that hits its card limit can stop buying things. The federal government's obligations keep arriving under laws that remain in force until Congress changes them.

Those obligations span the full range of federal activity. They include salaries for military personnel and civilian employees, payments to Social Security recipients, tax refunds and interest owed to holders of Treasury securities.

The power behind both sides of this arrangement sits with Congress. Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution gives Congress the authority to borrow money on the credit of the U.S., along with authority over taxes and spending. The debt limit is a separate statutory vote layered on top of those earlier decisions.

Future borrowing is shaped through the budget itself. Changing tax rates or reducing appropriations alters future deficits. Declining to raise the limit does not erase obligations that already exist.

The U.S. debt limit traces back to the Second Liberty Bond Act of 1917. That wartime law let the Treasury borrow to pay for World War I without returning to Congress to approve every bond issue. The single overall cap that exists today came later, through the Public Debt Act of 1939.

Before 1917, Congress typically authorized federal borrowing one issue at a time. A law would spell out the purpose of a loan and often its terms, such as the amount, the interest rate and the maturity. That approach suited a federal government that borrowed only occasionally and in modest amounts.

World War I changed the scale. The U.S. entered the war in April 1917. The cost of raising an army and supplying allies far outran tax revenue. Congress needed a faster way to raise money than passing a new bill for each sale of bonds.

The Second Liberty Bond Act, passed that September, gave Treasury Secretary William Gibbs McAdoo broad authority to issue bonds and other debt within limits Congress set. The government sold these Liberty Bonds directly to the public through large national campaigns. Ordinary households bought them alongside banks and businesses.

The 1917 law did not create one overall ceiling. It set caps on particular kinds of borrowing, and Congress adjusted those separate limits by category in the years that followed. The arrangement moved routine borrowing decisions from lawmakers to the Treasury. Congress still decided how much could be borrowed within each category.

The Public Debt Act of 1939 replaced that patchwork. It folded the separate limits into a single aggregate limit on federal debt. That change gave the Treasury freedom to choose the mix of bills, notes and bonds it issued, as long as the total stayed under the cap. The modern debt ceiling grew directly out of that 1939 framework.

That history explains why the ceiling works as a cap on total borrowing rather than a vote on individual loans. Lawmakers have raised, extended or suspended the limit many times since 1939, but the basic structure set that year remains in place.

Nearly all federal debt counts toward the debt limit. That covers money the government owes to outside investors and money it owes to its own trust funds, such as Social Security. The ceiling applies to the combined total, not to either piece on its own.

The first piece is debt held by the public. Most of it consists of marketable Treasury securities sold at auction. Treasury bills mature in a year or less. Treasury notes mature in two to 10 years, and Treasury bonds mature in 20 or 30 years. Savings bonds sold to households also fall into this category.

The buyers of that debt range widely. They include individuals, banks, pension funds, mutual funds, state and local governments, foreign governments and the Federal Reserve. Securities held by the Federal Reserve still count as debt held by the public, even though the Fed is part of the broader federal system.

The second piece is intragovernmental debt. Some federal programs collect dedicated revenue, such as payroll taxes, and credit it to trust funds. When a trust fund takes in more than it pays out, federal law directs it to invest the surplus in special-issue Treasury securities. These securities are not sold on the open market. Holders include the Social Security trust funds, Medicare's Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, the Civil Service Retirement and Disability Fund and the Military Retirement Fund.

Because both pieces count, the limit can bind even when debt held by the public sits well below it. Debt held by the public is the measure the Congressional Budget Office typically uses in its budget projections. The figure that matters for the ceiling, known as debt subject to limit, is larger.

The balance between the two pieces shifts over time. When Social Security collects more in payroll taxes than it pays in benefits, its trust funds buy new special-issue securities. That pushes debt subject to limit higher even if Treasury borrows nothing new from investors.

The reverse happens when a trust fund draws down its balance. The fund redeems its securities to pay benefits, and Treasury generally borrows from the public to raise that cash. Intragovernmental debt falls and debt held by the public rises. The total counted against the limit changes little.

The word nearly matters. Treasury reports debt subject to limit in its Monthly Statement of the Public Debt, and that figure differs slightly from total public debt outstanding. The gap comes from small technical adjustments, such as accounting for the discount at which Treasury bills are sold.

Extraordinary measures are accounting steps the Treasury Department uses to keep paying the government's bills for a period after federal debt reaches the statutory limit. They create temporary room under the cap. They do not raise the limit or give Treasury any new borrowing authority.

The tools work by reducing the amount of debt that counts against the limit. A large share of federal debt is owed to government trust funds and retirement accounts, which hold special Treasury securities. When Treasury stops issuing new securities to some of those funds, the debt subject to the limit falls or holds steady. That opens space to sell securities to the public and keep paying obligations.

The Thrift Savings Plan's G Fund is one of the main tools. The Thrift Savings Plan is the retirement savings plan for federal employees and members of the uniformed services. Its G Fund invests in special-issue Treasury securities. During a standoff, Treasury can suspend new investments in the G Fund.

The Civil Service Retirement and Disability Fund is another source of headroom. That fund pays pensions to retired federal civilian workers. Treasury can suspend new investments in it as well. Federal law also allows Treasury to redeem some of the fund's existing holdings ahead of schedule during these periods.

The process has a formal starting point. The Treasury secretary declares a debt issuance suspension period. That declaration is the legal trigger for using the retirement fund measures. Treasury notifies Congress when it begins.

Two smaller tools sit alongside the retirement funds. Treasury can suspend reinvestment of the dollar balance in the Exchange Stabilization Fund, which it uses for operations in currency markets. It can also halt sales of State and Local Government Series securities, which state and local governments buy to manage the proceeds of their own bond sales.

Federal law requires the affected funds to be made whole afterward. Once the limit is raised or suspended, Treasury issues the securities that were held back. It also credits the interest those securities would have earned. The restoration is designed so the funds do not lose money because of the maneuver.

The measures are finite. How much headroom they provide depends on the balances in the funds involved and on the pace of the government's tax receipts and spending. Once they are used up, only Treasury's remaining cash stands between the government and missed payments.

The X $TWTR-date is the day the Treasury Department would run out of both cash and extraordinary measures. After that point, it could no longer pay all of the federal government's obligations on time. The X-date is a projection, not a fixed deadline, and it moves as money flows in and out of the Treasury.

The X-date is a later and more consequential point than the day the debt limit is reached. Once debt hits the ceiling, Treasury can keep paying bills for a period by drawing down its cash balance and using accounting steps. The X-date marks the point at which those resources are gone.

No one can pin down the day in advance. It depends on how much the government collects in taxes and how much it pays out, and both totals swing from week to week. Federal cash flows are uneven. Large outflows such as Social Security benefits, Medicare payments, military pay and veterans' benefits cluster at particular points in the month. Tax receipts also arrive in bursts rather than at a steady pace.

The calendar plays a large role. Individual income tax payments due in mid-April can lift Treasury's cash position sharply. Quarterly estimated tax payments due in June add another inflow. A stronger or weaker tax season than forecast can move the X-date earlier or later.

Treasury keeps its operating cash in the Treasury General Account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It reports daily receipts, outlays and the account balance in the Daily Treasury Statement. Forecasters use those reports to track how fast the cushion is shrinking.

Three sources have produced estimates during past standoffs. The Treasury secretary has sent letters to Congress warning when the department expects to exhaust its measures. The Congressional Budget Office and the Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, have published their own projections. Those estimates have shifted when tax receipts and spending ran higher or lower than expected. They have sometimes been presented as a window of possible dates rather than a single day.

The federal government has never reached the X-date. What would follow has therefore never been tested. Treasury would still have cash arriving each day, but not enough to cover every payment due. That gap would force decisions about delaying payments to bondholders, beneficiaries, contractors or federal employees. No law sets out an order for making those choices.

The 2011 debt ceiling standoff ended when President Barack Obama signed the Budget Control Act on Aug. 2, 2011. Three days later, on Aug. 5, Standard & Poor's lowered the U.S. credit rating from AAA to AA+. It was the first time S&P had ever downgraded the country.

The dispute ran for months. Republicans won control of the House in the 2010 midterm elections, while Democrats kept the Senate and the White House. The two sides negotiated over whether an increase in the borrowing limit should be paired with deficit reduction, and on what terms. Talks stretched into the summer while Treasury relied on extraordinary measures to keep paying the government's bills.

Treasury had identified Aug. 2 as the day its borrowing authority would run out. The deal was signed on that same day, leaving almost no margin before the government risked missing payments.

The Budget Control Act raised the debt limit in stages. It also set caps on discretionary spending that ran through fiscal 2021. A third piece created the Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction, a panel of 12 lawmakers split evenly between the two parties. Its job was to propose further deficit reduction for Congress to vote on.

The law built in a penalty for failure. If Congress did not enact a committee plan, automatic across-the-board spending cuts known as sequestration would take effect. The committee announced in November 2011 that it could not reach an agreement. Sequestration began in March 2013.

S&P based its decision on two main concerns. It judged that the deficit plan fell short of what would be needed to stabilize the country's medium-term debt path. It also pointed to the brinkmanship of the standoff as a sign that U.S. policymaking had become less stable and less predictable. S&P paired the AA+ rating with a negative outlook, signaling that a further cut was possible.

AAA is the top grade on S&P's scale, and AA+ sits one notch below it. The other two major agencies did not follow in 2011. Moody's $MCO kept its Aaa rating but assigned a negative outlook, and Fitch affirmed its AAA rating. That left the U.S. with a split rating among the big three agencies for years afterward.

Markets reacted unevenly. U.S. stocks fell sharply in the first trading days after the downgrade. Demand for Treasury securities held up, though, and Treasury yields declined.

The Fiscal Responsibility Act, signed June 3, 2023, ended that year's debt ceiling standoff by suspending the borrowing limit until Jan. 1, 2025. The law also set caps on federal spending. Fitch Ratings then lowered the U.S. credit rating from AAA to AA+ on Aug. 1, 2023.

The act came out of negotiations between President Joe Biden and House Speaker Kevin McCarthy. The House passed the bill on May 31, 2023. The Senate approved it on June 1, and Biden signed it into law on June 3.

The act did not lift the cap to a new dollar amount. Instead, it switched the cap off for a set period. That approach is called a suspension, and it works differently from a straightforward increase. An increase writes a higher number into law. A suspension removes the number entirely until a chosen date.

While a suspension is in effect, the Treasury Department can borrow what it needs to cover the government's obligations without running into a fixed ceiling. When the suspension ends, the limit does not return to its old level. It resets to the amount of debt outstanding on that date.

That reset folds any borrowing done during the suspension into the new ceiling. On paper, a suspension looks like a pause. In practice, it works as an increase. Lawmakers avoid voting on a specific dollar figure, yet the limit still rises by whatever the government borrowed in the interim.

The spending caps applied to discretionary spending — the portion of the budget Congress sets through annual appropriations bills. The act set those caps for fiscal years 2024 and 2025.

Fitch had placed the U.S. on rating watch negative in May 2023, while the negotiations were still underway. Its downgrade arrived after the standoff was over. In explaining the decision, Fitch pointed to an erosion of governance, including the repeated standoffs over the debt limit. The agency also cited expected fiscal deterioration and a high and growing government debt burden.

At the time of the Fitch decision, Moody's $MCO still rated the U.S. Aaa, its highest grade.

A rating of AA+ sits one notch below AAA and remains investment grade. The downgrade did not signal a default. It reflected Fitch's judgment that the U.S. no longer met its standard for the highest rating it assigns.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, raised the federal debt limit by $5 trillion, to roughly $41.1 trillion. The increase restored Treasury's borrowing room after the cap had returned in January 2025 at roughly $36.1 trillion.

That January figure was not a number lawmakers chose. The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 had suspended the limit until Jan. 1, 2025. When the suspension ended, the ceiling came back at the level of debt then outstanding. The limit and the debt were the same amount. Treasury had no fresh capacity to issue new debt from the moment the cap returned.

Treasury began using extraordinary measures in January 2025 to keep meeting the government's obligations. Those accounting steps postponed a breach but did not add any room under the cap. A lasting fix required Congress to pass a new law.

That law was a broad tax and spending package. It extended individual tax cuts first enacted in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, alongside many other fiscal changes. Congress passed it through budget reconciliation. That procedure lets the Senate approve certain budget legislation with a simple majority. Reconciliation bills cannot be filibustered. As a result, the debt limit increase did not need the 60 votes most Senate bills require to move forward.

The 2025 change was an increase, not a suspension. A suspension sets a date when the limit comes back. An increase sets a dollar amount instead. The next deadline therefore depends on how fast federal borrowing climbs toward roughly $41.1 trillion, not on a date written into the statute.

The increase came after another change to the U.S. credit rating. Moody's $MCO lowered its U.S. rating from Aaa to Aa1 in May 2025. Moody's had rated U.S. government debt at Aaa since 1917. It had also been the last of the three major agencies to keep the U.S. at its top grade.

Three main alternatives to the debt ceiling have been proposed: invoking the 14th Amendment, minting a high-value platinum coin and repealing the cap entirely. None has been put into practice. Each remains a proposal rather than settled law.

The constitutional argument rests on Section 4 of the 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868 after the Civil War. Its text says the validity of the public debt of the U.S., authorized by law, shall not be questioned. The same section bars the U.S. and the states from paying any debt incurred in aid of insurrection against the country. Supporters of the 14th Amendment approach argue that a statutory cap cannot force the government to miss payments on debt Congress has already authorized. In their view, the limit would become unenforceable once Treasury could no longer meet those obligations.

No court has ruled on that argument. The amendment's text does not mention a borrowing cap. The statute that sets the debt limit remains in force.

The platinum coin idea comes from a provision of federal law, 31 U.S.C. 5112(k). That section gives the Treasury secretary authority to mint platinum coins and leaves their specifications to the secretary's discretion. Proponents argue this would let Treasury strike a single coin with a very high face value. Under the proposal, Treasury would deposit the coin at the Federal Reserve. Treasury keeps its main operating cash account, the Treasury General Account, at the Fed. It would then spend the resulting balance instead of issuing new debt. Treasury has never minted such a coin.

Abolishing the limit is the third option. The debt ceiling exists in statute, so Congress could repeal it through ordinary legislation. Borrowing would then follow from the spending and tax laws Congress passes, without a separate vote on the total amount the government owes.

Denmark offers a point of comparison. The country has a statutory debt limit, but it is set high enough that it does not bind.

The U.S. has followed a different path. Congress has kept its limit and adjusted it over time through increases and suspensions.

#5480. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5478. Western Sydney International Airport Opens After Bechtel-Led Delivery Program Completes Major Construction Works Seven Months Early

Australia's first major greenfield international airport in more than 50 years delivered ahead of schedule: a role model for future infrastructure delivery in Australia

SYDNEY, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport (WSI) opened to passengers on October 25, 2026, following a design, construction, and commissioning program led by Western Sydney Airport Corporation with Bechtel Australia as Delivery Partner that finished months ahead of schedule. The opening marks a new era of aviation, trade, and economic activity for Western Sydney and Australia.

Jetstar operated the airport's first commercial passenger service, flying from WSI to the Gold Coast. Passenger operations follow the start of freight services in July and cap 15 years of planning, seven years of construction, and a year of testing and operational readiness.

"I offer my warm congratulations to our partner, Western Sydney Airport Corporation, our contractors, and all the colleagues and partners who have come together to make this project such a success," said Darren Mort President of Infrastructure and Executive Director at Bechtel. "WSI shows what the integrated model can achieve when a customer, delivery partner, and contractors work as one team around a clear vision. Together, we transformed a 1,780-hectare greenfield site into a modern international airport, months ahead of schedule."

Since 2018, Bechtel has served as Delivery Partner to Western Sydney Airport Corporation, the company responsible for building and operating WSI. Under this model, Bechtel:

The program combined large-scale engineering with new approaches to sustainability and technology. It delivered Australia's largest earthworks program and reused nearly 6 million tonnes of sandstone from Sydney tunnelling projects that would otherwise have gone to landfill. More than 60 software platforms were integrated into one operating environment covering passenger processing, security, retail, and office systems. A 4.5-megawatt solar system, all-electric heating, and rainwater harvesting are built into the airport. And the new terminal includes extensive innovative elements, from the integrated domestic/international check-in area, a state-of-the art baggage system, and departure/arrival gates able to be used for both domestic and international flights.

The airport is designed to initially serve up to 10 million passengers a year, with capacity to expand as demand grows. It has already helped catalyze AU$19 billion in surrounding infrastructure investment and is projected to contribute AU$23.9 billion to Australia's gross domestic product by 2060.

Building on Bechtel's Commitment to Australia

"Today marks years of hard work, collaboration, and commitment from thousands of people, including more than 330 Bechtel colleagues across design, engineering, procurement, and project delivery," said Richard Freer, Managing Director of Bechtel's Public Infrastructure Business in Australia. "Excellent project set up, led by the Federal Infrastructure Department, strong front-end planning, disciplined project controls, and new ways of integrating complex systems kept multiple contractors and interconnected packages moving towards the same completion date. That's how we finished ahead of the schedule set back in 2018. Just as important, more than half of the workforce came from Western Sydney, so this airport was built by the community it now serves."

Bechtel has been serving Australian communities and customers for more than 70 years with projects spanning airports, rail, mines, mineral processing facilities, LNG installations, refineries, chemical plants, power stations, and telecommunications infrastructure. At peak construction on WSI, the project team brought together around 4,000 people; across the full construction period, more than 11,000 people worked on the project, with more than half drawn from Western Sydney. The program also engaged more than 360 local businesses and exceeded its workforce participation targets for local, diverse, First Nations and learner workers.

WSI is Australia's new 24-hour global gateway, providing domestic, international, and freight services, supporting Western Sydney's long-term growth and Australia's future aviation capacity.

Bechtel is a trusted engineering, construction, procurement, and project management partner to industry and government. Differentiated by the quality of our people and our relentless drive to deliver the most successful outcomes, we align our capabilities to our customers' objectives to create a lasting positive impact. Since 1898, we have helped customers complete more than 25,000 projects in 160 countries on all seven continents that have created jobs, grown economies, improved the resiliency of the world's infrastructure, increased access to energy, resources and vital services, and made the world a safer, cleaner place.

Bechtel serves the Energy; Infrastructure; Manufacturing & Technology; Mining & Metals; and Nuclear, Security & Environmental markets. Our services span from initial planning and investment through start-up and operations.

#5477. Financial institutions confront the complexities of scaling AI

AI in financial services is moving beyond the pilot phase as banks, capital markets firms, mortgage lenders and other organizations begin deploying the technology more broadly. The challenge is shifting toward managing AI responsibly at scale while meeting strict requirements for security, compliance and customer trust.

The AWS Financial Services Symposium highlighted that transition in May. As financial institutions expand their use of AI, they have opportunities to test new applications without committing to large-scale deployments, according to Scott Mullins, former general manager of AWS Worldwide Financial Services at Amazon Web Services Inc.

“You can spin this stuff up really quickly; you can experiment with it,” he said during the symposium. “You can show that it actually achieves the things that you want to achieve within specific policy guidelines and frameworks, and you can actually evaluate whether that governance is holding.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s ongoing coverage of the AWS Financial Services Symposium. (* Disclosure below.)

Moving AI from experimentation into production requires financial institutions to address a different set of challenges. Beyond demonstrating that the technology works, organizations must establish the governance and operational safeguards needed to support AI across regulated business processes, according to Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst for application development at theCUBE Research.

“Our AppDev research shows that 92% of organizations now integrate AI into at least one stage of the software delivery lifecycle, yet only about one-third have established the governance, security, and operational maturity required for production-scale AI,” he said. “In banking, capital markets and insurance, the gap is even more pronounced because compliance, explainability, and customer trust are non-negotiable. The next phase of AI adoption will be defined less by model performance and more by platforms that embed policy controls, auditability and security into AI-enabled workflows while improving customer experiences and operational efficiency.”

Infosys Ltd. is addressing those requirements through its AI platform, which incorporates safeguards and controls intended to help financial institutions deploy AI while managing risk, according to Rajaram R.K., vice president and head of sales for financial services at Infosys.

“It has the securities [and] it has the guardrails. It has the token economics … all the capabilities that an organization would need,” he told theCUBE.

Financial institutions face stringent regulatory requirements, making security, auditability and recovery essential to their operations. As banks, insurers and capital markets firms expand their use of AI, those requirements take on additional importance, particularly when automated systems begin influencing business decisions. Despite these challenges, financial institutions are among the sectors leading the way in AI adoption.

“The organizations that treat AI as a regulated business capability, not simply a technology initiative, will be best positioned to accelerate innovation while maintaining resilience and meeting evolving regulatory expectations,” Nashawaty said.

Applying those established risk-management practices to AI requires organizations to consider how automated systems access data, make decisions and operate within existing policies. The challenge is extending governance and operational controls to AI-enabled workflows without undermining the efficiency and innovation those systems are intended to deliver.

Financial institutions are finding practical applications for AI in customer service and employee productivity. At New York Life Insurance Co., reducing routine manual work is giving employees more time to provide personalized service and respond proactively to customers’ needs, according to Kristina Welke, vice president at New York Life.

“We really felt there was a lot of opportunity to support them, remove the manual work they do every day, enable them to provide that consultative support, be proactive versus reactive,” she told theCUBE.

Fifth Third Bank is using conversational AI to improve customer interactions and reduce average call-handling time. The bank is using Amazon Connect to support its customer-service operations, according to Kevin Anderson, product manager on the AI transformation team at Fifth Third Bank.

“Amazon Connect really lays the foundation as it solves for not only messaging but voice as well, allows for AI and automation,” he explained.

For financial institutions, scaling AI depends in part on modernizing the infrastructure that supports data-intensive workloads. Cloud platforms can provide the flexibility to deploy new capabilities while maintaining access to existing systems, making modernization an important consideration as organizations expand their AI initiatives.

Mortgage lender PennyMac Financial Services recently expanded its agreement with Amazon Web Services to accelerate modernization of its proprietary mortgage servicing platform, Plaisse. The partnership also includes plans to deploy enterprise-grade AI capabilities and further develop the platform.

As financial institutions modernize their infrastructure, they also need ways to move and manage data without disrupting existing operations. NetApp Inc. is addressing those requirements through storage and data-management capabilities designed to support migration, resilience and performance in AWS environments, according to Jacob Lim, cloud solutions architect at NetApp.

“We create value for customers by making it simple to migrate and run their data in AWS by combining proven NetApp ONTAP capabilities, such as space-efficient snapshots, near-instant data cloning capabilities with minimal storage overhead and storage performance,” he told theCUBE. “Then, there is also the highly efficient data replication and ransomware detection engine natively built into the operating system directly. Combined with AWS scale and elasticity, customers gained resilience, performance and operational simplicity in the cloud.”

Scaling AI in financial services brings new challenges

As financial institutions incorporate AI into daily operations, managing the complexity of those deployments is becoming an increasingly important challenge. According to PagerDuty’s 2026 State of AI-First Operations report, 59% of surveyed banks were actively incorporating AI into their operations, while another 34% were discussing implementation. As adoption expands, institutions must determine how to govern these systems, maintain data quality and integrate AI into existing workflows.

“I think you’re going to see AI really become: How do we govern, how do we use [and] how do we make sure the data’s clean? How does it become [about] helping us be more efficient in what we’re doing in day-in and day-out operations?” Todd McNabb, chief revenue officer of PagerDuty Inc., told theCUBE.

Technology providers are responding to the demand for faster enterprise AI deployment. AWS’ recently announced $1 billion investment in forward-deployed engineering, for example, is intended to help customers develop and deploy agentic AI applications more quickly. For financial institutions, however, the measure of success will extend beyond deployment speed to how effectively AI can operate within existing systems, regulatory requirements and business processes.

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the AWS Financial Services Symposium event. Neither AWS, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5476. How House and Senate vacancies are filled, and what changes in each chamber

Free daily briefing on global business news.

When a member of Congress dies or resigns, the Constitution, state law and chamber rules decide who fills the seat, who runs the office and how votes change

The Constitution treats an empty seat in the House of Representatives very differently from an empty seat in the Senate. A House district stays without a voting representative until its voters choose a replacement in a special election. In many states, a Senate seat can be filled by a governor's appointment before any ballot is cast.

That split comes from two parts of the Constitution. Article I, Section 2 sets the rules for House vacancies. The 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, moved Senate elections to a popular vote and set the rules for Senate vacancies.

Understanding what happens when a member of Congress dies or resigns means following several tracks at once. The seat itself is only one of them. A departing lawmaker also leaves behind a staff, a constituent office, committee assignments and a floor vote that no one can cast.

Each of those pieces runs on its own set of rules. State law sets the timing of special elections, and the governor issues the writ that calls one. In the House, the Clerk takes over administration of a vacant office and its staff. The Secretary of the Senate does the same job for an empty Senate office. Constituents can still get help with casework while they wait for a new member.

Committee seats open up, and party and chamber processes decide who fills them. Seniority, which shapes committee standing in both chambers, does not pass to whoever wins the seat next. A successor does not inherit the predecessor's place in line.

Vote math shifts as well. In the House, a vacancy lowers the whole number of the chamber, the figure used to calculate a quorum. Most House votes are decided by a majority of members present and voting. The Senate keeps working with an empty seat, and the vice president votes only when senators are equally divided. In a closely divided chamber, a single vacancy can narrow a party's working margin.

Resignation follows a set procedure too. A member usually sends a letter to the state's governor and to the chamber's presiding officer, and can choose the date it takes effect. Final pay, retirement and survivor benefits follow separate federal rules.

The 10 slides below cover a selection of these mechanics, from filling the seat to settling a member's pay. Each slide explains one piece of the process on its own.

A vacant seat in the U.S. House of Representatives can be filled in only one way: a special election. The Constitution gives no one the power to appoint a temporary replacement. That includes a governor, a political party and the House itself.

The rule comes from Article I, Section 2, Clause 4. It says that when a vacancy happens in a state's House delegation, the state's executive authority shall issue writs of election to fill it. In practice, that executive authority is the governor. A writ of election is the formal order that sets an election in motion.

The wording matters. The clause tells the governor to call an election, not to choose a person. The decision about who represents the district stays with its voters, just as it did for the member who left.

This design matches the House's original role. Article I, Section 2 says representatives are chosen by the people of the several states. From the start, the House was the one part of the federal government whose members were elected directly. An appointed House member would break that link between voters and their representative.

The process begins once the seat is formally empty. A member who dies, resigns or is expelled leaves the seat vacant. The Clerk of the House then notifies the executive of the member's state, which opens the path to a writ and a new election.

Until voters choose a successor, the district has no voting member in the House. No stand-in can cast floor votes or introduce bills on the district's behalf. Legislative representation for those residents waits for the special election.

The winner does not start a fresh two-year term. A special election fills only the rest of the departed member's term. The seat then appears on the ballot again at the next regular election.

Changing this arrangement would take more than a new law. The special election requirement is written into the Constitution itself. Allowing anyone to appoint a temporary House member would therefore require a constitutional amendment.

That makes the House different from the Senate, where a separate provision governs vacancies. Every House member who fills a vacancy arrives through the ballot box.

The 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, sets the basic rule for an empty Senate seat: the state's governor must issue writs of election to fill it. It also lets each state legislature authorize the governor to appoint a temporary senator until voters choose a replacement.

That two-part structure explains why Senate vacancies are handled differently from one state to the next. The Constitution supplies the framework. Each state legislature decides how much of it to use.

The amendment grew out of a larger change. Under the original text of Article I, Section 3, state legislatures chose U.S. senators. The 17th Amendment moved that choice to the voters, who now elect senators directly. The vacancy clause follows the same logic. Voters pick senators in regular elections, and they also get the final say when a seat opens early.

Before the amendment, the Constitution handled vacancies another way. If a seat opened while a state legislature was in recess, the governor could make a temporary appointment. That appointee served until the legislature met again and filled the seat. The 17th Amendment replaced that arrangement with the writ-of-election requirement.

The amendment's text makes any appointment temporary. An appointed senator holds the seat only until "the people fill the vacancies by election as the legislature may direct." The appointment bridges the gap until an election and does not replace one. The legislature also directs how that election takes place.

States are not required to allow appointments at all. The power belongs to the legislature to grant or withhold. Some states fill Senate vacancies only by special election, leaving the seat empty until voters act. Others authorize the governor to appoint someone and then hold an election later.

Because the amendment leaves these choices to each state, the details vary. The timing of the special election, any conditions on the governor's pick and the length of an appointee's service all depend on state law. The constant is that an election eventually decides who holds the seat.

The winner of that special election generally serves the remainder of the departing senator's six-year term. Senate terms are staggered under Article I, and a vacancy does not reset the cycle for that seat. A senator who wins a special election and wants to stay must run again when the original term ends.

The amendment also included a transition provision. Its final paragraph said it would not affect the election or term of any senator chosen before it became part of the Constitution. Senators already picked by state legislatures finished their terms under the old system.

In most states, a governor can name a temporary senator to fill a vacant seat. That appointee serves only until voters choose a successor in a special election. Each state legislature decides whether its governor has that power and what limits come with it.

The authority comes from a single clause of the 17th Amendment. It lets a state legislature empower the governor to make temporary appointments "until the people fill the vacancies by election as the legislature may direct." That wording leaves the details to each state.

Some states let the governor pick anyone who meets the constitutional requirements. Others attach conditions. A number of states require the appointee to belong to the same political party as the senator who left. Some go further and require the governor to choose from a short list of names submitted by that party.

Any appointee must meet the same qualifications as an elected senator. Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution requires a senator to be at least 30 years old. The appointee must also have been a U.S. citizen for at least nine years and an inhabitant of the state when chosen.

The appointment becomes official through paperwork. The governor issues a certificate of appointment, which is presented to the Senate as the new member's credentials. The Senate holds the final say on seating. Article I, Section 5 makes each chamber the judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members.

An appointee takes the same oath of office as an elected senator. Once sworn in, an appointed senator holds the same vote as any other member. The appointee can introduce bills and vote on legislation and nominations.

The appointment is temporary by design. State law sets when the special election takes place, and the winner serves out the remainder of the unexpired term. Some appointees run in that election to keep the seat. Others serve as placeholders and leave once the elected successor takes office.

Each state decides when and how its own House special elections run. The governor issues the writ that starts the process, but state election law shapes the calendar, the nomination method and the ballot. As a result, the wait for a new representative varies from state to state.

Federal law leaves the scheduling to the states. Under 2 U.S. Code Section 8, state law sets the time for holding an election to fill a House vacancy. Some states give the governor a fixed window in which to call the election. Others leave the governor wider discretion over the date.

Nomination rules differ just as much. In many states, voters choose party nominees in a special primary before the special general election. In others, party committees or conventions pick the nominees, and a single election follows. Some states use an all-candidate primary, in which every contender appears on one ballot regardless of party.

Those choices shape the calendar. A primary followed by a general election takes longer than a single election with party-selected nominees. Candidate filing deadlines, ballot printing and certification periods add further time. Ballots must also reach military and overseas voters early enough to be returned.

Some all-candidate systems add a runoff. If no candidate wins a majority in the first round, the top finishers meet in a second election. That step pushes the swearing-in date back further.

A governor may also place the special election on the same day as an already scheduled primary or general election. Combining the two spares local election offices the expense of running a separate vote. The trade-off is a longer stretch without a voting representative for the district.

The winner does not start a fresh two-year term. A special election fills only the remainder of the departing member's term, in the same district that member represented. Once the result reaches the House, the winner takes the oath of office and can begin voting. The seat then comes up again at the next regular election.

When a House seat becomes vacant, the Clerk of the House takes charge of the departed member's office and supervises its staff until a successor is sworn in. In the Senate, the Secretary of the Senate handles the administration of a vacant senator's office.

This arrangement keeps a district or state from losing access to help with the federal government while the seat sits empty. Phones stay answered, and constituent requests can still move forward in Washington and in local offices back home.

In the House, the authority comes from the chamber's own rules. They direct the Clerk to oversee the staff of a member who has died, resigned or been expelled. The Clerk does not represent the district or speak for its voters. The role is administrative, covering payroll, the office budget and the daily work of the remaining employees.

Casework is the main function that continues. A constituent who needs help with a Social Security claim, a veterans' benefit, a delayed passport or an immigration case can still contact the office. Staff can make inquiries with federal agencies for that person, much as they did before the vacancy.

The staff cannot act as a lawmaker. With no member in the seat, no one in the office casts votes, introduces bills or signs on as a cosponsor. Nobody in the office speaks for the district on pending legislation.

The staff jobs are temporary. Employees remain on the chamber's payroll during the vacancy, but a newly elected member picks their own team. The successor may keep some previous employees, hire new ones or combine the two.

The Senate follows a parallel path through the Secretary of the Senate, the chamber's chief administrative officer. In states where a governor can appoint a temporary senator, the appointee takes over the office and its staffing decisions once sworn in.

The member's own papers follow a separate rule. Congress treats a member's office papers as the member's personal property. Committee records, by contrast, belong to the chamber. After a death in office, the family or estate often decides where those personal files end up.

Timing also shapes the handoff. A member who plans a resignation can prepare staff and wrap up open cases in advance. A sudden death in office gives the staff no such warning.

A departing member's committee seats become vacant, and that member's seniority ends with the vacancy. Each party, working through its own internal rules and a vote of the full chamber, chooses who takes the open slots. A successor starts with no inherited rank and builds seniority from his or her own first day of service.

Committee membership belongs to the individual lawmaker, not to the district or the state. When a House member or senator resigns or dies, every assignment that person held opens up. That includes seats on full committees and on subcommittees. Congressional practice does not reserve those seats for whoever wins the special election or receives a governor's appointment.

In the House, each party fills its own committee slots. Republicans route assignments through their Steering Committee. Democrats use their Steering and Policy Committee. The full party conference or caucus then approves the selections, and the House adopts a resolution formally electing members to committees.

The Senate follows a similar path. Each party conference makes its selections, and the chamber ratifies them by resolution.

A party has options once a seat opens. It may give the slot to the incoming member, move a sitting colleague into it or leave it unfilled for a time. The parties negotiate the split of majority and minority seats on each committee, usually at the start of a new Congress. That ratio determines which party controls the vacant slot.

The departure of a committee chair carries more weight than the loss of a rank-and-file member. The majority party chooses a new chair through its own internal rules, followed by a House or Senate resolution. House rules also require each standing committee chair to designate a vice chair from the majority party. The vice chair presides over meetings and hearings when the chair is absent.

Seniority cannot be handed to anyone else. A successor's standing on a committee and in the chamber begins with his or her own swearing-in. That standing affects where a member sits on the committee dais and where the member falls in line for a future chairmanship or ranking-member post. In the Senate, seniority also sets the order in which senators choose office suites.

An appointed senator is treated the same way. Service counts from the day the appointee takes the oath, not from the day the former senator first took office.

A vacancy shrinks the whole number of the House, the base for calculating a quorum, but it leaves the rule for passing most bills unchanged. Those votes turn on a majority of members present and voting, not a majority of the full membership.

Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution makes a majority of each chamber a quorum to do business. Under House precedent, that majority is measured against members who are chosen, sworn and living. A seat left empty by death, resignation or expulsion drops out of the count.

The Speaker announces each vacancy and the adjusted whole number from the floor. With all 435 seats filled, a quorum is 218 members. With one vacancy, the whole number falls to 434, and a quorum stays at 218. With two vacancies, the whole number is 433, and a quorum drops to 217.

Delegates and the resident commissioner of Puerto Rico sit outside this calculation. They do not count toward a quorum of the full House. They also cannot vote on final passage of legislation.

Passing a bill follows a separate rule. A measure succeeds when the yeas outnumber the nays among members who vote. A tie defeats it. Members who are absent or who answer "present" do not affect the margin. An empty seat has the same effect on the tally as a member who skips the vote.

The practical effect shows up in party margins. When a vacancy falls in the majority party's ranks, that party has one fewer vote to spare on a measure that splits along party lines. A vacancy in the minority party gives the majority more room on the same kind of vote.

Some decisions require more than a simple majority. Passing a bill under suspension of the rules needs two-thirds of those present and voting. Overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds of members voting in each chamber, with a quorum present. In both cases, vacant seats are left out of the math.

The election of a Speaker has its own arithmetic. The winning candidate needs a majority of the votes cast for a person by name. Vacancies, absences and "present" votes all lower the number of votes needed to win the gavel.

The House presumes a quorum is present unless a member raises a point of order that one is not. A quorum call or recorded vote then measures attendance against the adjusted whole number.

A Senate vacancy does not stop the chamber from working. The Senate keeps debating and voting with fewer than 100 members, and the vice president still casts a vote only when senators are equally divided.

The tiebreaking rule comes from Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution. It names the vice president as president of the Senate but gives that officer no vote unless the chamber is evenly split. A vacancy leaves that limit unchanged.

A vacancy does change the arithmetic around a tie. With 99 senators in office, a vote in which every senator takes part cannot split evenly. One side will always hold at least one more vote than the other. Ties remain possible when senators are absent or decline to vote, so the vice president's role does not disappear.

The Senate's quorum also adjusts. Senate Rule VI defines a quorum as a majority of the senators duly chosen and sworn. An empty seat lowers that base. With 99 senators serving, 50 make a quorum, compared with 51 when all 100 seats are filled.

Final passage of most bills requires a simple majority of senators voting. Under that standard, a vacancy matters most through its effect on party balance. Take a Senate split 50-50, where the vice president breaks party-line ties. If one side loses a member, the other side holds 50 of the 99 filled seats. With full attendance, that side can win a party-line vote without the vice president.

Ending a filibuster follows a different rule. Senate Rule XXII sets the cloture threshold for most measures at three-fifths of the senators duly chosen and sworn. With 99 senators serving, three-fifths still rounds up to 60 votes. A single vacancy leaves that usual bar in place.

The affected state keeps one voice in the chamber. Every state holds two Senate seats regardless of population. A single vacancy cuts a state's Senate delegation in half until the seat is filled. Its remaining senator continues to vote on the floor. The empty seat casts no vote until a successor, whether appointed or elected, takes the oath of office.

A member of Congress resigns by putting the decision in writing. The letter usually goes to two recipients: the governor of the member's home state and the presiding officer of the chamber where the member serves.

Each recipient has a separate role. The governor is the state's executive authority. That is the official who issues the writ of election that starts the process of filling the seat. The presiding officer informs the chamber that one of its members is leaving.

In the House, the presiding officer is the Speaker. In the Senate, it is the vice president, who holds the title of president of the Senate under the Constitution.

The departing member picks the effective date. A resignation can take effect immediately, on the day the letter is delivered. It can also take effect on a specific future date named in the letter.

That choice controls when the seat legally becomes empty. The vacancy begins on the effective date. It does not begin on the day the member announces plans to leave or on the day the letter is written.

Until the effective date arrives, the lawmaker remains a sitting member. A member who sets a future date keeps the powers of the office in the meantime, including the right to vote on the floor and in committee.

The chamber does not hold a vote to approve a resignation. Colleagues and party leaders have no power to accept or reject it. The written notice is the act that matters.

The letter itself is usually short. It typically states the decision to resign and the date it takes effect. A member is not required to give a reason.

In the House, a resignation letter is typically laid before the chamber and printed in the Congressional Record. That creates a public, official record of the departure and its timing.

Resignation differs from expulsion. Under Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution, either chamber can expel a member only with a two-thirds vote.

A member's congressional salary stops when service ends, whether that happens through resignation or death. Retirement benefits a member has already qualified for are not erased by leaving early. A deceased member's family may qualify for survivor payments under federal retirement and Social Security rules.

Pay follows the same basic logic as other federal salaries. It is earned for time in office. A member who resigns is paid through the effective date of the resignation and no further. A successor is paid for that person's own service, not for the stretch when the seat sat empty.

Retirement coverage depends on when a member first entered federal service. Members who first arrived in 1984 or later are generally covered by the Federal Employees Retirement System, known as FERS. That system combines three parts: Social Security, a basic annuity and the Thrift Savings Plan. The Thrift Savings Plan is a 401(k)-style investment account. Members who entered earlier may be covered by the older Civil Service Retirement System.

Leaving office does not cancel a pension a member has already earned. A member needs at least five years of service to be eligible for a congressional annuity. A House member who serves a single two-year term therefore does not earn one. Eligible former members draw benefits once they meet their system's age and service requirements. Money a member contributed to a Thrift Savings Plan account stays with that person after departure.

A death in office brings a different set of provisions. Surviving spouses and eligible children can receive survivor benefits under the retirement system the member belonged to. The amount and eligibility depend on factors such as the member's length of service. Members also pay into Social Security. Their families may qualify for Social Security survivor benefits under the same rules that apply to other workers.

Congress has a long-standing custom of approving a separate death gratuity for a deceased member's survivors. The payment is not automatic. Lawmakers have traditionally provided it through legislation, often as a provision in an appropriations measure.

Members can also enroll in the Federal Employees' Group Life Insurance program, which pays out to the beneficiaries they name. None of these benefits pass to the member's successor. The new member starts building service credit and retirement eligibility from the first day in office.

#5475. GSMA MWC26 Doha welcomed over 10,000 attendees, as world-first ITU co-location puts MENA at the centre of global connectivity policy and innovation

MWC26 Doha brought together senior industry leaders, policymakers and regulators for three days of exhibition, discussion, networking and dealmaking in Doha

DOHA, Qatar, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MWC26 Doha closed today as over 10,000 attendees from 100 countries and territories convened in Qatar, proving the scale and ambition of the Middle East and North Africa's digital growth and transformation. Across three days of keynote sessions, conferences, and summits, and hosted in partnership with the State of Qatar's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT), delegates explored how embedded intelligence, next-generation infrastructure and national digital strategies are reshaping the Middle East and North Africa's role in the global connectivity ecosystem.

In a first-of-its-kind co-location, MWC26 Doha ran alongside the opening days of the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference (PP-26).

Sianne Ryder, CEO, Events and Industry Services, GSMA Ltd, said: "This week at MWC26 Doha, policymakers and regulators sat side by side with industry leaders and innovators to debate, connect and shape MENA's digital future. Co-locating with the opening days of ITU PP-26 created something unique: a place where those setting the global digital agenda could engage directly with the operators, technology companies and investors bringing it to life. The result was sharper conversations, stronger connections and a clearer path from policy to progress. We look forward to seeing the partnerships forged in Doha deliver impact across the region and beyond. Thank you to everyone who joined us - and especially to our hosts at MCIT."

GSMA now turns its attention to MWC27 Barcelona on 1-4 March 2027, with registration now open. We look forward to welcoming the region's connectivity ecosystem back to Doha, from 15-17 November 2027.
