#5474. What the U.S. government spends money on, from Social Security to interest

Free daily briefing on global business news.

See where federal tax dollars go, from Social Security and Medicare to defense and interest on the debt, in 10 major areas of the U.S. budget

Many federal payments are never voted on line by line in a given year. Social Security checks, Medicare claims and interest on Treasury debt go out under permanent law or binding obligations. They keep flowing whether or not lawmakers act. The difference between that spending and the money Congress approves annually is the starting point for understanding where federal tax dollars go.

Federal spending falls into two broad groups. Mandatory spending is set by standing law. The rules that decide who qualifies for Social Security or Medicare, and what they receive, stay in force until Congress changes them. Spending on these programs depends on how many people qualify and what the law entitles them to, not on a yearly vote.

Discretionary spending works differently. Congress sets it each year by passing appropriations bills, which fund agencies and programs for a single fiscal year. Defense is the largest part of this category. The rest covers a wide range of federal activity, from scientific research to much of veterans' health care. The federal fiscal year runs from Oct. 1 to Sept. 30. That means the budget calendar does not line up with the calendar year.

Borrowing adds a third layer. When spending exceeds revenue in a given year, the government borrows to cover the difference. That one-year gap is the deficit. The accumulated total of past borrowing is the national debt. The Treasury owes interest on the securities it sells to finance that debt. Those payments are a legal obligation rather than a program Congress votes on.

Knowing which group a program falls into helps explain the federal budget breakdown. It shows which costs lawmakers can adjust in one appropriations cycle and which require rewriting the underlying law. Financing is a separate question. Some programs draw on dedicated payroll or fuel taxes, while others rely on general revenue.

What follows is a selection of 10 major areas of federal spending and finance. It is not a ranking by size or a complete accounting of what the U.S. government spends money on. Each spending slide explains what a program or obligation does, who runs it, how it is paid for and whether it is mandatory or discretionary. The final slide turns to the revenue side, covering where the money comes from and how borrowing fills the rest.

Social Security sends monthly payments to retired workers, disabled workers and the families of workers who have died. Most of the money comes from payroll taxes collected under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act, better known as FICA.

The combined tax rate is 12.4% of wages up to an annual earnings cap. Workers pay 6.2% through paycheck withholding. Employers pay a matching 6.2%. The cap is adjusted each year to track average wage growth. Earnings above it are not subject to the Social Security portion of the payroll tax.

Self-employed people pay both halves themselves. Their contribution falls under the Self-Employment Contributions Act rather than FICA. The combined rate is the same 12.4%.

Payroll tax receipts are credited to two trust funds held at the Treasury. The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund pays retirement and survivor benefits. The Disability Insurance Trust Fund pays benefits to workers who can no longer work because of a qualifying medical condition. Any surplus in the funds is invested in special-issue Treasury securities.

The system largely operates on a pay-as-you-go basis. Taxes paid by today's workers fund the checks going to today's beneficiaries. The money is not saved in individual accounts.

Benefits go straight to individuals. The Social Security Administration calculates each payment from a person's lifetime earnings record. Higher lifetime earnings produce larger checks, up to a maximum. Retirement benefits can start as early as age 62 at a reduced amount. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. Waiting past full retirement age earns delayed retirement credits until age 70.

Survivor benefits can go to widows, widowers, dependent children and, in some cases, dependent parents. Disability benefits require enough recent work history to qualify. They also require a medical finding that the person cannot sustain substantial work.

Payments rise in most years through an automatic cost-of-living adjustment. The adjustment is tied to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Congress does not vote on each year's increase.

Social Security is mandatory spending. Its benefit formulas and eligibility rules are set in the Social Security Act, which President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed in 1935.

Some higher-income beneficiaries also pay federal income tax on part of their benefits. Much of that revenue is credited back to the Social Security trust funds. A portion goes to Medicare's hospital insurance trust fund instead.

Medicare is the federal health insurance program for Americans 65 and older and for some younger people with disabilities. Its coverage is split into parts: Part A pays for hospital care, Part B for doctor visits and outpatient services, and Part D for prescription drugs.

President Lyndon B. Johnson signed Medicare into law in 1965 as an amendment to the Social Security Act. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, an agency within the Department of Health and Human Services, runs the program. Medicare is classified as mandatory spending. Anyone who meets the eligibility rules set in law can enroll.

Age is the main route in, but it is not the only one. People who have received Social Security disability benefits for 24 months become eligible before 65. So do people with end-stage renal disease, which is permanent kidney failure, and people with ALS.

Part A is financed mainly by a payroll tax. The combined rate is 2.9% of wages, with employees and employers each paying 1.45%. Self-employed workers pay the full 2.9% themselves. Unlike the Social Security payroll tax, the Medicare tax has no cap on the wages it applies to. The Affordable Care Act added a 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages above set income thresholds. That tax took effect in 2013.

Part A revenue flows into the Hospital Insurance Trust Fund. Most enrollees pay no monthly premium for Part A. They qualify for premium-free coverage because they or a spouse paid Medicare taxes for at least 40 quarters, or about 10 years of work.

Parts B and D work differently. They draw on general federal revenue and on premiums paid by beneficiaries, through the Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund. Enrollees with higher incomes pay larger premiums for both parts.

Part D is the newest major piece. Congress created it in the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003, and coverage began in 2006. Private insurers that contract with Medicare deliver the drug plans. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 gave Medicare authority to negotiate prices for certain high-cost drugs.

Many beneficiaries get their coverage through Medicare Advantage, also called Part C. These private plans bundle Part A and Part B benefits, and most include drug coverage. Medicare pays the plans to provide those benefits.

Medicaid is a health coverage program paid for jointly by the federal government and the states. The federal share differs from state to state and is set by a formula called the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage, or FMAP.

That shared structure separates Medicaid from Medicare, which the federal government runs on its own. Each state administers its own Medicaid program within federal rules. States decide many details, including some optional benefits, payment rates for doctors and hospitals, and how people enroll. The federal government then reimburses its share of qualifying costs.

The FMAP formula compares each state's per capita income with the national average. States with lower incomes receive a larger federal match. Wealthier states receive a smaller one. Federal law sets a floor of 50%. No state covers more than half of its standard Medicaid costs on its own.

Federal Medicaid funding is mandatory spending, and it is open-ended. The federal government matches whatever qualifying amount a state spends rather than sending a fixed sum. Federal costs therefore rise and fall with enrollment and with medical prices in each state.

Medicaid covers several groups with limited incomes: children, parents, pregnant women, older adults and people with disabilities. It is also a major payer for long-term care in nursing homes. Medicare covers only limited skilled nursing stays. Many older Americans who need extended nursing home care qualify for Medicaid after spending down their savings to meet its eligibility limits.

The Affordable Care Act of 2010 let states extend Medicaid to most adults with incomes up to 138% of the federal poverty level. The federal government pays 90% of the cost for that expansion group. That is a higher match than the regular formula provides. Not every state has adopted the expansion.

The Children's Health Insurance Program, known as CHIP, fills a different gap. It covers children in families whose incomes are too high to qualify for Medicaid. Congress created the program in 1997. Unlike Medicaid, CHIP is funded through capped federal allotments to each state. Its federal match rate is higher than the regular Medicaid rate. States can run CHIP as part of Medicaid, as a separate program or as a combination of the two.

Medicaid itself dates to 1965. It was signed into law alongside Medicare as part of amendments to the Social Security Act.

Defense is the largest part of discretionary federal spending, and most of that money flows through the Department of Defense. Congress sets the level each year through the National Defense Authorization Act and a separate defense appropriations bill.

The two bills do different jobs. The National Defense Authorization Act sets policy and authorizes programs. It covers matters such as troop levels, military pay raises and which weapons programs may go forward. The appropriations bill provides the money the Pentagon can actually spend. A program can be authorized and still go unfunded if appropriators do not supply the dollars.

The Pentagon's budget is organized into a handful of broad accounts. Military personnel funding covers pay and allowances for active-duty and reserve troops. Operations and maintenance is the account that keeps forces ready. It pays for training, fuel, equipment repairs, base operations and the salaries of many civilian employees. A separate account, the Defense Health Program, runs military hospitals and clinics and the Tricare health plan.

Procurement covers the purchase of ships, aircraft, combat vehicles, missiles and munitions. Research, development, test and evaluation pays for designing and proving new systems before they are bought in quantity. Military construction pays for barracks, runways and other facilities. It moves through a separate appropriations bill that also funds the Department of Veterans Affairs.

Some national security spending sits outside the Pentagon. Nuclear warheads are designed, built and maintained by the Department of Energy through its National Nuclear Security Administration. That work counts toward the federal government's broader national defense budget category. It is not part of the Department of Defense's own budget. The Coast Guard also sits outside the Pentagon. In peacetime, it falls under the Department of Homeland Security.

Timing shapes how the money is spent. The defense appropriations bill is one of 12 regular spending bills Congress is meant to pass before each new fiscal year begins. When lawmakers miss that deadline, the Pentagon typically operates under a continuing resolution. That stopgap generally holds funding at the prior year's levels. It also generally bars new programs from starting until a full-year bill passes.

Net interest is the federal government's cost of carrying the Treasury securities it has sold, minus the interest income it collects. Federal law pays interest on the public debt through a permanent, indefinite appropriation, with no yearly vote required.

The calculation starts with interest on debt held by the public. That debt consists of securities owned by individuals, banks, pension funds, mutual funds, state and local governments, foreign governments and the Federal Reserve. Interest the government receives from other sources is then subtracted to reach the net figure.

Interest the Treasury owes to its own trust funds, such as those for Social Security, sits outside the net figure. Those payments move money from one government account to another. In the overall budget, they cancel out.

Budget presentations from the Congressional Budget Office list net interest as its own category, separate from mandatory and discretionary spending.

Two forces set the cost: how much debt is outstanding and what interest rates the Treasury pays. A larger debt raises the bill even when rates hold steady. Higher rates raise it even when the debt stops growing.

The mix of securities shapes how quickly rate changes reach the budget. Treasury bills mature in one year or less. Treasury notes run from two to 10 years, and Treasury bonds run 20 or 30 years. When a security matures, the Treasury usually sells a new one to repay the holder. The new security carries whatever rate the market sets at auction.

Debt weighted toward short-term bills reprices fast when rates move. A 30-year bond keeps the rate set at its original auction until it matures.

Some securities adjust on their own. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities raise their principal in line with inflation. The interest paid on them rises as that principal grows. Floating rate notes mature in two years. Their interest payments reset with the rate on 13-week Treasury bills.

Missing an interest payment would count as a default on U.S. government debt. That risk surfaces during standoffs over the statutory debt limit, the cap Congress places on total federal borrowing. Hitting the limit does not erase interest already owed. It restricts the Treasury's ability to borrow the cash needed to meet all of its obligations, interest included.

The Department of Veterans Affairs spends federal money in two main ways. It runs a nationwide health system through the Veterans Health Administration, and it pays benefits to veterans, including monthly disability compensation for conditions connected to military service.

The Veterans Health Administration owns and operates its own hospitals and clinics. It also employs its own doctors, nurses and support staff. That sets it apart from Medicare and Medicaid, which mostly pay outside hospitals and physicians for care. The VA also buys care from community providers. The VA MISSION Act of 2018 set the rules for when veterans can see community doctors at VA expense.

Much of the VA health care budget is discretionary. Congress sets that money each year through appropriations bills.

Disability compensation works on different terms. It is a monthly, tax-free payment to veterans whose illnesses or injuries were caused or made worse by their service. The VA assigns each eligible veteran a disability rating from 0% to 100%, in 10% steps. The payment rises with the rating. Veterans rated at 30% or higher can receive more if they have a spouse, children or dependent parents.

Disability compensation is mandatory spending. A veteran who meets the eligibility rules is entitled to the payment.

Education benefits trace back to the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, the original GI Bill. Its current main version, the Post-9/11 GI Bill, was enacted in 2008. It can cover tuition and fees and pay a monthly housing allowance to eligible veterans and service members. Some service members can transfer unused benefits to a spouse or children.

The VA home loan program also dates to the 1944 law. The VA usually does not lend the money itself. Instead, it guarantees part of a mortgage made by a private lender. That guarantee lowers the lender's risk if the borrower defaults. It also allows many eligible borrowers to buy a home with no down payment.

Compensation, education benefits and home loans are run by the Veterans Benefits Administration, a separate arm of the department from the health system. A third arm, the National Cemetery Administration, maintains national cemeteries and provides burial benefits for eligible veterans.

SNAP, Supplemental Security Income and the Earned Income Tax Credit are three major federal income-support programs, and each runs through a different agency. One provides food aid, one pays monthly cash and one delivers money through the tax system.

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program is run by the Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Service. It helps low-income households buy groceries. For decades it was known as food stamps. Congress renamed it SNAP in the 2008 farm bill. Benefits now arrive on an Electronic Benefit Transfer card, which works like a debit card at the checkout counter.

The federal government pays for the SNAP benefits themselves. States take applications and determine eligibility, and they share the cost of administering the program. Benefit levels are tied to the Thrifty Food Plan, a USDA estimate of what a low-cost, nutritious diet costs. Congress reauthorizes and revises SNAP through the farm bill, the same legislation that covers crop subsidies and other agriculture programs.

Supplemental Security Income is run by the Social Security Administration. It pays monthly cash to people with low incomes and limited assets who are 65 or older, blind or disabled. Congress created SSI in 1972, and it began paying benefits in 1974. It replaced earlier aid programs for older, blind and disabled people that the states had administered.

SSI is separate from Social Security disability benefits, even though the same agency runs both. SSI does not depend on a recipient's work history. It is paid from general tax revenue rather than from payroll-tax trust funds. Many states add their own supplement on top of the federal payment.

The Earned Income Tax Credit works through the tax code instead of a benefit office. Workers claim it on their federal income tax returns, and the IRS administers it. Congress enacted the credit in 1975. Only people with earnings from work can receive it. The credit grows as earnings rise, levels off, then phases out at higher incomes. It is larger for families with qualifying children.

The credit is refundable. When it exceeds a household's income tax liability, the IRS pays out the difference. That refunded amount counts as federal outlays. The part of the credit that only reduces a tax bill shows up as lower revenue instead.

All three programs are classified as mandatory spending.

Most federal money for roads, bridges and public transit moves through the Highway Trust Fund. Fuel taxes are its main source of revenue, including the federal gasoline tax of 18.3 cents per gallon.

The fund works differently from much of the federal budget. Drivers pay the gas tax at the pump as part of the price of each gallon. That money is credited to the trust fund instead of being pooled with general Treasury revenue. Spending from the fund is reserved for surface transportation.

Congress created the fund in 1956, the same year it authorized the Interstate Highway System. Lawmakers set its spending programs through surface transportation laws that typically cover several years at a time.

The fund has two parts. The Highway Account pays for building, repairing and replacing roads and bridges. The Mass Transit Account, added in 1982, supports bus and rail systems in cities and regions.

The federal government builds very little of this itself. The money reaches the ground mainly as grants to state and local governments. Those governments build and maintain most of the country's roads. They choose and plan projects, hire contractors and handle routine upkeep.

Two agencies inside the Department of Transportation handle the grants. The Federal Highway Administration oversees road and bridge funding. The Federal Transit Administration oversees money for transit systems.

The gas tax is a fixed charge per gallon, not a percentage of the pump price. Revenue depends on how many gallons are sold, not on what each gallon costs. A jump in fuel prices does not increase the tax collected on a gallon.

The rate is also not indexed to inflation, so each cent buys less construction over time. Cars that burn less fuel pay less tax per mile driven. Fully electric vehicles pay no federal gasoline tax at all.

Fuel taxes alone have not covered what the fund pays out. In recent years, Congress has transferred money from general revenue to keep the fund able to meet its obligations. As a result, part of the cost of highways and transit falls on taxpayers generally, not only on drivers at the pump.

The National Institutes of Health, part of the Department of Health and Human Services, funds biomedical research at universities, medical schools and laboratories across the U.S. NASA and the National Science Foundation pay for much of the government's other scientific work, from space missions to basic research in physics, biology and engineering.

All three agencies are funded with discretionary money. Their budgets can rise, fall or stay flat from one fiscal year to the next, depending on what Congress appropriates.

The agencies sit in different spending bills. NIH funding moves through the bill covering the departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education. NASA and the National Science Foundation are both funded through the Commerce, Justice, Science bill.

Most NIH money leaves the agency. It goes out as competitive grants to researchers at outside institutions, a category known as extramural research. Applications go through peer review. Panels of outside scientists score proposals before funding decisions are made. NIH also runs its own intramural research program, with government scientists working largely at its main campus in Bethesda, Maryland.

The agency is organized into 27 institutes and centers. Each one focuses on a disease, an organ system or a field of study. The National Cancer Institute and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases are two examples.

The National Science Foundation is an independent agency created by the National Science Foundation Act of 1950. It supports basic research and science education across most nonmedical fields, including mathematics, computer science, geosciences and the social sciences. It awards its funding largely through grants chosen by merit review. It also supports large research facilities, including telescopes and the research stations of the U.S. Antarctic Program.

NASA was created under the National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958. Its budget covers human spaceflight as well as science. The Science Mission Directorate oversees work that includes planetary science, Earth science, astrophysics and heliophysics, the study of the sun and its effects across the solar system. Its missions are built and run by NASA centers working with contractors and university partners.

Grants to universities generally cover two kinds of cost. Direct costs pay for salaries, equipment and supplies tied to a specific project. Indirect costs, also called facilities and administrative costs, cover shared expenses such as buildings, utilities and regulatory compliance. Each institution negotiates its indirect cost rate with the government.

Science funding is not limited to these three agencies. The Department of Energy's Office of Science supports a network of national laboratories. The Department of Agriculture funds research on crops, food safety and farming.

The federal government pays for its spending mainly with three taxes: individual income taxes, payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare, and corporate income taxes. Smaller levies add to those receipts, and the Treasury borrows whatever they do not cover.

The individual income tax has been a permanent part of the federal system since the 16th Amendment was ratified in 1913. It applies graduated rates to wages, salaries, business profits and investment income. Most workers pay it through withholding from each paycheck. The Internal Revenue Service collects it along with payroll taxes.

Payroll taxes follow a different logic. They are tied to wages and earmarked for specific programs. The money is credited to dedicated trust funds instead of being pooled with general revenue.

Corporate income taxes fall on the profits of companies organized as C corporations. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 replaced graduated corporate rates with a single flat rate, effective in 2018. Many businesses, including partnerships and S corporations, pass their income through to their owners. Those owners report it on individual returns and pay individual income tax on it instead.

Smaller streams round out federal receipts. Excise taxes apply to specific goods and activities, such as gasoline, tobacco, alcohol and airline tickets. Customs duties are tariffs on imported goods, collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection. When the Federal Reserve earns more than it spends on its own operations, it sends the excess to the Treasury.

Revenue has fallen short of spending in nearly every recent year. To make up each year's gap, the Treasury sells securities to investors, including individuals, pension funds, banks and foreign governments. Treasury bills mature in a year or less, notes in two to 10 years, and bonds in 20 or 30 years.

That borrowing accumulates in the national debt until it is repaid. A year in which revenue exceeded spending would produce a surplus instead, which could be used to pay down debt held by the public.

Congress also sets a statutory debt limit, a cap on the total amount the Treasury may borrow. The limit does not authorize new spending. It determines whether the Treasury can borrow to pay for obligations Congress has already approved. Raising or suspending the limit requires separate legislation.

#5472. /C O R R E C T I O N - Supermetrics/

In the news release, Supermetrics Launches Campaign Manager, Bringing AI-Powered Insights and Campaign Execution Together, issued 10-Nov-2026 by Supermetrics over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

New AI-powered capabilities help marketers move from answers to action across advertising platforms, with trusted data, human oversight and control over campaign decisions

HELSINKI, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Supermetrics, the marketing intelligence platform powering more than 200,000 businesses, today announced the launch of Campaign Management, a new solution designed to help marketers bridge the gap between understanding campaign performance and taking action with AI. By bringing cross-platform performance marketing data and campaign actions into AI chats, Supermetrics is helping businesses turn AI marketing recommendations into optimization actions with a simple in-chat approval.

For years, marketers have relied on increasingly sophisticated tools to understand campaign performance, yet acting on those insights often remains a fragmented, manual process. Teams must navigate multiple advertising platforms, reconcile disconnected data and translate recommendations into campaign changes, losing time and slowing their ability to respond to campaign issues and changing performance marketing priorities.

Campaign Management addresses this challenge by connecting marketing intelligence directly to campaign execution. Built on Supermetrics' established data infrastructure, the solution combines trusted, connected marketing data with AI-powered workflows, so marketers can identify opportunities, evaluate recommended changes and take action across advertising channels from whichever AI solution they currently use.

"There's pressure on every marketing team to put AI to work, but not everyone is starting from the same place," said Anssi Rusi, CEO of Supermetrics. "Some are still getting their data connected. Others are already using tools like Claude to analyze performance and work out what to do next. For those teams, the question is, 'Why do I have to leave this conversation to make the change?' That's who we're building Campaign Management for. They want to act on the recommendations where they're already working, while staying in control of what happens to their campaigns."

From Marketing Intelligence to Intelligent Action

Campaign Management represents the next step in Supermetrics' evolution from marketing data integration to AI-powered marketing intelligence and execution.

Rather than relying on isolated, platform-specific recommendations, Campaign Management is designed to help marketers make decisions informed by a broader view of their marketing performance and business priorities.

The solution introduces capabilities designed to help marketing teams:

Premier Cru Solutions, a six-person digital marketing agency serving premium and luxury wineries, is already saving around 30% of its time using Supermetrics Campaign Management and Supermetrics for Claude. The team builds, restructures and optimizes Google Ads and Meta campaigns from one chat, directing the saved time toward deeper client analysis. In one Google Search rebuild, the agency completed a campaign build estimated at 14 hours in two hours, before final fine-tuning.

"Getting our data into Claude with Supermetrics changed how we analyze," said Matthew Thompson, Founder and Head of Growth at Premier Cru Solutions. "Campaign Management is changing how we work. We find the problem and make the fix across Google and Meta from the same chat, and every change gets checked before it goes live. A Search build we estimated at 14 hours, took two. We aren't using that time to take on more clients. We're using the time and richer data to give our clients answers they may have never had before."

Building a More Connected Advertising Ecosystem

As advertising becomes increasingly complex, marketers need solutions that bring together data, intelligence and execution across the platforms where their campaigns operate.

Supermetrics' Campaign Management can manage campaigns across Google, Meta, LinkedIn, Microsoft Advertising,TikTok, Snapchat and ChatGPT Ads, reflecting the growing importance of trusted data connectivity and more actionable marketing intelligence.

"Snapchat is dedicated to helping businesses of all sizes reach new customers and drive growth. #5471. The White House isn't retreating on tariffs after an election wipeout

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Aide Jim Goyer said the administration will continue its pace, while Gary Cohn called tariffs a consumption tax on U.S. consumers

Jim Goyer, director of the White House Office of Public Liaison, spoke at the B20 USA Summit in Washington on Tuesday and said the administration will keep up its tariff pace through the end of President Donald Trump's term, according to CNBC.

Goyer argued that tariffs help bring industrial production back home, make supply lines more reliable and safeguard the country's security, according to CNBC. "We are just getting started," Goyer said.

Gary Cohn, IBM $IBM vice chairman and former director of the National Economic Council, offered a different view in an onstage interview with POLITICO Playbook co-author Dasha Burns at the summit. "Tariffs are a consumption tax on the U.S. consumer… The producers and the importers don't pay the tariff," Cohn said.

Cohn cited aluminum tariffs as an example. "You and I, if we're buying a new car, we are eating that cost," he said. On the elections, Cohn said, "The U.S. consumer voted their financial well-being."

Cohn believes Republicans and Democrats could reach a compromise on trade, according to CNBC. Cohn proposed that Trump and the Democrats who will soon control Congress could lock in permanent safeguards aimed at China, while tariffs on Canada are scaled back.

Dow Executive Chairman Jim Fitterling took the other side, according to CNBC. He conceded that tariffs can push prices higher but called them essential for guarding against unfair competition and defending domestic manufacturing.

Democrats emerged from the Nov. 3 midterm elections with their biggest Senate and House majorities since at least 2008, according to Reuters. They assume control once the incoming Congress is seated on Jan. 3.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday showed that 62% of Americans favor rolling back Trump's tariffs, according to Reuters. The poll put Trump's approval rating at 32%.

Democrats intend to take on the tariffs once they are running Congress in January, according to CNBC. Trump's ability to veto legislation, along with his sweeping authority over trade, could make the duties hard to undo.

Price pressures are building as the debate unfolds. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October after a 0.6% increase in September. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3%, matching September and August. Gasoline prices rose 37.4% over 12 months.

#5470. Mercor raises $750M at $20B valuation to take AI agent evaluation to enterprises

Artificial intelligence training data company Mercor.io Corp. today revealed that it has raised $750 million in new funding at a $20 billion valuation.

Mercor provides the human expertise used to train and evaluate AI models, drawing on a network of more than 5 million domain experts. Most of that work so far has been for frontier AI labs. The new funding is aimed at taking it to enterprises in every industry, which Mercor argues need their own way to measure whether an AI agent can be trusted with a job.

Co-Chief Executive Brendan Foody said “every job in the economy” will need its own AI agents and that companies will need a way to train and evaluate them on their own work. Mercor spent the past two years building that infrastructure with the frontier labs. The lab business has grown fast. Foody said in a post on X in July that annualized revenue had passed $2 billion in June.

Adarsh Hiremath, Mercor’s other co-chief executive, said a model can score well on a public benchmark and still fail on “the systems, policies and edge cases that define how a specific business runs.” For each enterprise customer, Mercor builds a custom benchmark that measures models against that company’s own standards. Post-training starts from there.

Part of that post-training runs on software from Deeptune Inc. Mercor bought the New York startup in July, and its team had spent the two years before that recreating hundreds of enterprise applications for AI agents to practice on. The company said the new money will pay for research and evaluation infrastructure, including more of those environments.

Mercor did not name a lead investor for the Series D round, which drew corporate money from Nvidia Corp., Salesforce Inc. and Zoom Communications Inc. Returning investors Benchmark Capital Management Co., Felicis Ventures Management Co. and General Catalyst Group Management also participated. Other investors in the round were Fundomo, G Squared Equity Management LP, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group Inc., XTX Ventures and funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management Inc.

The last round came in October 2025, when Felicis led a $350 million Series C round that valued Mercor at $10 billion. Foody’s blog post on the new round says it included a tender offer for employee shares, and the company has not said how the $750 million splits between that and fresh capital.

Frontier labs have been the main buyers of expert-driven training data so far, according to Jai Das, president, partner and co-founder of Sapphire Ventures. He expects that to change as open models get good enough for enterprises to build on, saying Mercor has built “something hard to replicate” from several years of work with the labs.

#5469. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5468. Homeowners are tapping home equity lines of credit at the fastest pace in decades

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Total U.S. household debt rose 1.8% to $19.1 trillion in the quarter, and 5.0% of outstanding debt was in some stage of delinquency

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported that home equity line of credit balances rose $23 billion in the third quarter, the biggest quarterly jump since 2005. The figures come from the bank's Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit, released on Tuesday.

Home equity line of credit, or HELOC, balances totaled $481 billion at the end of the quarter, up $59 billion from a year earlier. HELOC limits rose $31 billion in the quarter, continuing an expansion that began in 2022.

The quarterly rise was the 18th in a row, according to CNBC.

Total household debt grew $334 billion, or 1.8%, to $19.1 trillion. Mortgage balances increased $257 billion to $13.4 trillion, and mortgage originations reached $595 billion.

"Household debt levels rose moderately, led by increases in mortgage and home equity line of credit originations," Donghoon Lee, economic research advisor at the New York Fed, said in a statement. "Although delinquency transition rates for housing debts have crept up, the overall credit quality of these loans remains strong."

Overall, 5.0% of outstanding debt was in some stage of delinquency, up 0.3 percentage point from the previous quarter. The share of HELOC balances moving into serious delinquency, meaning 90 days or more past due, was 1.17%, compared with 1.27% a year earlier.

The increase in HELOC balances is occurring while the housing market remains stagnant and numerous owners are unwilling to trade away their low mortgage rates, according to CNBC. HELOCs let borrowers draw on their equity while keeping those rates.

"HELOCs let them borrow against their equity without giving up the low interest rate on their home," certified financial planner Douglas Boneparth, president and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, told CNBC.

HELOCs generally carry variable interest rates, according to CNBC. The average rate on a $30,000 HELOC stood at 7.49% on Nov. 4. Many HELOCs have a draw period during which borrowers typically pay only interest, followed by a repayment period that adds principal.

"Payments potentially could double overnight, and you really want to know that before you sign anything," Boneparth said.

The housing market has weakened since mortgage rates returned to 7% in mid-September, and an index tracking contract signings for previously owned homes hit a record low in September. Thirty-year mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, 110 basis points above a year earlier.

#5466. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5465. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”

#5463. The next AI question is who controls the intelligence

Free daily briefing on global business news.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

As AI becomes part of everyday interactions, the handling of information shared with conversational systems is becoming an important area of public and regulatory attention. In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission launched an inquiry into consumer-facing AI chatbots, seeking information about how companies process user inputs and how they use or share personal information obtained through users' conversations.

The scrutiny reflects a broader question about the relationship between users and increasingly capable AI systems. The FTC’s inquiry also examined issues including user engagement, monetization, safety, and the potential effects of AI companions, demonstrating that questions around conversational AI extend beyond the performance of the underlying technology.

Public attitudes provide another indication of the challenge facing the industry. A 2026 Pew Research Center survey found that 71% of U.S. adults believed greater use of AI would make their personal information less secure, while only 3% believed it would make their information more secure. The survey also found that 67% of Americans had little or no confidence that the federal government would effectively regulate AI.

That is the environment in which Michael Folk, founder of FolkTech AI, has chosen to build Serena. FolkTech AI describes its approach as local-first agentic AI, with Serena designed to run on the user's own hardware. The company states that Serena operates entirely on the user's machine, that conversations do not leave the device, and that an account is not required. Serena Business is designed to operate on hardware controlled by an organization.

For Folk, the architecture reflects a principle he has carried from his earlier career as a paramedic. He says his experience in emergencies showed him how consequential technology failures can become when decisions have to be made under pressure. That experience helped shape his determination to create an assistant that could remain useful without depending on a remote cloud connection.

“I learned early that reliability is not an abstract engineering goal,” Folk says. “When people are depending on technology in a critical moment, the system has to be there, and it has to behave in a way they can understand and trust. That experience stayed with me when I began thinking about what an AI assistant should be.”

Folk argues that the location of processing changes the relationship between an individual and an AI assistant. If conversations are processed locally, he says, the information does not have to cross an external network boundary to reach a vendor-operated endpoint. According to him, that approach does not eliminate every potential security risk associated with software or hardware, but it changes the data pathway that a user must consider.

Folk also sees continuity as an important part of the assistant experience. He describes Serena as being designed to retain relevant context over time, allowing interactions to build on previous conversations rather than treating every exchange as completely isolated. He also envisions proactive follow-up as part of the product's usefulness, with the assistant able to return to matters the user has previously discussed.

Those capabilities are part of Folk's broader view that an AI assistant should develop an understanding of context rather than simply retrieve information on demand. For businesses, that concept becomes the basis of Serena Business, which Folk describes as a "digital brain" capable of building relational knowledge around an organization's documents, procedures, and operational context. FolkTech states that Serena Business answers from an organization's own documents on hardware the organization controls.

The progression from Serena for individuals to Serena Business reflects FolkTech AI's stated strategy of building a broader ecosystem incrementally. Folk describes the company as deliberately product-led, with each stage extending the same local-first philosophy into another use case.

The company also has a social objective attached to that growth. Folk says FolkTech AI intends to donate a Serena consumer system with advanced educational content to communities without reliable internet access for every Serena Business product sold. He views local processing as particularly relevant to communities where continuous connectivity cannot be assumed. The initiative remains a company commitment, with its eventual reach dependent on execution and scale.

“AI should earn trust through what it is built to do,” he says. “If the intelligence is going to become part of your life, you should know where it lives, who controls it and what happens to your information. My goal is simple: build technology that works for people without asking them to give up control.”

#5462. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

Will CPI cause a sell-off across Asian stocks and Bitcoin? Asian stocks staged a sharp recovery this morning, but another US inflation report could put the rebound to the test. Investors are preparing for October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI), with expectations of slower monthly inflation offering some relief. However, rising Federal Reserve rate-hike bets and NVIDIA shareholders suing Jensen Huang have kept markets cautious.

The Korea’s KOSPI jumped 4.5% this morning trading, led by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index also advanced, while Singapore’s Straits Times Index joined the regional recovery. Bitcoin, meanwhile, remains below $75,000 ahead of the US inflation release.

South Korean stocks getting sent 📈 🤑 🥳 pic.twitter.com/KYd5V9Oh9d

Does this recovery have enough momentum to survive another inflation surprise? A hotter reading could revive concerns about borrowing costs, while weaker inflation might give risk assets room to recover. Will the latest CPI figures determine if the rebound continues, or will it cause a sell-off?

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics is scheduled to publish October CPI at 8:30 a.m. ET on November 10. Economists expect headline inflation to increase 0.3% month-over-month, slowing from September’s 0.6% rise. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, is forecast to increase 0.2%, compared with 0.3% previously.

Last year’s government shutdown prevented the BLS from collecting the necessary October 2025 data. Economists nevertheless estimate headline inflation would have reached 3.9% annually.

The stakes remain high because markets have increasingly priced in another Federal Reserve rate hike. Traders recently assigned an 84% to 85% probability to a December increase, following stronger employment data. The Fed’s benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75% to 4%.

A hotter-than-expected reading could strengthen the case for tighter monetary policy. Higher Treasury yields and a stronger dollar would potentially pressure Asian equities, particularly technology companies with valuations sensitive to financing costs.

South Korea’s KOSPI could face the greatest exposure. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are central to the global semiconductor supply chain, making the index particularly sensitive to changes in AI investment sentiment. Both companies helped drive today’s rebound, with their shares rising 5.1% and 6.8%, respectively.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index offers another important benchmark. Its technology-heavy components could face renewed pressure if investors reduce exposure to growth stocks. Singapore’s Straits Times Index provides a useful contrast, given its greater exposure to financial institutions and dividend-paying companies.

A cooler reading could produce the opposite reaction, easing rate concerns and supporting another regional advance.

Bitcoin is trading around $74,600 ahead of the inflation release, leaving it close to a crucial support zone. Our analysts identified the $73,000 level as an important level, with a sustained break potentially exposing $70,000.

A hotter CPI reading could intensify selling pressure as investors reassess interest-rate expectations. Bitcoin’s recent weakness also reflects fading institutional demand, with US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recording $1.28 billion in outflows last week.

A softer inflation report could trigger a relief rally, but it might not guarantee a sustained recovery. Stronger ETF demand and improved liquidity would still be necessary to support a meaningful reversal.

NVIDIA adds another complication. The chipmaker and CEO Jensen Huang is being sued in a proposed shareholder class action filed in California yesterday. Investor Mark Kistenmacher alleges that NVIDIA misled shareholders about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, and Jensen Huang are being sued in a class action lawsuit, accusing ‌them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang's ties with a suspected Chinese spy.The lawsuit claims that shareholders were misled about Huang's alleged relationship with a woman…

The complaint claims the alleged relationship created reputational and national security risks that investors should have known about. NVIDIA’s board had already announced an independent investigation, while the company had not immediately commented on the lawsuit.

NVIDIA shares fell 4.3% on Monday, erasing $190 billion in market cap. The decline arrived just as Asian semiconductor shares were attempting to recover from last week’s technology-led sell-off.

NVIDIA remains central to the AI investment cycle, and any deterioration in confidence surrounding the company could amplify concerns about semiconductor valuations and the sustainability of AI spending. That could leave Korean chipmakers particularly vulnerable if another inflation shock hits markets.

So, will CPI cause a sell-off? It depends on a few factors. We might need to watch core prices, Treasury yields, and the dollar for clues about the Federal Reserve’s next move. A cooler report could extend the recovery, but a hotter reading may expose how fragile confidence in Asian technology stocks and Bitcoin is.
