#5460. Trifecta explained: from horse racing to state and federal government

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A trifecta means one party controls a state's governorship and both legislative chambers — here's where the word came from and examples of states that held one in 2025

One word covers a bet at the racetrack, a state's balance of power and control of the federal government. That word is trifecta, and its meaning depends on where it shows up. At the track, it is a wager on the first three finishers in exact order. In a statehouse, it describes who controls the lawmaking process.

In U.S. state politics, a trifecta means a single party holds the governor's office and both chambers of the legislature. That alignment matters because a party with a trifecta can usually pass bills without votes from the other party. Budgets, tax law, school funding and election rules can all move through the legislature and onto the governor's desk without cross-party deals. In a state with divided government, the governor and lawmakers have to negotiate, or bills can stall.

The label has limits. A trifecta counts offices. It says nothing about how large a party's majorities are, whether its members agree with one another or what a state constitution requires for certain votes. One state also falls outside the standard definition. Nebraska elects its single-chamber legislature on ballots with no party labels.

This slideshow covers 10 angles on the term. It starts with the word itself and its roots in horse-race betting, including how the trifecta wager relates to the exacta and the superfecta. It then defines a state government trifecta and separates it from two related ideas: divided government and the triplex, a separate term used by Ballotpedia. It walks through examples of Republican and Democratic trifecta states as of 2025, as well as examples of states with divided government that year. Later slides explain Nebraska's structure, the limits of what a trifecta can deliver and how the same idea applies to the presidency and Congress.

The state examples here are a selection, not a full list. Party control can change at any general election. It can also shift through special elections, vacancies and party switches by individual lawmakers. Ballotpedia and the National Conference of State Legislatures track current status across all 50 states.

A trifecta is a set of three, most often three wins or three positions of control held at once. The word started as a horse-racing term and has since moved into politics, sports and everyday speech.

Its first syllable carries much of the meaning. Tri- is the standard prefix for three, the same one that appears in triangle, tripod and triathlon. The rest of the word comes from the betting vocabulary of American racetracks, which is where the term first took hold.

Three uses account for most of the word's appearances today. At the track, it still names a specific wager on the order in which horses finish. In U.S. state politics, it describes a single party holding the governor's office and both chambers of the legislature. In the federal government, it describes one party holding the presidency, the House and the Senate together.

Those three senses share a structure. Each involves three separate pieces, and each counts only when all three line up. Two out of three does not qualify. A party that holds the governorship and only one legislative chamber does not have a state trifecta.

Outside those formal settings, the word is used much more loosely. Sports fans and writers apply it to three titles, three trophies or three standout results in a single season. Business coverage may use it for a company hitting three goals at once. In casual use, there is no fixed rule about what the three things must be.

That looseness separates trifecta from tighter sports terms built on the number three. In ice hockey, a hat trick has a set meaning: one player scoring three goals in a single game. Trifecta carries no such fixed definition outside racing and government.

Context decides which meaning applies. A reference to a trifecta at the Kentucky Derby points to a bet. A reference to a trifecta in Austin or Sacramento points to party control of state government.

A trifecta bet wins only if the bettor names the horses that finish first, second and third in a race, in the exact order they cross the line. A ticket with all three horses right but in the wrong sequence loses as a straight trifecta.

The trifecta belongs to a family of exotic wagers. Each of these bets ties a single ticket to more than one finishing position. The trifecta sits in the middle of the group. An exacta asks the bettor to pick the first two finishers in order. A superfecta extends the same idea to the first four.

The name comes from that ladder of bets. Trifecta was formed from perfecta, a racing term for picking the top two finishers in order. Some U.S. tracks still call that two-horse bet a perfecta, while others call it an exacta. Replacing the opening syllable with "tri" signaled a third horse.

A boxed trifecta drops the order requirement. The bettor chooses a group of horses. The ticket pays if those horses fill the top three spots in any arrangement. That flexibility costs more per ticket. Boxing three horses covers six possible finishing orders. The ticket is priced as six separate trifecta combinations. Boxing four horses covers 24 combinations.

A keyed trifecta is a middle path between a straight bet and a full box. It fixes one chosen horse in a single position, often first. Several other horses can then fill the remaining two spots in any order. A key built from four horses covers fewer combinations than a full box of the same four.

At U.S. tracks, trifecta payouts come from pari-mutuel pools rather than fixed odds. All money bet on the trifecta in a race goes into a shared pool. The track deducts its takeout, and the rest is split among the winning tickets. The final payout is not known until betting closes. A result with long-shot horses in the top three tends to pay more. Fewer tickets hold that combination.

U.K. bookmakers offer a comparable bet on the first three finishers in correct order. There it is called a tricast.

A state government trifecta exists when one political party holds the governor's office and a majority in both chambers of the state legislature. The label counts three seats of power: the executive and the two lawmaking bodies.

Those three bodies are the ones that write and enact state law. In a two-chamber legislature, a bill has to pass the lower chamber and the upper chamber in identical form before it reaches the governor. The governor can then sign it or veto it. When one party controls every step in that chain, it can generally move a bill into law with votes from its own members alone.

The names of the chambers vary by state, but the test stays the same. California, New York, Nevada and Wisconsin call their lower chamber the Assembly. Virginia, Maryland and West Virginia call theirs the House of Delegates. Most other states use the name House of Representatives. The upper chamber is the Senate. Whatever the names, a trifecta requires one party to hold majorities in both chambers as well as the governorship.

A majority in a chamber typically lets a party choose that chamber's presiding leaders and set which bills come up for a vote. That is why the legislature counts as two separate pieces of the trifecta rather than one. Losing either chamber breaks the set, even if the party keeps the governor's office.

Majority size plays no part in the test. A party that holds the Senate by a single seat has a trifecta in the same sense as a party with lopsided majorities in both chambers. Two trifecta states can therefore differ widely in how much room the ruling party has to act.

Governors and legislatures together approve state budgets and set state tax rates. They also write state law on matters such as schools, roads and elections.

Two reference sources track which states have trifectas. One is Ballotpedia, a nonprofit online political encyclopedia. The other is the National Conference of State Legislatures, or NCSL, a bipartisan organization that serves state lawmakers and their staffs.

A state without a trifecta has divided government, meaning no single party holds the governor's office and both legislative chambers at once. A triplex is a separate measure. Ballotpedia uses that term when one party holds the offices of governor, attorney general and secretary of state.

Divided government can take more than one shape. A governor from one party may face a legislature run entirely by the other party. In another version, the two legislative chambers are held by different parties. One party controls the House, and the other controls the Senate. Either arrangement means there is no trifecta.

The two shapes create different pressure points. With a split legislature, a bill can pass one chamber and then fail in the other before it ever reaches the governor. With a governor facing an opposing legislature, both chambers can pass a bill and still see it vetoed.

The triplex looks at a different part of state government. Instead of the lawmaking branch, it covers three executive offices. The governor runs the executive branch. The attorney general is the state's chief legal officer. In most states, the secretary of state oversees elections and keeps official records, among other duties.

The governor is the only office the two terms share. A state can have a trifecta without a triplex, or a triplex without a trifecta. The two measures track different officeholders. Knowing one tells a reader nothing certain about the other.

Not every state fills these executive offices the same way. In New Jersey, the governor appoints the attorney general. Tennessee's attorney general is appointed by the state Supreme Court. Maine's legislature chooses its attorney general. The governors of Texas and Pennsylvania appoint their secretaries of state. Alaska, Hawaii and Utah have no secretary of state at all. In those three states, the lieutenant governor handles the duties that office would normally carry.

Those differences shape what a triplex reflects. In one state, it may come from voters electing all three officials. In another, it may come partly from appointments. Ballotpedia tracks triplexes separately from trifectas.

As of 2025, Republicans held the governor's office and both legislative chambers in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama, Oklahoma, Idaho and Utah. In each of these states, the governor who signs or vetoes bills and the two chambers that pass them belonged to the same party.

These six states are examples, not a complete roster. They span the South, the Great Plains and the Mountain West. They should not be read as a count of every state where Republicans held all three offices.

In Texas, the trifecta joined Gov. Greg Abbott $ABT with Republican majorities in the Texas Senate and the Texas House of Representatives. The Texas Legislature meets in regular session only in odd-numbered years. That made 2025 a regular-session year, when lawmakers write the state's two-year budget.

Florida paired Gov. Ron DeSantis with Republican control of the Florida Senate and the Florida House of Representatives. Unlike its Texas counterpart, the Florida Legislature holds a regular session every year.

Alabama's trifecta in 2025 ran through Gov. Kay Ivey and both chambers of the Alabama Legislature. Oklahoma's ran through Gov. Kevin Stitt, the Oklahoma Senate and the Oklahoma House of Representatives.

In the Mountain West, Idaho had Gov. Brad Little working with a Republican-led Senate and House in the Idaho Legislature. Utah had Gov. Spencer Cox alongside Republican majorities in both chambers of the Utah State Legislature. Utah's constitution limits the legislature's annual general session to 45 calendar days.

The governors in these examples had held office for different lengths of time. Abbott took office in 2015. Ivey became Alabama's governor in 2017, after the resignation of Robert Bentley. DeSantis, Stitt and Little took office in 2019, and Cox followed in 2021.

These alignments describe 2025. A single election can end a trifecta by changing the party of the governor or flipping one legislative chamber. Any of these six states could lose its trifecta after its next round of voting.

Democrats held the governor's office and both legislative chambers in California, Illinois, New York, Maryland, Colorado, Washington state and Oregon as of 2025. Massachusetts, Hawaii and Delaware were Democratic trifecta states that year as well. The states named here are examples, not a full tally.

In California, the 2025 trifecta paired Gov. Gavin Newsom with Democratic majorities in the State Assembly and the State Senate. California is the most populous U.S. state. Its party control therefore shapes state law for more residents than in any other state.

Illinois followed the same pattern under Gov. JB Pritzker. Democrats controlled both the Illinois House of Representatives and the Illinois Senate. Together those chambers form the Illinois General Assembly, which meets in Springfield.

New York's trifecta ran through Gov. Kathy Hochul and a legislature in Albany made up of the State Assembly and the State Senate. Democrats held both chambers in 2025.

Maryland's version included Gov. Wes Moore. The state's lower chamber goes by a less common name, the House of Delegates. It sits alongside the Maryland Senate in the General Assembly in Annapolis.

Colorado, under Gov. Jared Polis, gave Democrats the governorship and both chambers of the Colorado General Assembly in Denver. Oregon had the same arrangement under Gov. Tina Kotek. Democrats there held the House and the Senate of the Oregon Legislative Assembly in Salem.

Two states on the list changed governors in January 2025 without changing the party in charge. In Washington state, Bob Ferguson succeeded Jay Inslee. In Delaware, Matt Meyer succeeded John Carney. Both new governors are Democrats, and each state's trifecta continued through the handoff.

Massachusetts adds another Northeast example. Gov. Maura Healey worked with a legislature formally known as the General Court, which has a House of Representatives and a Senate. In Hawaii, Gov. Josh Green and Democratic majorities in the Hawaii State Legislature completed the set of three offices.

The examples cluster along the West Coast, in the Northeast and the Mid-Atlantic, and in Hawaii. Illinois and Colorado are the interior states in the group.

This status reflects 2025. Losing either legislative chamber or the governorship at a future election would end any one of these trifectas.

Nebraska is the only U.S. state with a unicameral, or single-chamber, legislature, and its members are elected on nonpartisan ballots. With one chamber instead of two, and no party labels on legislative ballots, the standard trifecta test does not map cleanly onto the state.

The usual definition asks whether one party holds the governor's office and both legislative chambers. Nebraska fails the second half of that test before party affiliation even comes up. The state has one chamber, not two. Its formal name is the Nebraska Legislature, and Nebraskans commonly call it the Unicameral.

The Legislature has 49 members, and they carry the title of senator. Nebraska voters approved the switch to a single house in 1934, and the new chamber first met in 1937. George Norris, then a U.S. senator from Nebraska, was the leading public advocate for the change. He argued that one house would make lawmaking more open. In his view, conference committees in a two-chamber system settled the final version of bills out of public view.

The ballot creates the second complication. Candidates for the Legislature appear without a party label. The two candidates who receive the most votes in the primary advance to the general election, regardless of party. A voter reading the ballot sees names, not parties.

The governor runs under different rules. Nebraska elects its governor on a partisan ballot, as other states do. The result is a state with one clearly partisan executive office and one legislative body that is nonpartisan by design.

That mismatch makes Nebraska an awkward fit for party tallies. Any party count for the Legislature has to rely on how individual senators are registered or affiliated outside the chamber. Those affiliations do not appear on the ballot, and the Legislature is not formally organized by party.

The structure also changes how laws pass or stall. Overriding a governor's veto in Nebraska takes 30 votes in the single chamber. There is no second chamber where a bill can die or a veto override can fail.

For readers comparing lists of trifecta states, Nebraska's placement reflects how a given tracker handles a nonpartisan body. It does not reflect a party result printed on a legislative ballot.

In 2025, Arizona, Wisconsin, Kansas, Kentucky, North Carolina, Vermont and Nevada were among the states with divided government. Each had a governor from one party and a legislature controlled wholly or partly by the other. No single party held all three centers of power in any of them.

Most of those examples paired a Democratic governor with a Republican-led legislature. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, was Arizona's governor in 2025. Tony Evers, also a Democrat, led Wisconsin. Laura Kelly held the office in Kansas, and Andy Beshear held it in Kentucky. Both are Democrats.

North Carolina fit the same pattern. Josh Stein, a Democrat, became governor in January 2025 after winning the 2024 election. He succeeded Roy Cooper, another Democrat who served alongside a Republican-led legislature. Republicans continued to control the legislature under Stein.

Vermont and Nevada ran in the opposite direction. Vermont's governor in 2025 was Phil Scott, a Republican. Nevada's was Joe Lombardo, also a Republican. Democrats controlled both states' legislatures.

Pennsylvania arrived at divided government by a different route. Its House and Senate were controlled by different parties in 2025. That split alone kept any party from holding a trifecta, whichever party held the governor's office.

Michigan and Minnesota also lacked a trifecta in 2025. Both states reached that position after the 2024 elections.

The states named here are examples rather than a complete list. Other states may also have had divided government in 2025. Ballotpedia and the National Conference of State Legislatures track each state's current status.

Election calendars shape how long each arrangement can last. Kentucky elects its governor in odd-numbered years. That means its executive branch can change hands in a year with no congressional races. Arizona, Wisconsin, Kansas and Nevada are scheduled to elect governors in 2026.

Vermont is one of only two states where governors serve two-year terms. New Hampshire is the other. That shorter cycle gives Vermont voters a chance to reshape the balance between governor and legislature every two years.

A trifecta gives one party the governor's office and both legislative chambers, but it does not guarantee that the party's agenda becomes law. Disagreements inside the party, constitutional thresholds and the courts can all stop a bill the majority wants.

Internal splits are a common obstacle. A party caucus does not speak with one voice. Lawmakers from rural and urban districts, or from moderate and hardline wings, can disagree on spending, taxes or social policy. When a majority is narrow, a handful of defections can keep a bill from passing either chamber. A governor can also veto a bill passed by lawmakers of the same party.

Constitutional rules set a second limit. Some state constitutions require a supermajority, rather than a simple majority, for certain actions. Tax increases and proposed constitutional amendments are two common examples. A party that holds all three bodies by slim margins may still need votes from the other party to clear those higher bars.

Courts act as a third check. State courts can strike down a law that conflicts with the state constitution. Federal courts can block a state law that conflicts with the U.S. Constitution or federal law. Holding a trifecta gives a party no direct control over those rulings.

Voters hold a further check in some states. Ballot initiatives let citizens propose laws directly. Referendums let voters approve or reject measures the legislature has passed. Both tools can move policy in a direction the governing party did not choose.

Divided states show the reverse side of the same question. Kentucky's constitution lets a majority of the members elected to each chamber override a governor's veto. That low threshold means a legislature controlled by the opposing party can still pass laws over the governor's objection. Many states set the override bar higher, often at two-thirds of members. In those states, a governor facing an opposing legislature has more room to block bills.

The trifecta label describes who holds the offices. Whether a given bill becomes law still depends on the vote count, the thresholds written into each state's constitution and the courts that review the result.

At the federal level, a trifecta means one party holds the presidency, a majority in the House of Representatives and a majority in the Senate. This arrangement is also called unified government.

The federal version mirrors the state version. The president takes the governor's place, and the two chambers of Congress take the place of the state legislature. When the presidency and Congress are split between the parties, the federal government is divided, just as a state government can be.

Federal control changes on a fixed calendar. All 435 voting seats in the House are up for election every two years. Senators serve six-year terms. Roughly one-third of the 100 Senate seats are on the ballot in each federal election. Presidential elections take place every four years. That staggered timing means a federal trifecta can form or end in a presidential election year or in a midterm.

Senate rules limit what a federal trifecta can accomplish. A majority party in the House can pass bills on its own, but most legislation in the Senate faces the filibuster. Ending debate on a filibustered bill takes 60 votes, more than a simple majority. Budget reconciliation bills are an exception and can pass the Senate with a simple majority. The vice president casts tie-breaking votes. That power can decide which party controls an evenly split Senate.

State trifectas can form and end through more routes than a regular election. General elections remain the most common path, with governors and legislators facing voters on set schedules. A special election to fill an empty seat can tip a narrowly divided chamber. A vacancy can shift the balance before anyone fills it if the departing member belonged to the majority. A lawmaker who switches parties can hand a chamber to the other side without a public vote.

These changes can arrive in the middle of a legislative session. A state listed as a trifecta in January may not be one by December. Election calendars also differ from state to state. Most governors serve four-year terms, but governors in New Hampshire and Vermont serve two-year terms. Virginia and New Jersey are among the states that elect their governors in odd-numbered years.

Any count of trifecta states is a snapshot tied to a specific date. Ballotpedia and the National Conference of State Legislatures both publish state-by-state data on party control. Their pages are the place to confirm the current number of Republican trifectas, Democratic trifectas and divided state governments.

#5459. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5458. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5457. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.

#5456. What House and Senate leaders actually do: 12 congressional leadership roles

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 12 congressional leadership roles show what House and Senate leaders actually do, from the Speaker's gavel to whip counts and Senate cloture votes

The Constitution names only a handful of officers to run Congress. Article I lets the House choose its own Speaker. It also makes the vice president the president of the Senate. It provides for a president pro tempore to preside when the vice president is away. Almost everything else about how the two chambers are led comes from party rules and long-standing custom.

That gap matters. The House majority leader, the Senate majority leader, the two minority leaders and the whips who count votes appear nowhere in the constitutional text. These posts still decide much of what happens on the floor. They set the schedule that determines which bills come up for a vote and when. They track where members stand before a roll call. They negotiate the terms under which debate begins and ends.

Knowing how congressional leadership roles work helps explain outcomes that can otherwise look puzzling. A bill can have broad support and still never reach a vote if the leaders who control the floor do not schedule it. In the Senate, ending debate on most legislation takes three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn. With all 100 seats filled, that is 60 votes. That means a majority leader often has to build a coalition larger than a simple majority. In the House, the Speaker must win a majority of the members voting for a named candidate. When all 435 seats are filled and every member votes for a named person, that number is 218.

These posts also reach beyond Capitol Hill. Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, the Speaker stands second in the line of presidential succession, after the vice president. The president pro tempore stands third. Party leaders in both chambers negotiate with the White House on budgets and other major legislation. They also work out differences when the House and Senate pass different versions of the same bill.

The 12 slides that follow cover a selection of leadership posts and practices across both chambers. They are not a complete list of every leadership position in Congress. Each one explains a single part of the leadership structure: what it is, where its authority comes from and how it shapes a bill's path to a final vote.

The Speaker of the House presides over the U.S. House of Representatives and leads its majority party. The Speaker runs floor debate, decides which members get recognized to speak and stands second in the line of presidential succession.

The post comes from Article I, Section 2 of the Constitution, which gives the House the power to choose its own Speaker. The clause stops there. It lists no duties for the office and sets no qualifications for whoever holds it.

That silence extends to membership. The Constitution does not require the Speaker to hold a House seat. Even so, every Speaker to date has been a sitting member of the chamber.

The full House elects the Speaker in a floor vote. The number of votes needed to win is not fixed. Members who are absent do not count toward the total, and neither do members who vote "present" instead of naming a candidate. Each absence or present vote lowers the bar a candidate must clear.

Once in the chair, the Speaker presides over floor proceedings. Much of that authority rests on recognition. A member who wants to speak on the floor needs the presiding officer to call on them, and the Speaker controls that call. That gives the Speaker a say over who is heard and when.

The Speaker also leads the majority party in the House. One person therefore fills two roles at the same time. The Speaker is the officer who runs the chamber's proceedings and the head of the party that controls it.

The post also ties into the presidency. Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, the Speaker follows the vice president in the line of succession to the presidency. That places the Speaker ahead of every member of the Cabinet.

Mike Johnson was elected Speaker on October 25, 2023.

The House majority leader is the second-ranking leader of the party that controls the House, behind only the Speaker. The core of the job is the floor schedule, which sets which bills the full House takes up and when.

No clause of the Constitution creates this office. Article I, Section 2 provides for a Speaker chosen by the House, but it does not mention a majority leader. The post exists under party rules. Its authority comes from the party that holds the majority, not from constitutional text.

Members of the majority party choose the majority leader, not the full House. The vote takes place inside the party's own organization rather than on the floor. Members of the minority party have no part in the choice.

Setting the calendar is the main task. The majority leader decides which measures get floor time in a given week. The same decision determines which measures wait.

That control over timing gives the post its influence. A bill has to reach the floor before the full House can vote to pass it.

The two top posts in the majority split their work. The Speaker presides and leads the party as a whole. The majority leader handles the narrower question of what the House takes up and in what order.

The House minority leader heads the party that does not hold a majority in the House. The minority leader is that party's nominee for Speaker and sets its strategy on the floor. Hakeem Jeffries has led House Democrats in this role since January 2023.

The job carries a formal duty at the start of every Congress. Before the House can take up any other business, the full chamber must elect a Speaker. Each party puts forward its own candidate for the gavel.

For the minority party, that candidate is its leader. Members of the party then cast their votes for the leader on the floor. The election is a public, member-by-member vote. Each party's support for its candidate goes on the record.

The minority holds fewer seats by definition. Its nominee can win the gavel only if the larger party fails to unite behind its own candidate. When the majority stays together, the minority leader's nomination falls short.

Most of the minority leader's work happens during regular business, after the Speaker is chosen. The majority party decides which bills reach the floor and when. The minority leader decides how the opposition responds once those bills arrive.

That response is the core of floor strategy. The leader can ask the party to oppose a bill as a group. The leader can also let members vote as they choose on a given measure.

The minority leader is also the opposition's main voice in the chamber. During floor debate, the leader makes the party's case against majority proposals and lays out its own priorities. For a party out of power in the House, the leader's floor speeches carry its message on major bills.

The post rests on the support of the party's own members. They elect the minority leader, and they can replace the leader under the party's rules.

A House whip counts votes and works to keep party members together on the floor. Each party in the House has its own whip. The job comes down to three tasks: finding out where members stand, getting them to the floor and pressing them to vote with the party.

Counting comes first. Before a measure reaches the floor, the whip's team asks members whether they support it, oppose it or remain undecided. The answers add up to a tally of where the party stands.

That tally tells party leaders whether they have the votes they need. On the majority side, it informs the leadership's judgment about when a bill is ready for a floor vote. On the minority side, it helps the minority leader shape the party's floor strategy.

A count is only as useful as it is accurate. A member counted as a supporter who then votes no can upset the leadership's plans.

Turnout is the second task. A member who backs the party position but misses the roll call adds nothing to the total. Whips press supporters to be present and to cast their votes when the roll call happens.

Persuasion is the third. When a member wavers, the whip works to bring that member back toward the party's position. The undecided column of the count shows the whip where that effort is most needed. This is the party discipline side of the role.

Deputy whips and regional whips share the workload. That network spreads the job of contacting individual members across a larger group. It also gives the whip more people to gather information and relay the party's position.

Both the majority and the minority run this kind of operation in the House. Each one serves its own party's leadership.

The title itself has roots outside the U.S. The word "whip" comes from the British Parliament. There, the term borrows from the language of fox hunting.

The Senate majority leader draws much of the job's power from one custom. When several senators seek the floor at once, the presiding officer recognizes the majority leader first. That priority lets the leader decide what the Senate takes up and when it votes.

The Constitution does not create the job. No clause in it mentions a Senate majority leader. The post comes from Senate tradition and party practice. The leader's main advantage is a custom of the chair rather than a written power.

Priority recognition is the core of the role. A senator needs recognition from the presiding officer before speaking or making a motion on the floor. By tradition, the chair grants that recognition to the majority leader ahead of other senators. The leader can use it to bring a bill or other business forward before anyone else gets the chance.

That first claim on the floor becomes agenda-setting power. The majority leader sets the order in which legislation reaches the floor. The leader also schedules votes, which shapes how the Senate spends its time.

Recognition also gives the leader first access to procedural tools. One of them is the cloture motion, a formal attempt to end debate on a measure. The majority leader can file that motion as part of moving business forward.

The majority party's senators choose their leader in an internal party election. That makes the job a double role. The leader manages the schedule for the full chamber while answering to the senators of one party. The title also depends on that party's standing. A leader holds it only while the party controls the Senate. If control of the Senate changes hands, the post passes to the leader chosen by the new majority.

John Thune has held the post of Senate majority leader since January 2025.

The Senate minority leader heads the party that holds fewer seats in the Senate. The core of the job is bargaining with the majority leader over how long the chamber debates a measure and which amendments get a vote.

Chuck Schumer has been the Democratic leader in the Senate since January 2017. His title has changed with his party's position in the chamber. The leader of the larger party holds the majority leader title. The leader of the smaller party holds the minority leader title. The party post stays the same. The label attached to it follows the seat count.

Many of the deals between the two leaders take the form of unanimous consent agreements. Under one of these agreements, the Senate proceeds on terms that no senator objects to. A single objection is enough to defeat a unanimous consent request.

That rule shapes the minority leader's position. An agreement that needs every senator's consent cannot move forward over the minority party's objection. The minority leader speaks for that party in the talks. That makes the minority leader the person the majority has to deal with when it wants the floor to run on agreed terms.

An agreement can fix the length of debate on a bill. It can also list the amendments that will be offered and voted on. Each agreement applies to a particular measure and lays out how that measure will move on the floor.

Those two items are the main subjects of the bargaining. Time on the floor determines how long a measure stays open to argument. A list of amendments determines which alternative ideas get a vote. For a party without a majority, a vote on its own proposal is one way to put its position on the record.

The minority leader does not set the Senate's agenda. That power belongs to the majority leader. The minority leader's influence runs instead through the terms negotiated for each bill.

The vice president is the president of the Senate under Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution, but casts a vote only to break a tie. When the vice president is absent, a senator elected as president pro tempore holds the chair.

This arrangement puts an officer who is not a senator at the head of the chamber. The Constitution assigns the vice president this role directly. The role does not depend on Senate rules or party custom.

The tie-breaking vote is the vice president's only voting power in the chamber. With 100 senators, a tie can occur, for example, when the full chamber splits 50 to 50. In that case, the vice president's vote decides the outcome. Outside a tie, the vice president does not vote.

The president pro tempore is a separate Senate office, and the chamber elects its holder itself. The post is one of the few congressional leadership positions the Constitution names. The others include the Speaker of the House and the vice president's role as president of the Senate.

By custom, the president pro tempore is the most senior senator in the majority party. Seniority, not a leadership race, usually settles who gets the title. That sets the post apart from the floor leaders, whom each party's senators elect.

The office also carries a place in the line of presidential succession. Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, the president pro tempore ranks third, after the vice president and the Speaker of the House. That order places the Senate's own presiding officer directly behind the House's.

The senator sitting in the chair on a given day is often neither officer. In practice, junior senators take turns presiding over the chamber. The rotation keeps the chair filled without requiring the vice president or the president pro tempore to be present.

Senate whips count votes and keep their party's senators present and informed ahead of key roll calls. In the majority party, the whip holds the number two leadership job, ranking just below the majority leader.

Each party in the Senate elects its own whip through its party conference, the name both Senate parties use for their members' organization. Before a vote, the whip works to learn where every senator in the party stands.

That tally tells the party's leader whether a bill or amendment has enough support to bring to the floor. It can also show that more work is needed first.

Attendance is the other core duty. A senator who is absent cannot vote. In a chamber of 100 members, a handful of missing senators can change the outcome of a close vote. Whips track who will be on hand and make sure members know when a roll call is coming.

Keeping senators informed runs in both directions. Whips relay the leadership's plans to rank-and-file members. They also carry those members' concerns back to the leader.

The Senate version of the job is more flexible than its House counterpart. A House whip serves a chamber of 435 members. A Senate whip works with a far smaller party group, and the role often extends beyond counting.

Helping the leader manage floor time is a frequent addition to that role. That work puts the whip in the middle of the chamber's daily floor business, alongside the majority leader who sets the agenda.

Counts also matter before cloture. The majority leader files cloture to end debate on a measure. Ending debate on most legislation takes a supermajority. A whip count shows in advance whether the votes are there.

The minority whip handles the same counting and attendance work for the opposition. A reliable count tells minority leaders how many of their senators will stand together on a given vote.

Party conferences and caucuses are the groups that choose each party's leaders in the House and Senate. Each group is made up of one party's members in one chamber. It elects that party's leaders, sets party positions and can remove or replace leaders under its own party rules.

The names differ by chamber and by party. House Republicans call their group a conference. House Democrats call theirs a caucus. In the Senate, both parties use the word conference. The label changes, but the basic job does not. In each case, the group meets as one body to make decisions for the party.

Several leadership posts rest on these elections. The House majority leader and the Senate majority leader both win their jobs through a vote of party colleagues. The full chamber does not vote on either post.

The Speaker of the House follows a different path. Article I, Section 2 gives the House the power to choose its Speaker. That means the full chamber casts the deciding vote. Each party still arrives at that vote with its own nominee, chosen inside its conference or caucus. On the minority side, that nominee is the House minority leader.

Winning a leadership election does not end a leader's dependence on the group. Leaders answer to the members who chose them. A conference or caucus can remove or replace a leader by following the procedures in its party rules.

The groups also do more than pick people. When a party's members meet, they work out the positions the party takes in its chamber.

The result is a two-level arrangement. On the floor, leaders hold the formal tools of their posts. In the House, the majority leader runs the floor schedule. In the Senate, the majority leader gets priority recognition by custom. Those tools last only as long as the party group behind a leader keeps that leader in the job.

Party leaders in Congress help decide which members get which committee seats. In the House, the majority party also controls the Rules Committee, the panel that sets the terms of debate for most major bills.

Each party in the House settles its own members' committee seats. It does this through a party committee that recommends assignments.

Party leaders have a say in that process. Their input shapes which panels a lawmaker joins and which policy areas that lawmaker works on.

The arrangement works the same way on both sides of the aisle. Majority and minority members alike reach their committees through their own party's assignment process. Their own leaders weigh in on those choices.

The Rules Committee is where leadership influence over procedure is most direct. Whichever party holds the House majority controls the panel.

The committee writes the terms under which most major bills are debated once they reach the House floor. Those terms govern how a measure moves through the full chamber.

Control of the panel gives the majority party's leadership a direct hand in floor procedure for its legislative priorities.

Cloture is the Senate procedure that ends debate on a measure. On most legislation, invoking it takes three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn, which is 60 votes when all 100 seats are filled.

The majority leader is usually the senator who files the cloture motion. The motion is a formal request to stop debating a pending measure and move it toward a final vote. Without cloture, debate on the measure can go on. A bill that a majority supports can stay stuck on the floor.

The wording of the rule matters. The base is senators duly chosen and sworn, not the number who show up for the roll call. In a full chamber, the target stays at 60 no matter how many members are present. A supporter who misses the vote does not lower the bar. In practice, an absent supporter has the same effect on the count as a no vote.

Vacancies work differently. A seat with no sworn senator drops out of the base. With enough empty seats, the number needed can fall below 60.

The current standard dates to 1975. Before then, the Senate needed two-thirds to invoke cloture. The 1975 change lowered the requirement to three-fifths. That rule still governs most bills.

The gap between a simple majority and 60 is where much of the leadership work happens. A bare majority of the full chamber is 51 senators. Reaching cloture takes nine more than that. Unless one party holds at least 60 seats, the majority leader has to find support from senators outside the party.

The need for 60 votes gives senators outside the majority leverage over a bill's wording and timing, even when the bill already has majority support.

Final passage comes after cloture and needs only a simple majority of senators voting. A bill that clears cloture has already shown it can draw more support than passage requires.

Congressional leaders serve as the main negotiators between Capitol Hill and the president, and between the House and the Senate. Leaders from both parties in both chambers meet with the president on major legislation such as budgets. They also work to settle differences when the two chambers pass different versions of the same bill.

This work differs from a leader's daily floor duties. On the floor, a leader manages one chamber. At the negotiating table, the same leader represents an entire party conference or caucus to the White House and to the other chamber.

The House and Senate often pass versions of a bill that do not match. One chamber may change spending levels, add new provisions or drop sections the other chamber approved. Those gaps have to be closed before the bill can move forward. Party leaders from both chambers take part in working out the final terms.

Each chamber's rules shape what a leader can promise. In the House, a bill passes with a majority of the members voting. In the Senate, ending debate on most legislation through cloture takes a supermajority. A deal that can clear the House on majority-party votes alone may still need minority-party support in the Senate.

That gap gives minority-party leaders a role in many negotiations. A Senate minority leader whose senators can block cloture holds leverage that a House minority leader often does not.

Leaders also have to know whether they can deliver the votes a deal requires. Whips in both chambers count votes and track where members stand. Those counts show leaders how much support an agreement can draw before it reaches the floor.

A leader at the table also answers to the party behind them. Leaders are elected by their party conference or caucus. Those groups can replace their leaders under party rules.

Talks with the president follow the same logic. The White House can set out priorities and push for specific provisions. The majority leadership in each chamber controls the floor schedule, however. An agreement reached with the president cannot become law unless the chamber leaders bring it to a vote and deliver enough support to pass it.

#5455. Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 5, 2026 at 2:27 pm

Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning, the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org, the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.

“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM, which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.

Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who took an interest in climate modeling before his death in 2018. His company, then known as Vulcan, launched the climate modeling project in 2019, and the group moved to Ai2 in 2021. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.

In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.

Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.

Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect date for the start of the climate modeling effort at Vulcan. It started in 2019.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5454. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”
