#5445. How Senate confirmations work, from nomination to final vote

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Senate confirmation process runs from nomination to final vote, and these 10 rules and stages explain how presidential nominees win or lose approval

A three-word phrase in the Constitution — "advice and consent" — gives the Senate a say over who runs federal departments and who sits on federal courts. It also covers who represents the U.S. abroad. The President picks the nominee. The Senate decides whether that pick takes office. That division of power gives two branches of government a role in every appointment that requires confirmation.

The Senate confirmation process is not a single vote. It is a chain of formal rules, committee customs and floor procedures. Each link can move a nominee forward or hold one back. Some steps are written into the Constitution. Others exist only in the standing rules of the Senate. A few are traditions that a committee chair can honor or set aside.

Those rules have not stayed fixed. The threshold for ending debate on nominees has dropped from a supermajority to a simple majority. The time allowed for debate after that vote has been cut for many lower-level posts. The 2013 and 2017 changes were each led by the Senate majority leader of the day.

This guide follows the path a nominee takes. It starts with the constitutional text and the kinds of jobs that need Senate approval. It then covers the questionnaires, financial disclosures and background checks that come before any hearing. Next come the committee hearing and committee vote. After that is the blue slip custom, which gives home-state senators a voice on some judicial and law enforcement picks.

From there the guide moves to the floor. It explains holds, cloture votes and the final tally, including what happens when the Senate splits evenly. The ninth section looks at nominations that fail, stall or get sent back to the White House. The 10th covers recess appointments and the bulk approval of military promotions. Both work outside the usual one-by-one vote.

Each section stands on its own. A reader who wants to know what a hold means, or why a vice president might cast the deciding vote, can go straight to that section. Together the sections show how a presidential choice becomes a confirmed official — and every point where that path can end.

Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution divides the power to fill top federal posts between two branches. The President nominates, and the Senate gives its advice and consent before an appointment is made.

The clause names specific categories of officials. It lists ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and justices of the Supreme Court. It then adds a broader category: all other officers of the U.S. whose appointments the Constitution does not otherwise provide for.

The order of the verbs matters. The President acts first by choosing a person and sending that name forward. The appointment comes only after the Senate has consented. A nomination on its own does not place anyone in office.

The phrase "advice and consent" is the constitutional footing for the Senate's role. Committee hearings, floor debate and confirmation votes on presidential nominees all rest on these words.

The same clause also limits how far Senate review reaches. It lets Congress decide that certain positions, which the text calls inferior officers, can be filled without the Senate's consent.

For those posts, Congress may vest the appointment power in one of three places. It can give the power to the President alone. It can give it to the courts. It can also give it to the heads of departments.

The decision rests with Congress rather than the President. Lawmakers determine which inferior offices skip Senate review and which of those three authorities makes the selection.

The result is a two-track system built into the same clause. Ambassadors, public ministers, consuls, Supreme Court justices and other officers not covered elsewhere go through both the President and the Senate. Inferior officers can go through a single appointing authority if Congress chooses that route.

Beyond those four named categories, the text does not list individual job titles. Which posts require the Senate's consent depends on the general category of officers and on the inferior-officer choices Congress makes.

Cabinet secretaries, ambassadors, federal judges, U.S. attorneys, U.S. marshals and senior military officers must all win Senate approval before taking office. These posts sit on the confirmed side of a line the Constitution draws between officers who need the Senate's consent and lesser officers who may not.

The roster spans the executive and judicial branches. Cabinet secretaries run the executive departments. Ambassadors represent the U.S. to foreign governments. Senior military officers lead the armed forces. Federal judges sit at three levels: district courts, circuit courts and the Supreme Court. Judges at all three levels need the Senate's consent.

U.S. attorneys and U.S. marshals belong on the list as well. Both posts are tied to individual federal judicial districts. A U.S. attorney leads federal prosecutions in a district. A U.S. marshal handles law enforcement work for the federal courts in a district. The Senate must sign off on both, just as it does for a Cabinet secretary or a judge.

Senate confirmation does not cover every federal job. The Constitution gives Congress a choice when it comes to inferior officers. Congress must make that choice by law. Lawmakers can place the power to appoint them with the President alone. They can also give it to the federal courts or to the heads of departments. When Congress takes one of those routes, the appointment does not go to the Senate.

Without a law vesting an inferior officer's appointment elsewhere, the default under the Constitution is nomination by the President with the Senate's advice and consent.

The result is a two-tier system. A nominee for a senior post, such as a Cabinet secretary or a federal judge, faces the Senate's full process before taking the job. That process runs from vetting through a committee review to a floor vote. An inferior officer whose appointment Congress has assigned to the President alone, a court or a department head does not.

A presidential nomination becomes official when the White House sends a formal nomination to the Senate. The Senate then refers it to the committee with jurisdiction over the post, where questionnaires, financial disclosure and background checks begin.

The formal nomination turns a president's choice into business the Senate can act on. Until that document arrives, senators have no pending nomination to consider. Once it does, the nomination does not go straight to the full chamber. It goes to a committee first.

Referral depends on the type of job. The Senate Judiciary Committee handles nominations for federal judges. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee handles ambassadors. The Senate Armed Services Committee handles military officers. The position, not the person nominated, decides which committee reviews the pick.

Vetting begins with paperwork. Nominees complete questionnaires for the committee reviewing them. Those documents put a written record of the nominee in front of senators before any questioning takes place.

Executive-branch nominees face an added financial step. People picked for posts in federal departments and agencies file financial disclosure. That disclosure is reviewed through the Office of Government Ethics. A nominee's finances are therefore on file before the Senate weighs the nomination.

Judicial nominees undergo an FBI background check on top of their questionnaires. That check covers people nominated to the federal bench, where judges are appointed to the courts rather than to an executive agency.

These requirements produce different paths for different posts. An ambassador nominee goes to Foreign Relations and, as an executive-branch pick, files financial disclosure reviewed through the Office of Government Ethics. A judicial nominee goes to Judiciary and undergoes an FBI background check. A nominee for a senior military post goes to Armed Services.

All of this happens before the committee holds a hearing or takes a vote. The questionnaires, disclosure filings and background checks form the record that committee members review once the nomination moves to that next stage.

A Senate committee reviews a nominee in two stages: it holds a hearing, and then it votes on how to report the nomination. That vote shapes what comes next, but it does not settle the outcome.

The hearing comes first. The nominee appears before the committee with jurisdiction over the post. Senators on that panel question the nominee directly before any vote takes place.

The two stages do different work. The hearing lets panel members put their questions to the nominee in person. The vote then asks those same members to record a position on the nomination.

The committee votes after the hearing ends. The question on the table is not whether the nominee gets the job. It is how the nomination will be reported to the rest of the chamber.

A committee has three options. It can report a nomination favorably. It can report it unfavorably. It can also report it without recommendation. Whichever option the panel picks, the nomination leaves the committee and heads to the floor.

Each option tells senators outside the panel something different. A favorable report signals that the committee backs the nominee. An unfavorable report signals that the committee opposes the pick. A report without recommendation moves the nomination along while the committee takes no position.

Only committee members take part in that vote. Its result reflects the judgment of one panel, not the view of the Senate as a whole. The floor is where the full chamber first weighs in.

None of these reports binds the chamber. A favorable report does not guarantee confirmation. An unfavorable one does not end a nomination. On the floor, any senator can vote, whether or not he or she sits on the committee.

The committee stage informs the decision rather than making it. The full Senate decides whether the nominee takes office.

The blue slip is a Senate Judiciary Committee custom that lets the two senators from a nominee's home state weigh in before the committee acts. It is a committee practice, not a rule of the full Senate.

The tradition works through consultation. When a nomination tied to a particular state reaches the Judiciary Committee, the senators who represent that state are asked for their view. Their answer signals whether they are willing to see the nomination move forward in committee.

The practice reaches beyond the courts. Under Chairman Chuck Grassley, the committee honored blue slips for district judges and for U.S. attorneys. For those posts, the views of home-state senators carried real weight in whether a nominee advanced. A senator who declined to return a favorable slip could keep that nomination from moving through the committee.

Circuit judges were treated differently. Starting in 2017, the committee did not apply the blue slip to circuit court nominees. A home-state senator who withheld support could not use the custom to hold up a circuit nomination in committee.

The split shows how a custom differs from a rule. The full Senate does not vote on the blue slip, and its standing rules do not require it. The committee chair decides how much weight the slips carry and for which kinds of nominees. That is why district and circuit nominees could be handled differently by the same committee.

A rule of the full Senate applies the same way no matter who leads a committee. A committee custom carries no such guarantee. A later chair can draw the lines in a different place, widening or narrowing the set of posts where home-state objections count.

The blue slip operates only inside the committee stage. It can shape whether a nomination advances in Judiciary. It does not replace the committee hearing, the committee vote or the final decision on the Senate floor.

A Senate hold is an informal notice from a senator that he or she intends to object if leaders try to move a nomination by unanimous consent. A hold can slow a nominee down, but it does not block a nomination outright.

The hold works through unanimous consent, the shortcut the Senate uses to skip formal procedural steps. Under unanimous consent, a matter moves forward only if no senator objects. A single objection is enough to stop the shortcut.

That power belongs to every member of the chamber. The objecting senator does not need to sit on the committee that reviewed the nominee. Any senator can refuse consent on the floor, regardless of party or seniority.

A hold announces that objection in advance. The senator does not have to wait for the nomination to reach the floor. Leaders learn ahead of time that consent will be refused. They can then decide whether to take the formal route instead.

The hold is not a vote, and it does not formally reject anyone. It is a statement of intent. Its force comes entirely from the right every senator already has to deny unanimous consent.

The majority still has a formal route around an objection. It can file for cloture, the procedure that brings debate on a nomination to a close. Once the majority takes that route, the nomination can advance without the objecting senator's agreement.

The practical effect of a hold is to force the slower path. A nomination that could have cleared the chamber by consent must go through formal procedure. That procedure includes a separate cloture vote before the final vote on confirmation. Every extra step uses floor time that unanimous consent would have saved. The decision shifts from a single senator's objection back to the majority.

A hold gives one senator influence over timing, not a veto over the nominee.

Cloture is the Senate procedure that ends debate on a nomination. For every type of nominee, it now takes a simple majority rather than 60 votes. Senate Rule XXII governs the process. Rule changes in 2013 and 2017 lowered the threshold, and a 2019 change shortened how long debate can run once cloture passes.

The Senate does not cut off discussion of a nominee by default. Until debate on a nomination formally ends, the chamber cannot move to a confirmation vote. A successful cloture vote closes that discussion and puts the nominee on a path to the final tally.

Before 2013, ending debate on a nomination required 60 votes. Under that threshold, a nominee with the backing of a majority could still stall if supporters could not reach 60. The minority party therefore held real leverage over which nominees reached a vote at all.

In 2013, Majority Leader Harry Reid led a change that set a simple-majority threshold for cloture on executive-branch nominations and lower-court judges. Supreme Court nominees were left out of that change. They still faced the 60-vote bar.

That exception did not last. In 2017, Majority Leader Mitch McConnell extended the simple-majority threshold to Supreme Court nominees. The Senate then confirmed Neil Gorsuch to the Supreme Court on April 7, 2017, by a vote of 54-45.

Passing cloture does not trigger an immediate confirmation vote. Senate rules allow a period of post-cloture debate first. In 2019, the Senate cut that window to two hours for most sub-Cabinet executive nominees and district judges.

Higher-level posts kept a longer runway. Up to 30 hours of post-cloture debate remains available for Cabinet-level nominees, circuit judges, Supreme Court justices and certain other positions. The gap shapes the floor schedule. The two-hour limit lets the chamber process lower-level nominees faster than the 30-hour maximum allowed for top posts.

A nominee is confirmed when a simple majority of the senators voting approves the nomination. If those senators split evenly, the vice president can break the tie. That power comes from Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution.

The phrase "senators voting" carries weight. The threshold is measured against the votes actually cast on the floor, not against the full membership of the chamber. A senator who is absent or does not vote is left out of the count. As a result, the number of yes votes needed to win can change from one roll call to the next.

A tie means neither side has a majority, and the nomination has not been approved. Article I, Section 3 gives the vice president a way to resolve that deadlock. The vice president's vote is then added to the final tally. That is why a tiebreak confirmation shows up as a one-vote margin.

Vice President Mike Pence used that power on Feb. 7, 2017. He broke a tie to confirm Betsy DeVos as Education Secretary. The recorded count was 51-50. Senators had divided 50-50 on the nomination, and Pence cast the deciding yes vote.

Two recent Supreme Court confirmations show the simple-majority standard working without a tiebreaker. Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed on Oct. 26, 2020, by a vote of 52-48. Ketanji Brown Jackson was confirmed on April 7, 2022, by a vote of 53-47.

In each case, more senators voted yes than voted no. That is all the rule requires. Neither count was tied. The vice president had no role in either outcome. Barrett won by four votes and Jackson by six.

The final vote is the Senate's actual decision on a nomination. Committee action, holds and cloture all come earlier in the process. None of them settles whether a nominee is confirmed. Only the floor vote does that.

A nomination can fail in three ways. The Senate can vote it down, decline to act on it, or let it go back to the President under the chamber's own rules. Each path ends a nomination without a confirmation, and each works through a different mechanism.

An outright rejection happens on the Senate floor. The full chamber takes a recorded vote, and more senators vote no than yes. Robert Bork's Supreme Court nomination ended this way in 1987, when the Senate voted 58-42 against him. The roll call put every senator's position on the record.

Cabinet nominees can meet the same end. In 1989, the Senate rejected John Tower as Defense Secretary by a vote of 53-47. A floor defeat is not limited to judicial nominees. A nominee to lead an executive department faces the same final test as a nominee to the high court.

A stalled nomination fails without any vote at all. Merrick Garland was nominated to the Supreme Court in March 2016. The Senate never held a hearing on Garland, and it never held a vote. His nomination produced no committee record and no floor tally. The Senate's role in appointments includes the option not to act.

The third path is procedural. Senate Rule XXXI governs nominations that are still pending when the chamber stops meeting for an extended stretch. If the Senate adjourns or recesses for more than 30 days, those nominations go back to the President. The Senate can prevent that by agreeing, through unanimous consent, to keep them in place.

A returned nomination is no longer before the Senate. No further committee or floor action can take place on it.

The unanimous consent requirement gives each senator leverage at this stage. One objection is enough to stop the Senate from holding pending nominations through a long break. That leaves the fate of those nominations outside the majority's sole control.

These outcomes separate a nomination that is defeated from one that runs out of time. A defeat requires more no votes than yes votes on the floor. A stall or a return requires only that the process stop before any final vote.

Two routes let a nominee take office without a separate, individual Senate roll call. Recess appointments, authorized by Article II, Section 2, Clause 3 of the Constitution, let the President fill vacancies while the Senate is away. Military promotions, in most cases, clear the Senate in bulk by unanimous consent.

The recess appointment power works differently from the standard nomination path. Under the ordinary process, a nominee moves through committee and then the floor before taking office. A recess appointment skips those steps while the Senate is not in session. The President acts alone, and the appointee can begin serving without a confirmation vote.

The central legal question is what counts as a recess. The Supreme Court addressed it in NLRB v. Noel Canning, decided in 2014. The justices held that a Senate recess lasting fewer than 10 days is presumptively too short for the recess appointment power. Under that standard, a break of a few days generally does not qualify.

The ruling put the Senate's calendar at the center of the issue. If the chamber never stays away long enough, the President has no qualifying recess to use. The Senate has used pro forma sessions to avoid long recesses. These are brief sessions held for form's sake during a break. They divide what would otherwise be one long absence into shorter stretches.

Officer promotions follow their own track on the Senate floor. Rather than hold a separate vote for each officer, the Senate groups promotions together. A single unanimous consent request can then clear the whole list.

That shortcut depends on every senator going along. The bulk method covers most military promotions, not every one. A nomination left out of the routine package has to move through the Senate's regular procedures instead.

The two routes rest on different foundations. Recess appointments turn on the calendar and the 10-day line drawn in Noel Canning. Bulk military approvals turn on routine agreement among senators.

#5444. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5443. Claude can now join video calls as an active, visible teammate in Anthropic’s latest push to reinvent white collar jobs beyond coding

Anthropic ‘s Claude Code reinvented the field of software engineering, turning AI into a must-have tool for programmers. Now the company is seeking to do the same across the corporate workplace with a new suite of office productivity tools launched on Tuesday.

The new products are an important part of Anthropic’s effort to broaden its base of paying customers and boost its revenue as it moves closer to a widely-anticipated initial public stock offering. The IPO, which could value Anthropic at roughly $1.4 trillion, is scheduled for as soon as next week, the company revealed separately on Tuesday.

To help create momentum around the product launch, Anthropic held a buzzy launch event in San Francisco Tuesday with hundreds of guests. Anthropic’s Chief Product Officer Ami Vora spoke on stage about how Claude has changed computer coding over the past year. Engineers can now delegate entire tasks to AI, but at the same time the work for most other teams has largely stayed the same, save for perhaps an email getting written faster, or a meeting being summarized.

The new products aim to bring the same AI benefits programmers have enjoyed “for over a year,” Vora said, to knowledge workers across corporations. Anthropic’s renewed push to attract corporate knowledge workers could put the company in closer competition with other software vendors such as Microsoft, whose shares were down more than 2% after the news was announced.

Anthropic’s vision is to turn Claude into an active member a team, rather than an optimization tool for individuals. For example, with Claude Meetings, professionals can add Claude to video calls as a “visible participant,” Anthropic said. The AI listens to the conversation and can “start on the work while people are still talking.” It lays out the proposed plan and timeline, answers questions in the call chat, and handles tasks such as pulling up last year’s numbers, using “the work apps people have connected,” Anthropic said. The results surface in claude.ai after the call.

Claude Meetings is in beta for Team and Enterprise plans, and starting with Google Meet, with plans to expand to other video platforms.

With Claude Whiteboards, humans can brainstorm ideas and collaborate with Claude. “A team talks through a messy plan out loud, and Claude turns it into a board with a timeline, owners and dates,” Anthropic said. Same goes for Claude Sheets, which are spreadsheets teams can build and edit alongside Claude, and can export to Excel or CSV files. Both these products are also in beta.

If these products can automate a meaningful portion of non-coding roles, they could encourage more businesses to sign up for Claude subscription plans. However, they could also create mayhem or burn tokens on AI-generated materials that never get used.

Anthropic is also seeking ways to deeply embed Claude in critical business functions. Another product called Claude Data, formerly Claude Dashboards, connects the AI to systems where companies keep their most important numbers, such as a data warehouse or CRM. Claude Data became available for paid plans today.

Similarly, new Claude Connectors “link Claude to the apps a company already uses, so Claude can pull information from them and take actions in them,” Anthropic said. Over 9,000 apps are available as Claude Connectors, such as Salesforce and Workday. “Teams already do much of their work in apps like these,” Anthropic said. “Now they can open the full app beside the conversation and ask Claude to work in it with them.” That means “no more switching tabs,” said Nicholas Lin, who leads product for knowledge work at Anthropic, on stage at today’s event.

Tuesday’s launch event came on the same day as Anthropic kicked off its pre-IPO roadshow with investors.

The idea of Claude revolutionizing non-coding roles in the same way it’s done for coding could energize the IPO and drive up the share price. Several sources we spoke to think Anthropic’s $70-$78 target share price is intentionally low, a tactic to set expectations and leave room to shatter them.

“Anthropic is moving forward with its IPO at a steeper discount than market initially anticipated,” said Lior Prosor, managing partner of Deep33, a deep-tech venture fund. “We think that is a smart pricing strategy. It gives nervous ‘AI-trade’ investors meaningful potential upside while securing the capital Anthropic needs to take full control of its destiny and fund its compute commitments.”

Also this week, Anthropic debuted new frontier models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, at a lower price with allegedly stronger performance than OpenAI’s latest frontier model, GPT-6 Astra. This also got investors’ attention.

“Anthropic has shown incredible advances recently and their announcement about Fable 5.2 yesterday suggests they could have a bigger impact in hardware domains like robotics than people might have given them credit for previously,” said Bastiaan Janmaat, General Partner at Lithos Capital.

#5442. From House charges to a Senate verdict: 10 parts of U.S. impeachment

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn how impeachment works in the U.S., from House charges and articles of impeachment to the Senate trial, the two-thirds conviction vote and what removal means

Impeachment is an accusation, not an eviction. When the House of Representatives impeaches a president or a federal judge, that official stays in office. Removal can come only later, and only if the Senate votes to convict. That distinction is the one most often blurred in headlines, cable segments and social media posts whenever the word starts trending.

The U.S. Constitution splits the job between the two chambers of Congress by design. The House acts something like a grand jury, deciding whether the evidence justifies formal charges. The Senate acts as the court, hearing the case and delivering a verdict. Each chamber has its own vote threshold, its own procedures and its own political pressures. An official can be impeached by the first and still be acquitted by the second.

The process is rare, but it is not theoretical. The House has impeached presidents four times, and three different men have faced a Senate trial as a result. None was removed. Federal judges are a different story: they are the only officials the Senate has ever convicted. Another president left office before the full House could vote at all.

The Constitution sketches the process in a few short clauses. Much of the detail has been filled in by practice. The House writes its own rules for investigating. The Senate sets its own procedures for trying cases. The Constitution never defines the key phrase describing impeachable conduct, and Congress has interpreted it case by case.

Understanding how impeachment works makes those open questions easier to follow. The 10 slides ahead walk through the process in order. They start with what the word means under the Constitution and who can be impeached. They then cover the grounds for charges, how the House opens an inquiry and how it votes on articles. Next come the Senate trial, the two-thirds bar for conviction and the penalties that follow a conviction. The final slides look back at the presidents who have been impeached. They also compare impeachment with two other routes by which a president can lose power: the 25th Amendment and resignation.

Each slide stands on its own. A reader can go straight to the stage of the process that matters most to them.

Impeachment is the formal act of charging a federal official with misconduct. It is not the act of removing that person from office. Under the U.S. Constitution, the House of Representatives brings the charges, and the Senate decides whether they hold up at trial.

News coverage and everyday conversation often use the word loosely, as if it meant being thrown out of office. That reading skips a step. An official who has been impeached has been accused, much as a criminal defendant who has been indicted stands accused. Neither has been found guilty of anything yet.

The comparison to a criminal case holds only in broad outline. Impeachment is a constitutional proceeding run by Congress, not a prosecution in a courtroom. The two chambers set many of their own procedures for it.

The House's authority comes from Article I, Section 2 of the Constitution. That clause gives the House "the sole Power of Impeachment." No other body can bring the charges.

The Senate's role comes from Article I, Section 3. That section gives the Senate "the sole Power to try all Impeachments." Only the Senate can hold the trial, and only the Senate can deliver the verdict.

Both clauses sit in Article I, the part of the Constitution that establishes Congress. That placement puts impeachment in the hands of the legislature. Courts and the executive branch do not bring the charges or decide the outcome.

The split between the two chambers has a practical consequence. An impeachment by the House, on its own, does not change whether the official holds the job. The person stays in office while the Senate considers the case. If the Senate acquits, the official keeps the position. The impeachment itself still remains part of the official record.

This two-stage design is the core of the process. Every later step — the inquiry, the vote on charges, the trial and any penalty — follows from the division of labor written into those two sections of Article I.

The Constitution allows Congress to impeach the president, the vice president and civil officers of the U.S. government. That coverage, set out in Article II, Section 4, also reaches federal judges. Members of Congress, by contrast, are generally not treated as civil officers who can be impeached.

The presidency draws the most attention, but it is one office among several on the list. Article II, Section 4 places the vice president in the same clause as the president. The two highest executive offices therefore face an identical process. Beyond them, the clause extends to the wider category of civil officers serving in the federal government.

Federal judges hold a distinct place on that list. Their position differs from that of elected officials in one basic way. Article III says federal judges hold office during good behavior. That language gives them no fixed term and no reelection campaign to face. Impeachment gives Congress a constitutional route to end that tenure.

The status of lawmakers was tested early in the country's history. In 1797, the House impeached Senator William Blount. The Senate dismissed the case in 1799 on jurisdictional grounds. A dismissal on those grounds turns on whether the Senate had authority over the case, not on whether the accusations were true.

Rank offers no protection under Article II, Section 4. The clause covers the most senior official in the executive branch, and nothing in its text shields any covered officeholder because of seniority. What the clause does limit is the basis for an impeachment. It ties the process to stated grounds, not to the importance of the person accused.

That structure gives the clause two separate filters. The first asks whether a person holds one of the covered offices. The second asks whether the conduct at issue fits the grounds the Constitution names. Both questions apply to every case brought under the clause.

The Constitution allows impeachment on three grounds: treason, bribery and "other high crimes and misdemeanors." It never defines that last phrase. Congress has given it meaning one case at a time.

The list appears in Article II, Section 4. That clause names the officials who can face impeachment and, in the same sentence, the conduct that can lead to it.

Treason and bribery are named outright. The third category works differently. No clause anywhere in the constitutional text supplies a definition, and no list of qualifying offenses accompanies it. A reader looking for a checklist of impeachable conduct will not find one in the document.

That gap leaves interpretation to Congress. When the House weighs articles of impeachment, its members decide whether the conduct described fits the phrase. When the Senate holds a trial, senators reach their own judgment on the same question. Each vote reflects how individual members read the phrase. The same conduct can draw different answers from different lawmakers.

One question has stayed open: whether an impeachable act must also be an indictable crime. An indictable crime is one that could be charged in a criminal court. Scholars and lawmakers have disagreed on this point. One reading limits the phrase to conduct that breaks a criminal law. Another treats it as broad enough to reach conduct that is not a crime. The Constitution does not resolve the dispute.

The two readings lead to different kinds of charges. Under the narrower reading, an article of impeachment would need to describe conduct that a prosecutor could also take to a criminal court. Under the broader reading, an article could rest on conduct such as a misuse of an office's powers, even where no criminal statute covers it.

The disagreement shapes how impeachment debates unfold. A defense that a charge describes no crime is an argument about this phrase. So is a claim that an official's conduct warrants removal whether or not it breaks a criminal law. Both depend on how members of Congress read a single phrase in Article II, Section 4.

An impeachment inquiry begins in the House of Representatives, where any member can introduce a resolution calling for an official to be impeached. The House Judiciary Committee has usually taken charge of the investigation that follows, though the Constitution sets no fixed procedure for this stage.

Filing a resolution is only a starting point. It does not charge anyone, and it does not commit the House to act. A single lawmaker can put one forward, but the chamber decides whether anything comes of it.

The committee's task at this stage is to establish what happened. It holds hearings and gathers evidence, building the factual record that any later charges would rest on.

The full House can also step in directly. Members can vote to authorize an inquiry, putting the chamber's formal backing behind the investigation.

The Constitution is silent on how any of this should be done. It gives the House the power to impeach but says nothing about who investigates, how evidence is collected or what steps must come before a vote. The House fills that gap itself by setting its own rules.

That arrangement means the inquiry stage is shaped by the chamber's choices rather than by a constitutional script. One inquiry can begin with a member's resolution and committee hearings. Another can begin with a floor vote authorizing the investigation. Both paths fit within the House's authority.

The inquiry is also distinct from what comes later. It is a fact-finding phase, not a trial, and it produces no verdict. No official is impeached during an inquiry. Impeachment itself happens only when the full House approves formal charges.

For readers following an impeachment in the news, the word "inquiry" marks this early, investigative step. It signals that the House is examining an official's conduct. It does not mean the House has decided to bring charges, and it does not mean the official faces removal.

The House impeaches an official by approving at least one article of impeachment, the formal written charge against that person. Each article needs a simple majority of House members voting. If all 435 members cast a vote, 218 votes are enough to pass an article.

Each article sets out one specific allegation of misconduct against the named official. A single impeachment resolution can carry one article or several.

The House does not vote on the package as a whole. Members vote on each article on its own. That allows a lawmaker to support one charge and oppose another. It also means a resolution can leave the House with some articles approved and others rejected.

The majority standard is tied to members voting, not to the full size of the chamber. The 218 figure applies only when all 435 seats are filled and every member votes. A vacant seat, after a death or resignation, cannot cast a vote. When fewer members take part, the number needed for a majority falls with them. If 410 members vote, for example, 206 votes would pass an article. A tie vote fails. A majority means more than half of the votes cast.

Approval of one article is enough. Once an article passes, the official has been impeached, regardless of what the Senate later decides.

After the vote, the House names managers to carry the case forward. The managers are themselves members of the House. They act as prosecutors once the matter moves to the Senate. They present the charges contained in the approved articles and argue for conviction.

Only the articles that win a majority travel to the Senate. The House delivers the approved articles to the Senate, which then organizes the trial. A charge the House rejects is not part of the impeachment. The Senate does not weigh it at trial.

A Senate impeachment trial turns senators into jurors who weigh the House's charges and decide whether to convict. House managers argue the case, the official's defense team answers it, and the Senate votes on each article separately.

That jury role begins with an oath or affirmation. Every senator takes one before hearing the case. Outside a trial, senators debate and pass legislation. During one, they sit in judgment of a specific official on specific charges. The affirmation exists as an alternative for senators who prefer not to swear an oath.

Who presides depends on who is on trial. When the president is the defendant, Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution requires the chief justice of the Supreme Court to preside. That requirement applies only to presidential trials. It places the head of the federal judiciary in the chair.

The prosecution comes from the House. Its case is presented by House members known as impeachment managers. In the Senate chamber, those managers lay out the evidence and arguments behind each charge. The accused official is represented by a defense team, which responds to the managers and argues for acquittal. Senators hear both sides before any vote is taken.

The verdict is not a single up-or-down vote on the whole case. Senators vote on each article on its own. The result can differ from one charge to the next. A conviction on any single article is enough to convict the official, even if the other articles fail. Each conviction vote requires two-thirds of the senators present.

Federal courts have left these procedures to the Senate. In Nixon v. United States, decided in 1993, the Supreme Court held that challenges to the Senate's trial procedures were nonjusticiable. In practical terms, that means courts will not hear such disputes. The Senate decides for itself how to run an impeachment trial. The case involved Judge Walter Nixon, not President Richard Nixon.

Convicting an impeached official takes the votes of two-thirds of the senators present, a requirement written into Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution. When all 100 senators vote, at least 67 must vote to convict.

The threshold is measured against attendance, not against the full size of the chamber. An absent senator does not count toward the base used to calculate two-thirds. If 99 senators are present, conviction takes 66 votes. If 98 are present, 65 votes would fall just short of two-thirds, so conviction still takes 66.

The same math shows how few votes it takes to stop a conviction. With every senator voting, 34 votes against an article are enough to defeat it. The blocking number stays at 34 when 99 senators are present, because 66 votes would still be needed to convict. That means a bloc of just over one-third of the chamber can end the case on that charge.

The Senate standard sits well above the simple majority the House uses to impeach. The same two-thirds standard applies whether the accused official is a president, a federal judge or another civil officer.

The higher Senate number has a political consequence. Conviction generally requires votes from senators of both parties. For one party to convict on its own, it would need at least 67 seats, with all 100 senators present and every member of that party voting together.

Seat counts show how much cross-party support a conviction needs. A party holding 50 seats, with all 100 senators present, would need at least 17 votes from outside its ranks. A party holding 60 seats would still need seven. In practice, the side pressing for conviction has to persuade members of the opposing party.

That threshold has never been reached in a presidential case. No president has been convicted by the Senate.

If no article reaches two-thirds, the official is acquitted on every charge and keeps the job.

A Senate conviction removes the official from office. The Senate can also bar that person from holding federal office in the future. The Constitution allows no other penalty in an impeachment case.

Article I, Section 3 limits judgment in cases of impeachment to removal from office and disqualification from holding federal office. The Senate cannot impose a fine, order prison time or seize property as part of an impeachment judgment. An impeachment trial decides whether someone may hold federal office. It does not decide whether that person is punished as a criminal.

Removal comes with the conviction itself. Once the Senate convicts on an article, the official loses the office.

Disqualification works differently. It is optional, and the Senate has decided it through a separate vote. That vote has required only a simple majority. The case of Judge Thomas Porteous shows how the two steps fit together. The Senate removed Porteous from the federal bench in 2010. Then, in its own vote, it barred him from holding future federal office.

The two penalties do different things. Removal ends the official's time in their current post. Disqualification looks forward and closes off future federal office.

Leaving office through impeachment does not end the possibility of criminal charges. Article I, Section 3 states that the convicted party remains "liable and subject to Indictment, Trial, Judgment and Punishment, according to Law." Prosecutors may bring an ordinary criminal case over the same conduct. Such a case would run through the regular courts under criminal law, not under Senate trial rules.

The president's pardon power has a specific limit here. Article II, Section 2 lets the president grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the U.S., "except in Cases of Impeachment." A president cannot use a pardon to undo an impeachment or reverse a Senate conviction. No pardon can restore a removed official to office or lift a bar on future federal service.

Three U.S. presidents have been impeached by the House of Representatives: Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump. The Senate acquitted all three men every time, and none was removed from office.

Andrew Johnson was the first. The House impeached him in 1868, which sent the case to the Senate for trial. Senators acquitted him by a single vote. One more vote to convict would have removed him from office.

Johnson's case stood alone for 130 years. The House did not impeach another president until 1998.

That president was Bill Clinton. The House impeached him on December 19, 1998. His Senate trial ran into the next year. Senators acquitted Clinton on February 12, 1999, less than two months after the House vote. He stayed in office. He remains the only president impeached in the 20th century.

Donald Trump became the third impeached president about 21 years after Clinton. The House first impeached him in December 2019. The Senate acquitted him on February 5, 2020.

The House impeached Trump again on January 13, 2021, roughly 13 months after the first time. The Senate acquitted him one month later, on February 13, 2021. Trump is the only president to face two impeachments. They came in consecutive years, the shortest gap between any two presidential impeachments.

The second trial centered on a single article of impeachment. Senators voted 57 to 43. A majority of the chamber sided with conviction. The tally still fell short of the two-thirds threshold the Constitution sets for a guilty verdict.

Richard Nixon is absent from this list because the full House never voted to impeach him.

Federal judges have a different record. They are the only federal officials the Senate has convicted. The House has impeached 15 federal judges, and eight of them were convicted. The other seven ended without a conviction. No presidential impeachment has ended that way.

Impeachment charges an official with misconduct. The 25th Amendment addresses a president who cannot do the job, and resignation is a voluntary exit. The three are often mentioned together, but they work in different ways and serve different purposes.

The 25th Amendment was ratified in 1967. It governs presidential disability and succession. Its focus is whether the president is able to serve, not how the president has behaved in office.

Section 4 of the amendment allows the vice president and a majority of the cabinet to declare that the president is unable to serve. That decision starts inside the executive branch. Impeachment, by contrast, begins with charges brought by the House of Representatives.

The 25th Amendment is not a punishment process. It does not accuse the president of wrongdoing. It involves no articles, no prosecutors and no trial. An impeachment, on the other hand, is a formal accusation that an official has committed an offense serious enough to justify removal. The 25th Amendment applies only to the president, while impeachment reaches the vice president, federal judges and other civil officers as well.

Resignation works differently from both. When an official steps down, the impeachment process usually ends without a Senate verdict. No senator votes to convict or acquit. The question of guilt is never formally resolved.

Richard Nixon followed this path. He resigned on August 9, 1974. By then, the House Judiciary Committee had approved articles of impeachment against him. The full House never held a floor vote on those articles. Nixon was never impeached by the full House.

Resignation does not always stop Congress, though. In 1876, the House impeached William Belknap, the former secretary of war, despite his resignation. The case went to a Senate trial, and the Senate acquitted him.

Of the three routes, impeachment is the only one that runs through both chambers of Congress. It is also the only one that ends in a vote on specific charges.

#5441. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5440. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5439. One mom tallied 23 hours a week of household work. Then she built a company to turn ‘invisible labor’ into a paid profession

Kelly Hubbell worked full-time in tech sales and raised two children when the overwhelm set in. She didn’t need a nanny—both kids were in daycare—but the household work kept piling up, and she was desperate for support.

So she made a list of everything she did to keep the house running. It added up to 23 hours a week. Most of that time, Hubbell realized, wasn’t the chores themselves. It was the mental work of planning them.

“I just thought, wouldn’t it be awesome if I could clone myself?” Hubbell said.

Instead, she went looking for what she called a “house manager,” someone who could take over the logistics and errands she had been cramming into her evenings and weekends. She found one.

“It completely changed my life,” Hubbell said. “Overnight, I felt like I could be a present parent, and I had relief from the mental load, because I was able to fully hand off tasks.”

That relief became a business. In 2023, during her third maternity leave, Hubbell founded Sage Haus, a white-glove service that helps parents hire a house manager and set up the “home-management systems” that make handing off work possible. Its pitch arrives as women hold more U.S. payroll jobs than men for only the third time in the country’s history, while still shouldering most of the planning that keeps a household running.

Sage Haus isn’t alone. “House manager” now turns up in job listings on Indeed and Care.com, and other agencies have emerged to place house managers with busy parents.

The difference between a house manager and a babysitter is ownership. A babysitter who noticed your child had outgrown their shoes, took your credit card, and bought a new pair without asking would be overstepping. For a house manager, that is the job.

That kind of help doesn’t come cheap. Sage Haus families typically pay a house manager $25 to $45 an hour for 15 to 20 hours a week, according to the company, or roughly $20,000 to $47,000 a year. Full-time house managers generally earn $50,000 to $120,000, depending on location and scope, and Sage Haus charges families a flat placement fee rather than a percentage of salary.

Those rates run well above the broader market. House manager job postings on Indeed average about $23 an hour.

The services are marketed to dual-income families who simply don’t have enough hours in the day. Hubbell said many of the women she has worked with told her that before they hired help, they feared they would have to leave careers they loved to take care of their homes.

That fear has data behind it. KPMG research found that mothers of young children cut hours or left work at higher rates than fathers, pushed by return-to-office mandates and scarce, expensive childcare.

In the U.S., mothers handle 71% of household mental-load tasks, the cognitive work of planning meals, arranging activities, and keeping family life on schedule, according to a 2024 study by researchers at the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne. Fathers report handling 45%; the shares overlap because some tasks are shared.

In a world where someone from an app will deliver your dinner or build your IKEA furniture, Sage Haus wants to break the taboo around hiring help at home.

“We are putting a value on what has historically been invisible labor on the backs of mostly women, and that makes a lot of people uncomfortable,” Hubbell said. “Part of our mission is to normalize this, to take out the shame and the guilt around getting the kind of support that we need.”

In 2024, Hubbell quit her job to run Sage Haus full time. The company now has more than 60 employees and works with about 100 families a month across the U.S. and Canada, she said.

Sage Haus also draws on a network of more than 7,000 house managers and sells a $99 House Manager Certification course, which teaches them to anticipate needs, practice discretion, and become an integral part of a household.

Hubbell sees the role as a career path in both directions. She thinks house managers could move into corporate administrative work, and she has watched executive assistants switch into house management.

“I do believe that it takes high executive functioning to be in this role,” Hubbell said.

The work being handed off was never small. In 2020, Oxfam estimated that the unpaid care work done by women and girls worldwide is worth at least $10.8 trillion a year. In the U.S. alone, unpaid household labor is worth up to $6 trillion a year, about a fifth of GDP, and none of it appears in official growth figures.

Perhaps paying someone to make your grocery list is a late-stage-capitalist offering for families that have it all. But while hiring help has long been considered a luxury, companies like Sage Haus are asking why work traditionally done by women was ever free in the first place.
