#5438. What executive orders can and can't do: 10 powers and limits explained

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A guide to what executive orders can and can't do, covering 10 points on presidential authority, emergency powers, court challenges, congressional limits and revocation by later presidents

An executive order carries the weight of the presidency, yet none of its power is its own. The authority behind it comes from the Constitution or from a law Congress has already passed. That borrowed footing explains both how much an order can accomplish and where it stops.

Executive orders shape daily life in ways that are easy to miss. They tell federal agencies which laws to enforce first and how to read ambiguous statutes. They set terms for the civil servants who run the government and for the companies that sell it goods and services. A single signature can change how a regulation is drafted or how a federal contract is written.

That reach draws heavy news coverage. It also leaves many readers with a reasonable question: are executive orders law? The short answer is that they carry legal force inside the executive branch, but they are not statutes. Congress writes statutes. The president directs the people and agencies that carry them out.

Understanding what executive orders can and can't do starts with three checks built into the U.S. system. The Constitution sets the outer boundary. An order that violates it is invalid, no matter how sweeping its language. Congress holds the power to make laws and to fund the government. That means it can narrow an order's reach or override it outright. The federal courts decide disputes over whether a president stayed within those limits. The Supreme Court has struck down presidential action that went beyond them.

The fourth limit is the next president. An order does not expire when the president who signed it leaves office, unless its own text says so. But the next president can revoke or rewrite it with a new order, without any vote in Congress.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of these powers and limits. They begin with where an order's authority comes from, then turn to agency enforcement, federal workforce and contractor rules and national emergency declarations. Later slides cover lawmaking and spending, constitutional rights, judicial review and congressional action. The last two address states and private citizens, then revocation by a later president. Each slide stands on its own.

Every executive order must rest on one of two foundations. One is a power the Constitution gives the president in Article II. The other is a power Congress has delegated to the executive branch through a statute. An order that rests on neither cannot be enforced.

An executive order is a written directive from the president to the federal government. It tells officials and agencies what to do. It is not a law passed by Congress, and its strength depends entirely on the source it cites.

The Constitution never uses the phrase "executive order." The practice grew out of the broad grant of power in Article II. That article opens by vesting "the executive Power" in a president. It also makes the president commander in chief of the armed forces. And it directs the president to "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed."

Those clauses give the president room to manage the executive branch. They do not give unlimited room. An order grounded in Article II has to fit within powers the Constitution actually assigns to the office.

The second foundation is delegation. Congress often writes statutes that authorize the president to act in a specific area. When an order relies on such a law, its reach depends on the statute's wording. If the law grants narrow authority, the order is narrow too.

Many orders state their legal basis in the opening lines. A typical order cites the Constitution and the laws of the U.S. as the source of the president's authority. That citation tells agencies and courts where the power to act comes from.

Executive orders are numbered in sequence and published in the Federal Register, the federal government's daily journal of official documents. The Federal Register Act of 1935 requires publication of presidential orders that have general applicability and legal effect. Publication creates a permanent public record that anyone can read.

The numbering system arrived long after the practice began. The State Department started assigning numbers in 1907. It worked backward to cover earlier orders, designating an 1862 order from President Abraham Lincoln as Executive Order 1.

A president can use an executive order to tell federal agencies how to carry out laws Congress has already passed. That includes which cases to prioritize, how to read an unclear provision and how firmly to enforce a rule.

This power follows from the president's position at the head of the executive branch. Cabinet departments and most federal agencies answer to the White House. An order is the formal, written way a president gives them instructions.

The main limit is that the order works inside existing law. It shapes how an agency uses authority it already has. It does not hand the agency new authority that Congress never granted.

Enforcement priorities are a common use. A statute may cover far more conduct than an agency has staff or budget to police. An order can tell the agency where to focus first and which cases to set aside.

Interpretation is a second lever. Laws often leave gaps or use broad terms. An order can steer agencies toward one reading of that language. That reading then guides their regulations and decisions. Courts can still review whether an agency's reading fits the statute.

Executive Order 9981 shows how far this kind of direction can reach. President Harry Truman signed it on July 26, 1948. It declared a policy of equality of treatment and opportunity for everyone in the armed services, without regard to race, color, religion or national origin.

Truman did not need Congress to pass a new law first. He acted under his authority as commander in chief, which Article II of the Constitution gives the president. That authority covers the military. An order to the armed forces fell squarely within it.

The order also created a presidential committee to recommend how the services should put the new policy into practice. It called for changes as rapidly as possible without impairing efficiency or morale. Full desegregation of the services took years after the signing.

The example illustrates a broader pattern. An order carries the most weight when it addresses officials the president already supervises, using powers the president already holds.

A president can use executive orders to set workplace rules for the federal workforce and for companies that do business with the government. The president runs the executive branch. That role includes oversight of how the government hires its workers and how it buys goods and services.

Executive Order 11246, signed by President Lyndon Johnson in 1965, set nondiscrimination requirements for federal contractors. Companies that wanted government business had to accept those terms as a condition of their contracts.

The order did not cover every employer in the U.S. Its reach came through the contracting relationship. A business with no federal contract fell outside its terms. That is the basic logic of contractor orders. The government sets conditions on the deals it signs.

Johnson's order was amended in 1967 by Executive Order 11375, which added sex discrimination to the covered categories. The change came through a new order, not through an act of Congress.

Contractor orders often rest on the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949, commonly called the Procurement Act. That law gives the president authority to set procurement policy for the executive branch. Courts have treated it as a basis for many contractor requirements.

That authority has limits. In 1995, President Bill Clinton issued Executive Order 12954, which barred certain contractors from permanently replacing striking workers. In Chamber of Commerce v. Reich, decided in 1996, a federal appeals court held that the National Labor Relations Act preempted the order.

The president has more direct control over the federal workforce itself. A federal statute, 5 U.S.C. 7301, lets the president prescribe rules of conduct for executive branch employees. In 1962, President John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 10988, which allowed federal employees to bargain collectively through unions.

Orders like these can change hiring practices, workplace standards and contract clauses without new legislation. They still operate inside the civil service and procurement laws Congress has written. When an order conflicts with one of those statutes, the statute controls.

A national emergency declaration does not give the president new power on its own. Under the National Emergencies Act of 1976, a declaration activates authorities that other federal statutes already tie to an emergency.

The declaration and the power are two different things. The act lets the president declare a national emergency, but that step works like a key rather than a source of authority. What the president can do afterward depends on the separate laws Congress wrote to take effect during an emergency.

The act also sets procedural requirements. A president must publish the declaration in the Federal Register and send it to Congress. The president must also name the specific statutory provisions he or she plans to use. If no law connects an action to an emergency, the declaration cannot supply that power.

One widely used example is the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977. Once an emergency is declared over a foreign threat, that statute lets the president block assets and restrict financial transactions. Many U.S. sanctions programs rest on it. Without a declaration, those powers stay unavailable.

A declared emergency does not last indefinitely by default. It ends automatically after one year unless the president publishes a notice in the Federal Register continuing it. Presidents routinely file these renewals. Some emergencies have stayed in effect for decades.

Congress has its own way to end an emergency. Lawmakers can pass a joint resolution that terminates the declaration, and that resolution is subject to a presidential veto. The act originally allowed termination by concurrent resolution, which does not go to the president. After the Supreme Court struck down legislative vetoes in INS v. Chadha in 1983, Congress switched the mechanism to a joint resolution in 1985.

Whether a president can take a given step during a declared emergency turns on the underlying statute. Congress decides in advance which powers an emergency can unlock. The president decides when to declare one.

An executive order cannot make new law, impose a tax or fund a program Congress has not paid for. The Constitution gives those powers to Congress, and an order cannot transfer them to the president.

Article I opens by vesting "all legislative Powers herein granted" in a Congress made up of a Senate and a House of Representatives. The president's formal part in passing a bill comes after Congress acts, when he signs it or vetoes it. An order that tries to create a new legal duty for the public, with no statute behind it, steps outside the executive role.

Money follows the same logic. Article I, Section 9 says no money may be drawn from the Treasury except through appropriations made by law. That provision is known as the Appropriations Clause. It means the executive branch cannot spend federal funds simply because a president wants a project done.

The taxing power also sits with Congress. Article I, Section 8 lists the power to lay and collect taxes among the powers of Congress. Article I, Section 7 adds that bills for raising revenue must originate in the House. A president cannot create a new tax by signing an order.

What an order can do is steer money Congress has already provided. Appropriations laws often leave agencies room to choose among eligible projects or to set priorities within a funding stream. A president can use an order to direct how agencies use that discretion. The direction must stay inside the amount, purpose and time period Congress set.

Federal statutes reinforce these constitutional limits. The Antideficiency Act bars federal officials from spending or committing money beyond what Congress has appropriated. Officials who break it can face administrative discipline. Knowing and willful violations can also carry criminal penalties.

The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 addresses the reverse situation, in which a president wants to hold back money Congress has approved. Under that law, a president may propose canceling funds, a request known as a rescission. If Congress does not approve the proposal within 45 days of continuous session, the money must be made available for spending.

Together, these rules set the boundary. An executive order can organize, prioritize and direct the work of federal agencies. Creating a program, a tax or a new source of funding requires a bill that passes both chambers and becomes law.

An executive order that conflicts with the Constitution has no legal force. Presidential directives rank below the Constitution, and a court can declare an order invalid when it violates a constitutional right or limit.

That rule follows from the document's own structure. Article VI makes the Constitution the supreme law of the land. Article II requires each president to take an oath to preserve, protect and defend it. A directive from the same office cannot outrank the text its author swore to uphold.

The Bill of Rights adds specific limits. The Fifth Amendment bars the federal government from depriving any person of life, liberty or property without due process of law. An executive order is federal action. That guarantee applies to it just as it applies to a statute passed by Congress.

No order can amend the Constitution either. Article V requires an amendment to be proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress or by a convention called at the request of two-thirds of the states. Ratification then takes three-fourths of the states. The president has no formal role in that process.

A written limit does not always stop an order when it is issued. Executive Order 9066 is a cautionary example. President Franklin Roosevelt signed it in February 1942. It authorized the removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast.

The Supreme Court upheld the use of that order in Korematsu v. United States in 1944.

The Court repudiated Korematsu in Trump v. Hawaii in 2018. The majority opinion in that case stated that Korematsu was wrong the day it was decided.

The sequence shows that a ruling in an order's favor is not necessarily the final judgment on its constitutionality. A later Court can reject the earlier reasoning outright. The Constitution's limits apply to every executive order, whichever president signs it.

Federal courts can strike down an executive order that goes beyond the president's legal authority. The leading case is Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer. On June 2, 1952, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that President Harry Truman lacked the power to seize the nation's steel mills during the Korean War.

The case grew out of a labor dispute. In April 1952, the United Steelworkers union was preparing to strike. Truman feared a shutdown would cut off steel needed for weapons and ammunition in Korea. He issued Executive Order 10340. It directed Secretary of Commerce Charles Sawyer to take possession of the mills and keep them running.

The steel companies sued. They argued that no statute and no clause of the Constitution allowed the president to take private property this way. The government countered that the president held inherent power to act in a national emergency. It also pointed to his role as commander in chief.

Justice Hugo Black wrote the majority opinion. He held that the president's power to issue an order must come from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself. Neither supported the seizure. Black rejected the idea that the commander-in-chief role let the president take private property to keep a labor dispute from halting production. That kind of policy choice, he wrote, belonged to Congress.

Truman complied with the ruling and returned the mills to their owners. Chief Justice Fred Vinson wrote the dissent, joined by Justices Stanley Reed and Sherman Minton.

Justice Robert Jackson wrote a concurring opinion that has outlasted the case itself. He sorted presidential action into three tiers. Power is at its strongest when the president acts with authorization from Congress. It falls into an uncertain middle zone when Congress has said nothing. It is at its weakest when the president acts against the expressed or implied will of Congress.

Jackson placed the steel seizure in the third tier. Congress had considered seizure as a tool for labor emergencies and chose other methods instead. Those methods included the procedures in the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947.

Courts still use Jackson's framework when an executive order is challenged. The Supreme Court relied on it in Dames & Moore v. Regan in 1981, a case over the agreements that ended the Iran hostage crisis. It applied the framework again in Medellín v. Texas in 2008. The test asks the same basic question in each case: what has Congress said, and does the president's action fit within it?

Congress can undo an executive order in three ways. It can pass a law that supersedes the order, change the statute the order relies on or cut off the money needed to carry it out. Each route requires a bill that clears both chambers and survives a possible presidential veto.

The most direct option is a superseding statute. An executive order ranks below an act of Congress. When the two conflict on a matter within Congress's constitutional authority, the statute controls. Lawmakers can write a bill that bars the policy an order sets out. They can also require agencies to act in a different way.

A second option targets the order's foundation. Many orders rest on power that Congress delegated through a specific statute. If lawmakers amend or repeal that statute, the delegated authority can narrow or disappear. An order built on it can then lose its legal footing, even if the new bill never names the order.

The third option uses the power of the purse. Congress can attach language to an appropriations bill stating that no funds may be spent to implement a particular order. An agency cannot carry out work that has no money behind it. Lawmakers can write these limits into the regular spending bills that fund the government.

Every one of these routes ends at the president's desk. Under Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution, a bill passed by both chambers goes to the president. The president can sign it or veto it. A president can veto a bill that would reverse one of his or her own orders.

The Constitution gives the president 10 days, Sundays excepted, to act on a bill. If Congress adjourns during that window and prevents the bill's return, the unsigned bill does not become law. This is known as a pocket veto. Congress has no chance to override it.

Overcoming a regular veto takes a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate. The Supreme Court held in Missouri Pacific Railway Co. v. Kansas that this means two-thirds of members present and voting, provided a quorum is present. When neither party holds that many seats, an override needs votes from both parties.

The legislative route works differently from a lawsuit. A court asks whether an order was lawful. Congress can change the law going forward, whether or not the order was valid when the president signed it.

An executive order binds the executive branch, not the public at large. Private citizens and state governments feel its effects indirectly, through what federal agencies do in response, such as issuing regulations, changing enforcement priorities or writing contract terms.

That limit follows from what an order is. It is an instruction from the president to the officials who carry out federal law. A cabinet department or a federal procurement office can be told what to do. A shop owner, a landlord or a commuter is not part of that chain of command.

The route to the public usually runs through an agency. An order might direct a department to draft a rule on a particular subject. Under the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946, many such rules go through public notice and comment before they take effect. Once finalized, the rule can carry legal force for individuals and companies.

In that case, the obligation on a private person comes from the regulation and the statute behind it. The order supplied the direction. It did not, by itself, create a duty for anyone outside government.

States stand on different footing. The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states, or to the people, the powers the Constitution neither delegates to the federal government nor denies to the states. States are separate sovereigns with their own legislatures, courts and executives.

A president cannot order a state legislature to pass a law, repeal one or adopt a policy. Governors do not report to the White House.

In Printz v. United States (1997), the Supreme Court held that the federal government cannot command state officers to administer or enforce a federal regulatory program. That case involved an act of Congress. The principle limits the federal government as a whole, not only the president.

Federal money is another route to influence states, and it has its own limits. Conditions attached to federal funding for states must be authorized by Congress. A president cannot add new strings to state grants on presidential authority alone.

In South Dakota v. Dole (1987), the Supreme Court upheld a law tying a portion of federal highway funds to states setting a minimum drinking age of 21. That condition came from Congress and was written into statute.

The practical test of an order's reach is whom it addresses. When the answer is a federal agency, the public feels the effect only after that agency acts within the authority the law gives it.

Yes. A president can revoke, amend or replace any executive order by signing a new one. That power belongs equally to the president who issued the original and to every successor who follows.

The reason is structural. An executive order is not a statute. It is a directive from the head of the executive branch to the people who work in it. Whoever holds that office can change the directive. A new president does not need the consent of the predecessor who signed the original order.

The new order does the work. It typically names the earlier order by number and states that it is revoked in whole or in part. A partial revocation can strike specific sections while leaving the rest in force. The replacement order is published in the Federal Register like any other. That gives the public a written record of what changed and when.

A change in administration does not end an order on its own. An executive order stays in force after the president who signed it leaves office. Unless its own text sets an end date or a condition for expiring, it does not lapse with the passage of time. An order that no successor revisits can remain in effect across several administrations.

Revocation also looks forward, not backward. Actions taken lawfully while an order was in effect stay valid after it is withdrawn. A contract signed, a policy carried out or a decision made under the old order is not erased by the new one.

Rules that agencies formally adopted to carry out an order can be harder to unwind. A final regulation issued through notice-and-comment rulemaking generally has to be rescinded through a similar process. A new executive order can direct an agency to begin that work. It cannot delete the regulation by itself.

Statutes sit on firmer ground. A law passed by Congress and signed by a president can be repealed only by Congress. A policy first set by executive order becomes harder to reverse if lawmakers later write it into a statute.

#5437. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5436. Anthropic inks $3.4 billion deal for gas-powered data centers—the largest of its kind—to secure AI autonomy ahead of planned IPO

In late September, investment banking company Piper Sandler released a short memo saying it had served as a financial advisor for San Antonio-based equipment supplier OnePWR Solutions on its $3.4 billion sale of its power generation platform to a “frontier AI lab.”

Now, the AI lab in question has been revealed. Anthropic is committing $3.4 billion to secure gas-fired power generators for its expanding data center operations—the largest direct investment in power generation equipment by an AI company, according to the Financial Times.

The deal involves 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty natural gas generators from OnePWR Solutions, according to the FT. Anthropic agreed to the transaction, taking over generator commitments that OnePWR had previously made with Caterpillar. The arrangement also includes engineering and construction capabilities necessary to install the equipment. The generators are expected to become available in the next two years.

Meanwhile, Anthropic is preparing for its IPO, with the company filing its S-1 with the SEC in September. In the registration statement, Anthropic disclosed approximately $900.9 billion in aggregate committed spending on computing and infrastructure, which would include purchase commitments and lease agreements. Of that amount, about $451.6 billion is expected to be spent before 2030, with most of the remaining commitments extending through 2045. Another $70.7 billion is due within the 12 months following Sep. 30, according to the amended S-1 filed in November.

The company is seeking a $1.3 trillion valuation, selling 825 million shares at a range of $70 to $78 a piece.

The S-1 also outlined key concerns for Anthropic, of which gas-powered data centers were included. The company warned that the dependence on natural gas could put the data center buildout under threat of volatile prices.

“As data center operators increasingly rely on natural gas-fired generation, and because behind-the-meter and on-site arrangements are feasible only in some jurisdictions given the applicable regulatory frameworks, we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas,” the filing read.

Anthropic and OnePWR Solutions did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune.

The commitments outlined in Anthropic’s S-1 reflect the company’s effort to secure its own computing capacity needed to develop and operate its AI models. Currently, Anthropic’s infrastructure strategy spans several technology suppliers including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Nvidia, and AMD.

But the S-1 describes a strategy called “Anthropic Direct,” in which the company can lease chips directly and place them in dedicated data centers on its behalf. According to the filing, it allows Anthropic to separate its “commitments for data center capacity” from its “commitments for the compute infrastructure deployed inside them.”

“Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs,” the S-1 reads, “this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain.”

The filing also makes it clear electricity and power are becoming a major constraint on that expansion. Anthropic warned that transformers, turbines, generators, substations, and other electrical equipment can take years to procure, with manufacturers facing higher prices, tariffs and limited production capacity. Alongside those concerns, the company also acknowledged it may need to purchase long-lead-time power generation at prices above market rates.

Anthropic specifically disclosed that some planned data center facilities rely on dedicated natural gas-fired generation, exposing it to fluctuations in fuel lines, pipeline capacity constraints, and disruptions to natural gas supplies.

While Anthropic just agreed to the largest acquisition deal for power generation equipment as of yet, it’s not the only AI-forward company looking to secure its own power generation.

In December 2025, Alphabet—the parent company of Google—acquired energy developer Intersect Power for $4.75 billion. Intersect had been working with Google to colocate data centers with new electricity generation, and the deal gave Google greater control over how quickly it could bring new power generation online.

Elon Musk’s xAI also turned to natural gas turbines to power its Colossus data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi after the existing grid connections couldn’t provide sufficient power.

Meanwhile, Meta has pursued on-site natural gas generation for its Ohio data center campus, working with energy infrastructure company Williams on a project worth approximately $1.6 billion in energy generation equipment, according to the Milken Institute.

And Microsoft signed a 20-year agreement with Constellation Energy in September 2024 to purchase electricity from the Three Mile Island nuclear facility in Pennsylvania, a $16 billion agreement.

Amazon has also pursued data center energy capacity through an agreement with Talen Energy, a nuclear-powered data center campus adjacent to the Susquehanna nuclear power plant in Pennsylvania.

“We’re making the largest private sector investment in state history–$20 billion–to bring 1,250 high-skilled jobs and economic benefits to the state, while also collaborating with Talen Energy to help power our infrastructure with carbon-free energy,” AWS Vice President of Global Data Centers Kevin Miller, said in a Talen Energy press release at the time.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5434. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”

#5433. How the Congressional Review Act lets Congress overturn agency rules

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Congressional Review Act lets Congress cancel federal agency rules, and these 10 explainers cover how it works, from major rules and Senate fast-track votes to the lookback period

Congress writes the laws, but federal agencies write many of the detailed rules that carry the force of law. Lawmakers routinely hand agencies the authority to fill in details on workplace safety, financial markets, energy use and much more. That delegation raises a basic question about accountability. Once an agency finalizes a rule, how can Congress take back a specific decision it never voted on?

The Congressional Review Act is Congress's statutory answer. Passed in 1996 and signed by President Bill Clinton, the law gives Congress a set procedure to overturn individual rules issued by executive-branch agencies. It does not require lawmakers to rewrite the underlying statute. Congress instead passes a short measure called a joint resolution of disapproval, aimed at a single rule.

Both chambers must pass the same resolution, which then goes to the president. That final step shapes much of how the law is used. The president can veto the resolution, and overriding a veto takes two-thirds of each chamber. Successful uses have mostly come when the president and congressional majorities share a party and the targeted rule came from a predecessor.

Timing also shapes the outcome. The law sets windows for introducing resolutions and for using a special Senate procedure that sidesteps the filibuster. Through the lookback period, rules submitted late in a congressional session can become targets for the next Congress. That leaves rules finalized late in an administration exposed when power changes hands.

A successful disapproval has lasting effects. The canceled rule is treated as though it never took effect. The agency also faces limits on issuing a similar rule later, under statutory language that has never been precisely defined.

The law produced no successful disapproval until 2001. That first success stood alone for years. That changed in 2017, when a Republican Congress and President Donald Trump used it to overturn many Obama-era rules.

The 10 slides that follow explain how Congress cancels federal rules under this law. They cover what counts as a rule, how agencies report to Congress, the special treatment of major rules and the procedures in each chamber. They also explain the president's role and what happens after a disapproval. Each slide stands on its own, so readers can start with whichever part of the process they need.

Congress passed the Congressional Review Act in 1996, and President Bill Clinton signed it into law on March 29 of that year. The law gives Congress a formal way to overturn rules that executive-branch agencies issue under powers Congress handed to them.

The act did not arrive as a standalone bill. Lawmakers enacted it as one part of a larger package, the Contract with America Advancement Act. Clinton's signature on that broader measure put the review process into federal law.

The statute is codified at 5 U.S.C. sections 801 to 808. Those eight sections hold the full framework, from how agencies report new rules to what happens after Congress acts on them. That placement gives the process a fixed legal address. Lawmakers and agencies work from the same set of provisions each time a rule comes up for review.

The law responds to a problem that starts with delegation. Congress often writes statutes in broad terms. It then assigns the detailed work of carrying them out to federal agencies.

Those agencies write rules that fill in the specifics. Congress does not vote on each of those rules before an agency issues it. The authority to write them comes from statutes Congress has already passed.

The 1996 law added a check rather than a rewrite of that system. Agencies kept the rulemaking authority Congress had already granted them. What changed was that Congress gained a set procedure for answering a finished rule.

The law's scope follows from that arrangement. It applies to rules from executive-branch agencies acting under authority Congress delegated. The branch that granted the power keeps a statutory path to cancel a particular use of it.

The Congressional Review Act covers a wide range of agency actions. Its definition of "rule" comes from the Administrative Procedure Act, the law that sets out how federal agencies make regulations.

That borrowed definition is broad. A document does not need to carry the label "regulation" to fall within it. What matters is whether the document meets the statutory terms.

The review law then carves out three categories. The first is rules of particular applicability. These are actions aimed at a specific party or circumstance rather than at the public generally.

The second exclusion covers rules about internal agency management. Such rules stay outside the law only if they do not substantially affect parties outside the agency. A directive that reaches no one beyond the agency's own operations would meet that condition.

The third exclusion covers rules of agency organization, procedure or practice. A similar condition attaches. These rules escape review only if they do not substantially affect the rights or obligations of outside parties.

The qualifier in the last two exclusions limits their reach. A procedural or management rule that changes what outside parties must do, or what they are entitled to, does not fit either exemption. Such a rule remains subject to review.

Guidance documents have been a point of dispute. Agencies issue guidance to explain how they read a statute or how they intend to apply it. Whether a given guidance document qualifies as a rule under the review law has been contested.

The Government Accountability Office has issued opinions on such questions. Those opinions address whether a particular agency document meets the statute's definition of a rule. Each opinion applies the statutory definition and its three exclusions to one specific document.

The definition sets the threshold for everything else in the statute. An agency action that falls outside it cannot be overturned through a joint resolution of disapproval under this law.

Federal agencies must send each new rule, along with a report on it, to both chambers of Congress and to the Comptroller General before the rule can take effect. That delivery opens Congress's chance to review the rule under the Congressional Review Act.

The Comptroller General heads the Government Accountability Office, or GAO. The submission therefore goes to three recipients: the House, the Senate and the head of the GAO. Each receives the rule itself and the agency's report on it.

The duty is not limited to the costliest regulations. It applies to every action that meets the law's definition of a rule, whether or not the rule is classified as major. A routine regulation and a sweeping one face the same delivery requirement.

Finalizing a regulation is not the agency's last step. A rule cannot take effect until the agency has completed this submission. The requirement ties a new rule's legal effect to Congress being told about it.

Congress treats receipt of the rule as the start of its review clock. The deadline for introducing a disapproval resolution counts forward from that date. The window for the Senate's expedited procedure also runs from receipt, together with the rule's publication.

The date of receipt therefore anchors the whole review. Every later procedural deadline depends on it. A lawmaker weighing a challenge first needs to know when Congress received the rule.

Rules that agencies never formally submitted have been a recurring issue under the law. The problem follows from how the review clock works. If Congress never formally receives a rule, the event that starts the review period has not happened. The delivery step is what links an agency's rulemaking to Congress's power to overturn it.

A major rule under the Congressional Review Act generally cannot take effect until 60 days after it is submitted to Congress or published in the Federal Register, whichever comes later. The waiting period applies only to rules that meet the law's definition of major.

An agency does not apply the label to itself. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs makes the determination. Its finding rests on what a rule is likely to do once it is in force.

The first trigger is a dollar threshold. A rule is major if it is likely to have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more.

A second trigger looks at prices. A rule also qualifies as major if it is likely to cause a major increase in costs or prices.

The third trigger covers wider economic harm. A rule qualifies if it is likely to have significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity or innovation. Likely significant adverse effects on U.S. competitiveness also count.

Each trigger stands on its own. A rule with an expected annual effect below $100 million can still be major if it is likely to significantly harm employment or competition.

The 60-day clock runs from the later of two dates. One is the day the agency submits the rule to Congress. The other is the day the rule is published in the Federal Register. If an agency publishes a rule and submits it to Congress afterward, the countdown starts on the submission date.

The delay gives lawmakers time to examine a high-impact rule before it takes effect. Rules that fall short of the major tests are not held by this 60-day pause.

The Government Accountability Office works on a tighter deadline. It must send Congress a report on each major rule within 15 days. That deadline falls inside the 60-day waiting period.

A joint resolution of disapproval is the one tool the Congressional Review Act gives lawmakers to cancel a federal agency rule. The statute fixes its wording: Congress disapproves a named rule, and that rule shall have no force or effect.

The prescribed text is a single sentence with blanks. It states that Congress disapproves the rule submitted by a named agency relating to a stated subject, "and such rule shall have no force or effect." Drafters fill in the agency and the rule. They add nothing else.

That fixed text sets the resolution apart from an ordinary bill. Lawmakers do not draft new policy language or amend the regulation section by section. They name one rule and reject it.

The design narrows what a resolution can do. It cannot strike some provisions of a regulation and keep others. It cannot substitute different requirements. The only outcome it offers is disapproval of the named rule in full.

That all-or-nothing structure shapes the vote itself. A lawmaker who supports most of a regulation but objects to one provision cannot use the resolution to fix that provision. The choice is to keep the entire rule or cancel the entire rule.

The uniform wording also keeps the debate narrow. Every resolution follows the same template, so there is no policy language to negotiate. The question before each chamber is whether the named rule should stand.

Because the prescribed text names one rule, lawmakers who object to several agency regulations draft a separate resolution for each one. Each of those resolutions then moves through Congress on its own and succeeds or fails on its own.

Timing is the second constraint. A member must introduce the resolution within 60 days of continuous session after Congress receives the rule. The count runs in days of continuous session, not calendar days.

That distinction means the deadline cannot be read off a calendar. The window depends on when Congress formally received the rule. It also depends on how many days Congress remains in continuous session afterward.

The Congressional Review Act gives the Senate a fast track for disapproving agency rules. A discharge petition signed by 30 senators can pull a resolution out of committee. A simple majority can then pass it, and it cannot be filibustered.

That combination sets the Senate path apart from the route most legislation travels. Ordinary bills usually depend on committee action to reach the floor. They can also be held up by extended debate on the floor.

The discharge petition addresses the first obstacle. A committee that does not act on a joint resolution of disapproval cannot keep it from moving. Once 30 senators sign the petition, the measure comes out of committee and heads toward a floor vote.

Floor debate on the resolution is limited under the statute. That limit addresses the second obstacle. Senators who oppose the resolution cannot use open-ended debate to prevent a final vote from taking place.

No supermajority is needed at the final vote. A party holding a narrow Senate majority can pass a disapproval resolution with its own members' votes. Support from the minority party is not required.

The expedited process is available for a limited time. It lasts for 60 Senate session days after the rule is received by Congress and published.

A session day counts only when the Senate actually meets. Recesses and adjournments do not add to the total. As a result, the window can run longer than 60 calendar days.

The count depends on two events, receipt and publication. A rule that has reached Congress but has not yet been published has not started the Senate window.

Once the 60 session days pass, the fast-track procedures no longer apply to that rule. Senators who want to use the discharge petition and the majority-vote threshold must act inside the window.

The Senate fast track governs only one chamber. A disapproval resolution passed this way still needs approval from the House and the president before it becomes law.

A Congressional Review Act resolution must pass the House and the Senate and then win the president's signature to cancel a federal rule. Unlike the Senate, the House gets no statutory fast track for these measures.

The difference between the chambers is written into the law itself. The statute builds an expedited path for the Senate. It provides no matching procedure for the House. A disapproval resolution introduced in the House gets no special protection from the Congressional Review Act.

House leadership fills that gap with its own tools. The usual route is a special rule reported by the Rules Committee. That special rule sets the terms for bringing the disapproval resolution to the floor. As a result, the timing of a House vote rests with the chamber's leadership rather than with a deadline in the statute.

Passage in one chamber is not enough. Both the House and the Senate must approve the same resolution before it reaches the president.

The president then has two choices: sign the resolution or veto it. A signature enacts the disapproval. A veto returns the measure to Congress.

Overriding a veto takes a two-thirds vote in each chamber. Both the House and the Senate must clear that threshold separately. A resolution that passed either chamber by a narrow margin will not reach two-thirds without added support. That math makes a veto difficult to overcome.

The presidential step shapes how the law works in practice. A president is unlikely to approve a resolution that cancels a rule from the president's own administration. Successful use of the Congressional Review Act has mostly come under one set of conditions.

The president and the congressional majorities belong to the same party. The targeted rule came from a predecessor's administration. Under that alignment, both chambers can pass a disapproval resolution and the president can sign it. That pattern links the law's real-world use to changes in party control of the White House.

Once a Congressional Review Act disapproval becomes law, the targeted rule is treated as though it never took effect. The agency that wrote it also loses the power to reissue a rule that is "substantially the same" unless a later law specifically authorizes it.

Those two consequences point in opposite directions in time. One erases the rule's past. The other limits what the agency can do next on the same subject.

The "never took effect" treatment reaches backward. The rule does not simply end on the date the resolution becomes law. For legal purposes, it is handled as if it had never been in force.

The reissue bar reaches forward. An agency cannot return months later with a near-copy of the disapproved rule. To write something substantially similar, it needs Congress to pass a new law that specifically allows it. Like any other legislation, that law must clear both chambers. It must then either win the president's signature or survive a veto.

The open question is the phrase itself. The statute does not define "substantially the same." It offers no test for how far a replacement must depart from the original before it falls outside the ban.

That gap leaves the scope of the restriction unsettled. An agency weighing a new rule on a subject Congress has already disapproved has no statutory definition to consult. It has to judge for itself how close is too close.

The Congressional Review Act adds a further limit. It states that actions and omissions under the law are not subject to judicial review. That language narrows the usual path of asking a court to decide what a statute requires.

The result pairs a firm prohibition with an undefined standard. A disapproved rule cannot come back on the agency's own authority. The boundary between a barred near-copy and a permissible new rule remains unsettled in the statute's text.

The Congressional Review Act's lookback period gives a new session of Congress a chance to review rules that arrived late in the previous one. It applies to rules submitted within 60 legislative days in the House, or 60 session days in the Senate, before sine die adjournment.

Sine die adjournment is the formal end of a session. A chamber adjourns without setting a date to return. The lookback window counts backward from that point.

Rules caught in the window are treated as though they were submitted on the 15th session day of the next session. That legal fiction resets the timing. The review clock starts over in the new session.

The restart reaches the introduction deadline too. Lawmakers have 60 days of continuous session after a rule is received to introduce a joint resolution of disapproval. Under the lookback, that period runs from the 15th session day of the new session.

The Senate's fast-track window restarts as well. Senators get a fresh 60 session days to use the expedited procedure against rules that reached Congress in the final stretch of the prior session.

The window is measured in days a chamber actually meets, not calendar days. The House count uses legislative days. The Senate count uses session days. Each chamber keeps its own calendar, so the two windows can open on different dates.

No one can pin down the start of the lookback window while a session is still under way. It depends on how many days each chamber meets before final adjournment. The start date is fixed only after the fact, once the calendar is complete.

That uncertainty matters for agencies finishing rules late in a session. A rule sent to Congress near the end of a session may or may not fall inside the window. The answer turns on a schedule that has not yet played out.

Rules that arrive earlier in a session do not get this second chance. They follow the ordinary review timeline instead.

Congress first used the Congressional Review Act successfully in 2001, overturning the Occupational Safety and Health Administration's ergonomics rule. Successful use then stayed rare until 2017, when a Republican Congress and President Donald Trump overturned many Obama-era rules.

The ergonomics rule came from OSHA, the workplace safety agency within the Department of Labor. Congress passed a joint resolution of disapproval against it. President George W. Bush signed the measure on March 20, 2001. With his signature, the resolution became law and the rule was canceled.

That first success arrived just under five years after President Bill Clinton signed the CRA on March 29, 1996. For that entire stretch, the statute had not canceled a single regulation.

The disapproval had lasting consequences for OSHA. Under the law, the ergonomics rule is treated as though it never took effect. The agency also cannot issue a rule that is "substantially the same" unless a later act of Congress specifically authorizes it.

For years after 2001, the ergonomics repeal stood as the only successful use of the CRA. Lawmakers kept the power to introduce disapproval resolutions throughout that period.

Use of the statute rose sharply in 2017, 16 years after the ergonomics vote. President Donald Trump took office that year alongside a Republican Congress. Those majorities used the CRA to overturn many rules finalized under the Obama administration.

The 2017 surge fit the conditions under which the CRA has mostly worked. The president belonged to the same party as the congressional majorities and was willing to sign their disapprovals. The rules in question had been issued by a predecessor rather than by the sitting administration.

That alignment matters because the president can veto a disapproval resolution like any other joint resolution. Overriding a veto requires two-thirds of each chamber. Without shared party control, a resolution that clears both chambers can still fail at the president's desk.

#5432. Delaware’s federal court forced litigation funders into the open. Its most important court still lets them hide

Sonnenfeld is one of the nation’s most recognized experts on corporate governance. Sonnenfeld and Tian  have co-authored Trump’s Ten Commandments (Worth/Simon & Schuster)

We warned in the pages of Fortune last week that the corporate flight from Delaware would only accelerate on the heels of Delaware Chancery Court Vice Chancellor Travis Laster’s controversial and widely criticized decision in the highly watched Cloudflare case. Since then, Virtu Financial has announced its own relocation from Delaware to Texas on Nov. 4, following the recent exits of at least 30 companies over the last two years. Virtu’s move comes as it too is embroiled in pending litigation in Laster’s court, after Laster denied Virtu’s motion to dismiss.

As we’ve written previously, the boards of companies moving out of Delaware most often cite the same concern: they can no longer predict how the state’s Chancery Court, once prized for its consistency and predictability, will treat them, amidst a series of decisions widely construed as judicial overreach. The legislature has tried to correct this problem through SB21, but certain Chancery judges continue to seemingly defy the will of the legislature, and the Delaware Supreme Court has inadvertently undermined their own efforts to overturn erroneous decisions by remanding cases back to the same judges.

But a second blind spot gets far less attention, and it may matter just as much. A Delaware company can be hauled into the Court of Chancery today with no way of knowing who is paying for the lawsuit against it, whether that backer controls settlement, or whether it is a competitor or a foreign state amidst a surge in litigation backed by litigation finance firms.

The legal philosopher Jeremy Bentham wrote that “publicity is the very soul of justice.” One of the quiet strengths of the American legal system is how much of that ideal it has honored. Our courts function in the open, with public proceedings, published rules, and disclosure requirements designed to ensure that judges, litigants, and the public can understand who is driving a case—and why. Those features are not procedural niceties; they are cornerstones of trust in the judiciary itself. Delaware’s century-old promise to corporate America rested on the same idea: boards and litigants could see the rules and the players before they acted. Undisclosed third-party litigation funding cuts against that promise in the one court that matters most to American business.

A growing, mostly invisible market of litigation finance which has become perverted away from original noble intention

The global litigation finance market was estimated at $20.6 billion in 2025, with forecasts that it will more than double over the next decade, and U.S. commercial funders alone managed roughly $16 billion in assets at the end of 2024. This is a market which has already grown exponentially, as it barely existed merely two decades ago. At its best, litigation funding expands access to justice for plaintiffs who could not otherwise afford to be heard, a noble founding intent as it was envisioned by the widely admired founders of the field. But as litigation finance firms have proliferated exponentially over recent years, the actual practice of litigation finance has frequently become perverted from those noble founding aims, with key challenges including that too often, it is opaque, undisclosed, and strategically deployed. It obscures the real parties who have an interest in dragging out litigation and obfuscates what ulterior motives they may have, distorts the incentives that are supposed to drive a case toward resolution, and risks undermining the integrity of the courts themselves.

Unlike the contingency-fee arrangements familiar to American law, many third-party investments by litigation finance firms involve opaque layered structures of who gets paid, and complex ownership that remain invisible to judges and opposing parties. No federal statute or rule requires disclosure of even the existence of a litigation funder—let alone whether that litigation funder holds sway over litigation strategy or settlement decisions, as they sometimes do.

Real risks of undisclosed hidden litigation finance, including most alarmingly to national security

The potential harms are concrete from undisclosed litigation finance firms underwriting litigation. First, an outside litigation funder’s investment return thresholds can push it to resist settlement and prolong disputes, at real cost to litigants and to judicial resources. Second, a funder may not be motivated by financial profit at all. An undisclosed entity can underwrite suits to impose burdensome costs on a competitor for competitive harm, and when the money answers to a foreign state, the concern becomes one of national security. A December 2024 Government Accountability Office report found stakeholders pointing to funders from China, Saudi Arabia, and France, while conceding that the full extent of such funding is unknowable given how little is disclosed. The industry’s ties to foreign capital are not speculative, as one firm has announced a “strategic capital relationship” with a sovereign wealth fund, while another is now majority-owned by a consortium led by Mubadala, Abu Dhabi’s sovereign investor. Our courts are open by design, but openness should not mean naïveté.

This isn’t hypothetical. A Shenzhen-based firm led by the general counsel of Chinese electronics giant TCL was revealed to be financing patent suits against Samsung in U.S. courts , and Samsung later alleged that the funder had misused its confidential information to compete unfairly.

America’s famously broad civil discovery magnifies the danger. Justified by the principle that both sides should have access to the facts, discovery is estimated to account for 50% to 90% of the cost of litigating a case. That lets a funded plaintiff run up a defendant’s bill as an end in itself, or as a way to operationally hinder a competitor by requesting a document dump of sensitive strategic files of limited relevance to the actual litigation at hand, but of huge importance to sensitive industry and strategic competition. Indeed, when a lawsuit is secretly financed by an entity with strategic or geopolitical motives, discovery can become nothing more than a mechanism for extracting sensitive information under the protective cover of judicial process, with that sensitive information subsequently used by hostile foreign powers to undermine American companies unfairly.

Delaware’s federal court has already proved disclosure works

Patent litigation shows the pattern at scale. Patent cases absorbed 32% of new litigation-funding commitments in 2024, up from 19% a year earlier and the largest single category, and roughly 30% of patent suits are now estimated to be funded. Most of the large technology companies the GAO interviewed said that more than half the patent suits filed against them involve confirmed or suspected third-party funding. The suits increasingly come from non-practicing entities that make no products but acquire patents to monetize them in court: in 2025, NPEs filed 55% of all district-court patent cases and 90% of those in the high-tech sector.

Because the U.S. Supreme Court held in TC Heartland that a corporation “resides” for patent-venue purposes only in its state of incorporation, Delaware’s federal district court is a default venue for patent suits against Delaware corporations. In April 2022, Chief Judge Colm Connolly ordered parties before him to disclose any litigation funder and whether it controls litigation or settlement decisions. The results were revealing. Patent filings in the district fell 41% over the following two years, against a 15% national decline, and funded patent cases in his courtroom virtually disappeared. It was Connolly’s order that surfaced the profoundly disturbing Chinese TCL-linked funder behind the Samsung suits mentioned previously. Transparency, it turns out, discourages the litigation that least wants to be seen.

Delaware’s state courts have been slower to follow. To their credit, on Sept. 30, 2026, the Superior Court amended its rules to permit discovery into a funder’s existence, identity, and control rights while shielding the funding agreement itself absent a showing of good cause. But the Court of Chancery—the most important court in the nation for corporate disputes—has adopted no corresponding rule and proceeds case by case. Its judges have taken notice of the problem. In Burkhart v. Genworth, a putative class action decided in 2024, Vice Chancellor Nathan Cook ordered the plaintiffs to produce their funding agreement in full, warning that such cases are “especially ripe for a third-party funder to exercise improper control over the litigation.” That ruling shows the court understands the stakes, but a single order in a single case by one of the court’s seven judges, won only after a motion to compel, falls well short of a universal disclosure requirement.

The gap matters, because Chancery is where corporate America’s stockholder litigation lives, as the single most important court for American businesses in the entire country. When a court and defendants do not know who stands behind a complaint, it cannot fully assess conflicts of interest, police litigation conduct, or tell whether decisions are being driven by the named plaintiff or by an undisclosed backer with very different and ulterior objectives. None of this is a criticism of judges, who can only manage what is disclosed to them. The problem is structural – and easily fixable by the Delaware Chancery Court.

The case for reform is increasingly difficult to ignore. Members of Congress have pressed the judiciary to move faster. The chairman of the House Oversight Committee urged the Judicial Conference in 2024 to consider mandatory disclosure, citing foreign money in U.S. lawsuits; a bipartisan Senate bill introduced in 2023 would require any foreign funder to disclose its role and bar sovereign wealth funds from financing U.S. litigation; and four senators introduced legislation this February requiring disclosure in federal class actions and multidistrict litigation.

Regulators and states are moving too. The International Trade Commission proposed in April to require disclosure of funders in Section 337 proceedings, the arcane but consequential cases that determine whether foreign goods can be blocked from the U.S. market. Ohio enacted a law in July requiring funders to register and disclose their agreements, barring them from influencing how a lawsuit is handled or settled, and prohibiting foreign funders outright. North Carolina on June 22 became the first state to prohibit third-party litigation investment altogether. More than 20 states have now enacted laws regulating the practice, and New Jersey’s Assembly passed a disclosure bill in June.

Transparency is the remedy. Full, universal disclosure simply ensures that judges and litigants know who the real stakeholders are and what their motives may be —just as they already do when funders back class actions in the Northern District of California, when creditor groups organize in a bankruptcy, and when an investor accumulates more than 5% of a public company. Capital markets function on disclosure, not secrecy. Shareholders disclose ownership. Political donors disclose contributions. Judges disclose conflicts. The notion that litigation funders should be uniquely exempt makes no sense.

Boards leaving Delaware cite the increasing unpredictability of the Delaware Chancery Court and the cost of stockholder litigation, but undisclosed litigation funding feeds both. The fix is a Chancery rule modeled on Chief Judge Connolly’s order, requiring parties at the outset of a case to disclose whether a funder exists, who it is, and whether it controls strategy or settlement.

Justice Louis Brandeis observed that sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants. Delaware built its reputation by letting everyone see the rules. It should let everyone see who is paying to litigate under them.

Disclosure: The authors presented their research on dual class shares to a special committee of Cloudflare’s board, a Delaware company currently in litigation in the Court of Chancery.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld is the Lester Crown Professor in Management Practice and Senior Associate Dean at Yale School of Management.

Steven Tian is the director of research at the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute.
