#5431. How a bill becomes law in the U.S., from introduction to veto override

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How a bill becomes law in the U.S., from a lawmaker's introduction through committee, floor votes and the president's desk, explained in 10 consecutive steps

The U.S. Constitution gives Congress the power to write federal law, but it also sets strict conditions on that power. Article I, Section 7 lays out a narrow path. A bill has to pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form. Then it goes to the president, who can sign it, veto it or, in some circumstances, let it take effect without a signature.

Understanding how a bill becomes law helps explain much of what appears in the news about Capitol Hill. A headline about a committee hearing, a stalled vote or a veto threat describes one specific point in a longer sequence. Knowing where that point sits makes it easier to judge what could happen next. It also shows why a proposal that sounds popular can still go nowhere.

The process filters legislation at nearly every stage. Many bills are introduced, referred to a committee and never heard from again. Others clear one chamber and stall in the other. Even a bill that passes both chambers can still be vetoed by the president.

Each stage serves a different purpose. Some stages decide which proposals get attention at all. Others shape the text through amendments and negotiation. A few function as checks, giving one chamber or one branch of government the chance to block what another has approved. The House and Senate also run their floors under different rules. The same bill can move quickly in one chamber and slowly in the other.

The 10 slides that follow walk through the steps in the legislative process in the order a typical bill encounters them. The path starts with a lawmaker formally introducing a bill. It runs through committee work, floor debate in each chamber and the effort to settle differences between the House and Senate versions. It ends with the president's decision and, in some cases, a final vote by Congress to override a veto.

That sequence describes the usual route, not the only one. Congressional procedure includes exceptions that can speed a bill up or let it skip a stage. The Senate can pass measures by unanimous consent. House members can use a discharge petition to pull a bill out of committee. Budget reconciliation runs under its own procedures. Each slide explains one stage on its own terms. A reader can start anywhere in the process.

Every federal bill starts when a sitting member of the House or Senate formally introduces it. That lawmaker becomes the bill's sponsor, the person responsible for it at every later stage.

The idea itself can come from almost anywhere. A president can ask Congress for a new program. A business group, a union, a city government or a citizen advocacy organization can draft language and shop it around Capitol Hill. Executive agencies also send proposed legislation to Congress. None of these outside players can put a bill into the system on their own, though. A lawmaker has to agree to sponsor it.

Drafting usually happens before introduction. Members and their staffs can get help from the Office of the Legislative Counsel. Each chamber maintains its own version of that office to turn policy goals into statutory text. The office works on a nonpartisan basis.

The sponsor can also recruit cosponsors, other members who sign on to show support. Lawmakers who join on the day of introduction are known as original cosponsors. Others can add their names later. A long cosponsor list signals backing, but it does not by itself move the bill forward.

In the House, introduction is a physical act. The member places the bill in the hopper, a wooden box near the rostrum in the House chamber. Members can do this only when the House is in session. In the Senate, a senator typically submits the bill to the clerks at the presiding officer's desk. A senator can also introduce it after being recognized on the floor.

Each bill then gets a number. House bills carry the prefix H.R., and Senate bills carry S. Numbering starts over with each new two-year Congress. That means H.R. 1 in one Congress has nothing to do with H.R. 1 in the next. Any bill not enacted by the time a Congress ends expires. A sponsor who wants to keep pushing it must reintroduce it under a new number.

The Constitution places one limit on where a bill can start. Article I, Section 7 requires that all bills for raising revenue originate in the House of Representatives. The Senate can still propose or concur with amendments to those bills, as it can with any other legislation.

After a bill is introduced, it goes to a committee, where lawmakers assigned to its subject area review it first. In the House, the Speaker refers the bill to one or more committees on the advice of the parliamentarian. In the Senate, the presiding officer makes the referral.

The choice of committee depends on subject matter. Each chamber's rules spell out which committee covers which policy areas. In the House, Rule X $TWTR sets out those jurisdictions. In the Senate, Rule XXV does the same job.

A bill dealing with federal courts or criminal law would typically go to a Judiciary Committee, a panel both chambers have. A House bill on telecommunications or public health might go to the Energy and Commerce Committee. A tax measure in the Senate would usually land at the Finance Committee.

The parliamentarian plays a central role in those decisions. Each chamber has its own parliamentarian, a nonpartisan official who advises on rules and precedents. The parliamentarian's office reviews the text of a new bill and recommends where it belongs. In the Senate, the presiding officer generally follows that recommendation.

A single bill can cover several policy areas at once. The House handles that through multiple referral, which sends the bill to more than one committee. The Speaker usually designates a primary committee and can set time limits for the others. The Senate typically sends a bill to the one committee whose jurisdiction covers most of its subject matter. Senate Rule XIV also lets a senator skip referral and place a bill directly on the Senate calendar.

Referral shapes what happens next. A committee chair largely controls the panel's agenda. That means the chair has wide say over whether a bill receives any attention.

Most bills go no further than committee. A committee can simply take no action on a measure, and that inaction alone can end its chances. A bill that is still pending when a two-year Congress ends expires. Its sponsor can reintroduce it in the next Congress. The new version receives a new bill number and starts over with a fresh committee referral.

A committee often hands a newly referred bill to one of its subcommittees for closer study. Lawmakers there may hold hearings with witnesses, then meet for a markup session where they propose, debate and vote on amendments to the bill's actual wording.

Full committees cover broad subject areas, and subcommittees split that work into smaller pieces. A House panel such as Energy and Commerce handles policy ranging from health care to telecommunications. It divides that territory among smaller groups of members. Each subcommittee works on a narrower slice of policy and builds expertise in it.

The subcommittee chair has wide control over the schedule. The chair decides whether to hold a hearing, which bills get attention and in what order they move. Members of the minority party can request witnesses and offer amendments, but the majority sets the agenda.

Hearings are the fact-finding stage. Witnesses can include officials from federal agencies, academic specialists, industry representatives, advocacy groups and people directly affected by a proposal. Witnesses usually submit written testimony in advance and then answer questions from members. The hearing record becomes part of the bill's paper trail. Hearings are not required, and some bills go straight to markup without one.

Markup is where the text itself changes. The session starts from a base text. That text may be the bill as introduced, or a substitute version offered by the chair. Members then offer amendments section by section. Each amendment is debated and decided by a vote of the members present. Those votes can be taken by voice or recorded by name.

Amendments range from small fixes, such as changing a word or a date, to rewrites of entire sections. A markup can also adopt an amendment in the nature of a substitute. That device replaces the bill's whole text with a new version in a single vote.

When a subcommittee finishes its markup, it can vote to forward the bill to the full committee for further action. Practice varies across the House and Senate. Some committees skip the subcommittee step entirely and hold hearings and markup at the full-committee level instead.

A bill typically reaches the House or Senate floor only after the full committee votes to report it. That vote usually comes with a written committee report explaining what the bill does and why. A bill the committee never reports usually dies there.

The reporting vote follows markup. Committee members decide by majority vote whether to send the measure to the full chamber. They can attach the amendments adopted during markup. A committee may also bundle those changes into a single amendment in the nature of a substitute. That amendment replaces the original text with a rewritten version.

A committee can report a bill favorably, unfavorably or without recommendation. A favorable report is the common outcome.

The committee chair controls much of the committee's schedule. A chair who does not take up a bill can keep it from ever reaching a reporting vote.

The committee report is a public document with its own number, labeled H. Rept. in the House and S. Rept. in the Senate. It typically describes the bill's purpose, summarizes its provisions and lays out the changes it would make to existing law. Members who disagree with the majority can add minority or additional views. In the House, reports generally include a cost estimate from the Congressional Budget Office. Courts and federal agencies sometimes consult these reports later to understand what lawmakers intended.

Once reported, a bill goes onto a calendar of pending business. The House uses the Union Calendar for most bills that raise or spend money and the House Calendar for many others. The Senate places reported bills on its Calendar of Business.

House members have one formal way around a committee that will not act. A discharge petition can pull a bill out of committee once 218 members sign it, a majority of the full 435-seat House. The petition can be filed only after the bill has sat in committee for 30 legislative days. Signatures on discharge petitions have been public since 1993.

A bill that stays in committee does not wait indefinitely. Any measure not enacted by the end of a two-year Congress expires. Its supporters must reintroduce it in the next Congress for it to be considered again.

Before most major bills reach the House floor, the House Rules Committee writes a special rule that decides how long members can debate and whether they can offer amendments. The full House must vote to adopt that rule before debate on the bill begins.

This step has no counterpart in the Senate. It places a formal gatekeeper between committee approval and a floor vote in the House.

A special rule takes the form of a House resolution, numbered with the prefix H.Res. It typically sets a fixed block of debate time and divides that time between the bill's supporters and opponents. It can also waive procedural objections, known as points of order, that might otherwise stall the measure.

The rule's amendment terms come in three main forms. An open rule lets any member offer an amendment that is germane to the bill. A structured rule allows only the amendments the Rules Committee lists in its report. A closed rule bars floor amendments entirely, so the House votes on the bill largely as written.

Members who want changes usually submit their proposed amendments to the Rules Committee in advance. The committee then decides which ones, if any, will reach the floor. That decision determines which changes the full House can consider at all.

The majority party's leadership chooses the majority's members of the committee. That arrangement gives the Speaker significant influence over which bills move and on what terms. Votes to adopt a rule usually break along party lines. If a rule fails, the bill cannot come up under those terms, and debate on it does not begin.

The House typically debates the rule itself for one hour before voting on it.

Some bills skip the Rules Committee altogether. Under a procedure called suspension of the rules, the House limits debate to 40 minutes and permits no floor amendments. Passage under suspension requires a two-thirds vote of members present and voting.

A bill passes the House when a simple majority of members present and voting supports it, as long as a quorum is on hand. Floor debate follows the terms of the rule the chamber adopted for that bill. A winning vote sends the measure to the Senate.

The Constitution defines a House quorum as a majority of members. With all 435 seats filled, that is 218. Much of the amending work happens in the Committee of the Whole House on the state of the Union. This procedural device lets the full membership act with a quorum of 100.

Debate time is usually split between two floor managers, one from the majority and one from the minority. They are often leaders of the committee that handled the bill. Each manager yields minutes to colleagues who want to speak. The rule controls how long this lasts and which amendments, if any, members may offer.

Votes can be taken by voice, by division or by recorded vote. The Constitution lets one-fifth of members present demand that the yeas and nays be entered in the journal. Recorded votes have used an electronic system since 1973. Members insert voting cards into stations on the floor. The first vote in a series stays open for at least 15 minutes.

Before final passage, the minority can offer a motion to recommit. If adopted, it sends the bill back to committee. A tie vote defeats the question. Passage requires more yes votes than no votes.

Not every bill travels this route. Measures considered under suspension of the rules skip a special rule. They allow no floor amendments and get 40 minutes of debate. In exchange, passage requires two-thirds of members present and voting.

Once the House approves a bill, clerks prepare an engrossed copy that reflects every adopted amendment. That certified text goes to the Senate as an act of the House. A bill that began in the Senate reaches the House only after Senate passage. It then moves through these same House steps.

A bill on the Senate floor can pass with a simple majority, but ending debate on it usually takes 60 votes. As a result, the cloture vote, not the final passage vote, is often the harder threshold for legislation to clear in the U.S. Senate.

Senate debate is generally open-ended. Unless senators agree to limits, a bill can stay on the floor as long as members keep talking or keep procedural objections alive. Using that freedom to delay or block a final vote is called a filibuster.

Limits on debate often come through unanimous consent agreements. These agreements can set how long debate runs and which amendments receive votes. A single senator's objection can keep such an agreement from taking effect.

When consent fails, supporters of a bill turn to cloture, the formal process for ending debate under Senate Rule XXII. A cloture motion must carry the signatures of 16 senators. The vote on it takes place one hour after the Senate convenes on the second day after the motion is filed.

Invoking cloture on most legislation requires three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn. With all 100 seats filled, that equals 60 votes. The threshold is measured against sitting senators rather than those present. An absent senator therefore offers no help to the side trying to reach 60.

A successful cloture vote does not end consideration on the spot. Rule XXII allows up to 30 more hours of consideration before the final vote. Passage itself then needs only a simple majority of senators voting. If that vote ties, the vice president, serving as president of the Senate, can cast the deciding vote under Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution.

The cloture rule dates to 1917. For decades, it required two-thirds of senators present and voting. In 1975, the Senate replaced that standard with the current three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn.

Budget reconciliation bills are an exception to this process. They move under limited debate time and cannot be filibustered. They therefore do not need 60 votes to reach a final vote.

Both chambers of Congress must pass the exact same text before a bill can go to the president. When the House and Senate approve different versions, lawmakers have three ways to close the gap. One chamber can accept the other's text, the chambers can trade amendments, or a conference committee can negotiate a compromise.

Acceptance is the most direct route. If one chamber is willing to take the other's version as written, it passes that text. The two chambers are then in agreement, and no further negotiation is needed.

The second route is an exchange of amendments. One chamber amends the other's bill and sends it back. The receiving chamber can agree, propose its own amendment to that amendment, or insist on its position. This back-and-forth is informally known as "ping-pong." It lets leaders settle differences without appointing a formal negotiating panel.

The third route is a conference committee. This is a temporary panel made up of members from both the House and the Senate. The Speaker names the House conferees, and the Senate's presiding officer appoints the Senate conferees. Conferees usually come from the committees that handled the bill.

Conferees from each chamber vote as a separate delegation. A compromise moves forward only when a majority of the House conferees and a majority of the Senate conferees sign the conference report. That report contains the agreed text. A joint explanatory statement accompanies it and describes how the negotiators resolved each difference.

Both chambers then vote on the conference report. Neither the House nor the Senate can amend it on the floor. Members accept or reject it as a whole. If either chamber votes it down, the disagreement stays open. The bill cannot go to the president in that form.

Once the two chambers agree on identical text by any of these routes, the chamber where the bill started prepares a final official copy. That copy is called the enrolled bill. The Speaker of the House and the presiding officer of the Senate sign it. Only then is the measure ready to be sent to the White House.

Once Congress presents a bill, the president has 10 days, Sundays excepted, to act on it. A signature makes the bill law, a veto sends it back, and inaction can produce either outcome depending on whether Congress is still in session.

That deadline comes from Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution. The clock starts when the bill is presented to the president, not when the final floor vote takes place. Before presentment, the identical text approved by both chambers is prepared as an enrolled bill. The Speaker of the House and the presiding officer of the Senate sign it before it goes to the White House.

Signing is the most direct route. With the president's signature, the measure becomes law. Presidents sometimes sign major legislation at public ceremonies. The legal effect comes from the signature itself, not the event around it.

A regular veto takes a different path. The president returns the bill to the chamber where it originated, along with the president's objections. The Constitution directs that chamber to enter those objections in its journal and reconsider the measure. The president acts on the bill as a whole and cannot approve some provisions while rejecting others.

A president can also decline to act. If 10 days pass, Sundays excepted, while Congress is in session, the bill becomes law without a signature. In that situation, the president's silence counts as acceptance rather than rejection.

The outcome changes when Congress has adjourned. If lawmakers have left and the president does not sign within the window, the bill does not become law. This is called a pocket veto. The Constitution's text describes it as a case in which Congress, by its adjournment, prevents the bill's return.

The difference between the two kinds of veto shapes what happens next. A regular veto puts the bill and the president's objections back in front of Congress, which can try to reverse the decision. A pocket veto leaves no returned bill for lawmakers to reconsider. Supporters of a measure blocked this way have to introduce it again as a new bill and restart the process.

A presidential veto does not have to be the final word on a bill. Congress can override it if two-thirds of each chamber votes to pass the bill again. That is a far higher bar than the simple majority needed the first time.

The Constitution spells out the override procedure. The vetoed bill returns to the chamber where it started, along with the president's objections. That chamber records the objections in its journal and reconsiders the bill. If two-thirds agree to pass it, the bill moves to the other chamber. The second chamber must also reach two-thirds.

The Constitution requires override votes to be taken by yeas and nays. Each member's name and vote are entered in that chamber's journal. Every override attempt is therefore a recorded vote. There is no option for an anonymous voice vote.

If every seat is filled and every member votes, an override takes 290 of 435 House members and 67 of 100 senators. The threshold is measured against members present and voting, provided a quorum is present. The exact number can shift with absences and vacancies. The Supreme Court upheld that reading in Missouri Pacific Railway Co. v. Kansas.

If the first chamber falls short, the veto stands. The second chamber then has nothing to vote on. Overrides are rare. A bill that clears both override votes becomes law over the president's objections.

Once a bill is enacted, whether by signature or by override, it receives a public law number. The first part of that number identifies the Congress that passed it. The second part reflects the order in which it was enacted during that Congress.

The new law is first issued as a slip law, a standalone printed copy of the single measure. It is later compiled in the Statutes at Large, the permanent chronological record of the laws Congress passes. Laws of general and permanent effect are then folded into the U.S. Code, which arranges federal law by subject. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel of the House handles that codification.

#5430. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5429. ‘It’s just about fairness’: United’s CEO doubles down on a wealth tax despite his $32 million pay

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby took home about $32.3 million in total compensation last year, according to Fortune’s reporting on United’s proxy statement. He says people like him should be paying more, starting with a tax on the wealth they already hold.

In a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times in mid-October, Kirby said wealth inequality “has become a danger to our society” and called for a national wealth tax, plus inheritance taxes that “get close to 100% at some level.” “I would pay them,” he added.

The remarks drew swift pushback, much of it aimed at his paycheck. Fox Business asked United how Kirby squared his pay with his warnings about inequality; the company didn’t respond.

Kirby doubled down a few days later on CNBC’s Squawk Box, framing the idea as a matter of fairness.

“I think a wealth tax… is just about fairness…. If you’re wealthy enough, you can put money aside, and by the way, I think it would apply to me, put money aside, let it grow forever, never realize income on it, you can let it grow forever and it never gets taxed,” he said.

That is the gap Kirby wants to close. The federal system taxes income: in 2025, the top rate of 37% applied to single filers’ taxable income above $626,350, according to the IRS. Investments that rise in value but are never sold aren’t taxed.

Kirby’s view stands out because of who holds it. He runs a company on the 2026 Fortune 500 that brought in $59.1 billion in revenue last year.

He stressed that these were personal views and that he has no interest in politics or policymaking. If it were up to him, he said, he would prefer a system “where we had lower income taxes, and higher taxes, or some kind of taxes, on the gain in wealth.”

In practice, the idea draws pointed objections. Mariana Trujillo, managing director of government finance at the Reason Foundation, a libertarian-leaning think tank, tells Fortune it would undercut the very growth it’s meant to share.

“Taxing accumulated wealth discourages investment and entrepreneurship — the very forces that have made our lives better than those of our grandparents and great-grandparents. Economic progress, not the state, has driven improvements in our material condition. A wealth tax discourages the very thing it aims to promote,” she says.

Trujillo draws a sharp line between the two ideas Kirby floated. An inheritance tax hits wealth once, when it changes hands. An annual wealth tax hits it every year, and she argues that gives the wealthiest Americans, and their capital, a reason to leave.

“An annual wealth tax is entirely different from an inheritance tax…. People move out of states and countries for tax reasons. National wealth taxes failed in Europe, where countries including France, Sweden, and Germany abandoned them amid concerns about capital flight, administrative costs, and disappointing revenues.”

A few European countries have held on: Norway, Spain, and Switzerland still levy net wealth taxes, according to the Tax Foundation.

Trujillo also had a message for Kirby himself. “If Kirby believes his wealth could be better used to improve others’ lives, he is free to put it toward that purpose,” she said. “But I hope he recognizes that his compensation reflects the perceived value of his contributions to his company and, therefore, to society at large. Wealth does not need to be redistributed to be productive; it is already the result of creating value for others.”

Kirby has argued that a state-by-state approach is doomed. “We should have a national wealth tax—it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he told the Times, as Fortune reported.

California just tested a state version. In the Nov. 3 election, voters rejected Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of state residents worth more than $1 billion. The Associated Press called the race on Nov. 9, with 52.8% of voters opposed, according to CalMatters.

The measure had high-profile backers, including six Nobel Prize–winning economists who argued it could kick-start similar efforts elsewhere. But opponents spent about $378 million against it, while the yes campaign raised $33.5 million, and Silicon Valley voters broke against it even as Los Angeles and San Francisco voted yes.

Trujillo sees the result as a verdict on the idea itself. “California’s wealth tax proposal failed at the ballot box for good reasons: first, because voters recognized it may reduce government revenue as people leave, and second, because they saw it as discouraging investment and innovation, which make our lives better.”

Kirby says the emails he received about his comments split about evenly for and against. If California is any guide, the rest of the country isn’t far off.

#5428. Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 5, 2026 at 10:41 am

Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.

Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200, has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post. It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March.

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg.

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.

Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.

“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.

The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.

“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.

“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”

#5427. A tabloid scandal bankrolled a Long Island Democrat, mostly with out-of-district money. A Hollywood-linked tycoon backed a Republican who beat him.

Leaked photos were supposed to end Chris Gallant’s campaign. Instead, they bankrolled it. After the New York Post published archived images of the Democrat modeling bondage gear for a San Francisco leather retailer, his fundraising took off.

In the quarter the photos surfaced, Gallant raised more than the incumbent. His October quarterly FEC report shows $929,825 in receipts for July through September. Rep. Nick LaLota reported about $609,000 for the same period.

The money bought a close loss, not a win. LaLota won a third term in New York’s 1st Congressional District last Tuesday, 51.1% to 48.9%, a margin of nearly 7,000 votes with 560 of 561 election districts reporting. Gallant first held out for absentee ballots, then conceded Wednesday. LaLota’s margin shrank from about 11 points in 2024 to about two, in a year Democrats swept to control of Congress.

Nor was the money especially local. A Fortune review of both campaigns’ raw 2026 FEC filings through Oct. 14 found that in-district donors accounted for about 16% of LaLota’s money from named individuals and just over a third of Gallant’s.

The post-leak surge followed the same pattern. In the 32 days after the Post story ran on Sept. 13, Gallant reported $276,055 in itemized contributions. Only $65,997 of it, about 24%, came from individuals inside NY-1, and almost half of that came from 62 donors in the Hamptons. Donors in Manhattan and California gave $73,606 combined, more than every donor inside NY-1 put together.

In NY-1, the people who funded the race and the people who voted in it were often different. Both campaigns were bankrolled mostly by donors outside the district, including major Wall Street, Hollywood and tech names. Even the men on the ballot live beyond its lines: both reside near Amityville, on Long Island’s South Shore, which means neither could vote for himself.

NY-1 runs from Suffolk County’s North Shore villages to the East End, with vineyards and farms on the North Fork and the Hamptons on the South Fork. In between lie Smithtown and Brookhaven, where suburban neighborhoods give way to woods and residents are largely commuters, law enforcement and small-business owners.

Each summer, the South Fork fills with the people who run Wall Street and corporate America. That makes the district one of the country’s busiest political ATMs, where financiers and industry titans host fundraisers for both parties. Suffolk County donors gave more than $45 million to campaigns in the 2020 cycle alone, according to OpenSecrets data CNBC cited.

In August, Vice President JD Vance raised more than $5 million from young Republican donors at the Southampton home of Omeed Malik, president of 1789 Capital and a prominent Trump donor.

LaLota, a Navy veteran and former Suffolk County elections commissioner, was first elected in 2022 to succeed Lee Zeldin and was re-elected in 2024, defeating former CNN anchor John Avlon by about 11 points. In that race, LaLota criticized Avlon for his dual residency between Sag Harbor and Manhattan.

Gallant, 37, is an Army National Guard Black Hawk pilot, a former FAA air traffic controller at JFK, a former union leader and a volunteer firefighter. He won the June primary with about 63% of the vote against Lukas Ventouras, a 25-year-old law student who lives in the district and had raised about $124,000, most of it in unnamed small-dollar gifts. Gallant later picked up endorsements from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

After the Post story, Gallant’s attorney, Sara Azari, who previously represented former Rep. Eric Swalwell after misconduct allegations, confirmed the photos were authentic and consensual. Gallant told the New York Times he hoped it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” and the campaign began selling “Make Politics Sexy Again” merchandise. LaLota stuck to calling Gallant “weak and woke” and needling him for declining to debate.

Asked by Fortune about the surge, Gallant answered through Slingshot Strategies, a consulting firm that promises “a proven track record of shifting the conversation” for candidates facing “overwhelming odds” and “difficult fights.”

He said the Post story “backfired on them” and that the Times interview let voters see “a proud gay man who refused to be ashamed of his identity, and it resonated.” On LaLota’s outside money, he said, “I never had to rely on outside interests to try and buy this seat.” About a third of his own money from named donors came from inside the district.

LaLota cast the surge as a product of the controversy itself. “On the same days my opponent was backing out of debates, he was monetizing his BDSM and pornographic modeling past,” he said in a statement to Fortune. “Instead of boasting how kinky he is, as he did to the Times, he owes Long Islanders an explanation for choosing vanity and fundraising over debates and accountability.”

Fortune analyzed itemized contributions dated in 2026 in both campaigns’ raw FEC filings through Oct. 14, so the comparison covers the same stretch of the race for both candidates. Repeat donors were counted once, refunds subtracted and conduit entries adjusted so no gift was counted twice. The FEC does not require campaigns to name individuals who give $200 or less in a cycle, so those donors are excluded. Fortune placed donors inside or outside NY-1 based on the mailing city they listed, which may differ from where they vote. Individuals may give $3,500 per election this cycle, or $7,000 for the primary and general combined. Fortune tallied the filings by hand, then used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to clean the raw files and check the calculations.

LaLota had the bigger war chest. Through Oct. 14, he had raised $4.5 million and had $2.31 million in cash on hand. Gallant had raised $1.7 million and had $426,000 on hand.

The sharper contrast was where the money came from. Of the 785 named donors in LaLota’s 2026 filings, 29% listed mailing addresses in the district. Together they gave $207,161, only 17% of what he raised from named individuals. PACs and other committees supplied $1.18 million, about a quarter of his total for the cycle.

Gallant’s support was more local, but not by much. Of his 1,031 named donors in the 2026 raw file, 390 (38%) listed addresses in NY-1 and nearly $300,000, about a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals this year. Counting gifts from 2025, his itemized individual total for the cycle is $1.15 million.

Half of that in-district money, about $159,000, came from the Hamptons and Shelter Island, the East End enclaves where wealthy New Yorkers have long kept second homes. In East Hampton Town, half of the 22,562 housing units are no one’s usual residence, according to the Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 American Community Survey, which counts second homes as vacant. In Brookhaven, the figure is only about 9%.

Outside the district, 218 Manhattan donors gave Gallant $215,600 and 85 Californians gave about $93,000. Thirteen listed San Francisco.

The photos worked as a fundraiser, just not a local one. Between Sept. 13 and Oct. 14, Gallant reported 677 itemized contributions totaling $276,055: $229,050 from 484 individual donors and $47,005 from PACs, party committees and other sources.

That haul, all in the campaign’s final month of reporting, is about 16% of the $1.7 million he raised this cycle and nearly a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals in 2026. About a third of it arrived in the first four days after the leak.

On Sept. 15, two days after the leak, the New York State Democratic Committee transferred $25,025 to the campaign. That same day, the campaign paid Azari, a celebrity attorney who specializes in crisis and media strategy.

Among the contributions that followed: $500 on Sept. 15 from Howard Sacarob, head of U.S. tax at Royal Bank of Canada, and $3,500 on Oct. 4 from Ryan Fitzpatrick, Corcoran’s regional vice president for Downtown Manhattan.

On Oct. 7, the New York Times published its analysis of the photo scandal. That day, Robert Saum, the World Bank Group’s regional country director for Eastern Europe, a role based in Kyiv, gave $1,000. He lists an Arlington, Va., address.

Steven Holley, COO of the New York investment manager Select Equity Group and a Sullivan & Cromwell partner, gave $1,000 on Oct. 9. Sacarob, Fitzpatrick and Holley all list New York City addresses, outside the district.

The San Francisco-based CEO of Mr. S Leather, the retailer behind the photos, gave $1,000 on Oct. 10.

Not all of Gallant’s best-known donors gave after the Post story. Fortune checked the names below against the dates in his filings.

Wall Street: Stephen Mandel, who founded the Greenwich hedge fund Lone Pine Capital, gave the $3,500 maximum on Sept. 14, the day after the story ran. Susan Mandel of Greenwich, listed as not employed, gave $3,500 the same day.

Old money and real estate: Katharine Rayner, the Cox Enterprises heiress whose fortune of about $4.9 billion (Forbes) rests on her estimated 17% stake in the family company, gave $3,500 on Sept. 15. She had also given $2,000 in July, and her cycle total is listed at the $3,500 limit.

Another maximum gift came on Sept. 26 from Michael Raynes, a developer who restores architecturally significant properties in Miami. In late 2022, he sold a historic estate in Southampton for $20 million. He lists a Miami Beach mailing address.

Wall Street: Charles Myers gave the $3,500 maximum at the end of 2025, when Gallant was still facing a primary. He is founder and chairman of Signum Global Advisors, a geopolitical research firm that advises financial institutions and touts “representation across the political spectrum.” He previously served as vice chairman at Evercore ISI and advised Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign.

Jason Carroll, co-founder of the high-frequency trading firm Hudson River Trading, gave $3,500 on Sept. 8, five days before the leak. Eric Knight, a senior trader at Jane Street, gave $7,000, covering both the primary and the general.

Hollywood and media: Kevin Huvane, co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency, gave $3,500 on June 30. Jeffrey Bewkes, the former Time Warner chairman and CEO who sold the company to AT&T in 2018, gave $3,500 on Aug. 12.

Local: Nancy Goroff, an organic chemist and former chair of Stony Brook University’s chemistry department, gave the maximum on June 29, days after Gallant’s primary win. Goroff lives in a modest New England saltbox overlooking Stony Brook Harbor, valued at about $1.1 million. She ran for a similarly drawn seat in 2020 and lost to Zeldin, now the Trump administration’s EPA administrator.

Goroff also backed “Team KCQ,” North Fork educator Kathryn Casey Quigley’s progressive bid to oust Suffolk County Democratic Chairman Rich Schaffer. Casey Quigley won about 43% of the weighted county committee vote on Sept. 22. Her campaign accused Schaffer of “backroom deals” with the local Conservative Party, which had harshly condemned Gallant’s photos.

Wall Street: Charles Schwab, founder of the brokerage bearing his name, a Fortune 500 company, gave LaLota $13,600 over the past two cycles, the maximum allowed. His mailing city: Palm Beach, Fla.

Crypto and defense: Faryar Shirzad, Coinbase’s chief policy officer and a deputy national security adviser under George W. Bush, gave $3,500 from a Washington, D.C., address. Palmer Luckey of Newport Beach, Calif., who founded defense contractor Anduril after selling Oculus to Facebook for about $2 billion, gave $7,000.

Global money: Leonard Blavatnik, the Ukrainian-born British American billionaire behind Access Industries, gave LaLota $3,500 in March. FEC reports list another $7,000 in aggregate from his wife, Emily.

“Though I have never met him, I appreciate his support,” LaLota said. His spokeswoman suggested Blavatnik may be drawn to LaLota because Russia’s Foreign Ministry put LaLota on a May 2023 list of 500 Americans barred from the country, a distinction the congressman “wears as a badge of honor.”

Blavatnik’s recent contributions also include Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and the Equality PAC, which backs LGBTQ+ candidates.

His contribution forms give an address of 40 W. 57th St. in Manhattan, about 105 miles from the estate the press calls his.

The July 2025 sale of 408 Further Lane in Amagansett, which Behind the Hedges reported as the most expensive residential sale in Hamptons history, lists Brise Lointaine LLC as the new owner.

The seller, Terry Semel, ran Warner Bros. when Stanley Kubrick filmed his masked Long Island society for the studio. Semel had bought the property from Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman in 2005 for $43 million.

Property records from the real estate data service PropertyShark, reviewed by Fortune, list the arm’s-length price as $115,000, three zeros shy of the reported $115 million. East Hampton’s 2026 tax roll still billed Semel’s Windsor Digital Studio LLC. The town assessor’s office said it did not update the roll until July 2026.

The East Hampton Town Clerk’s office confirmed Brise Lointaine LLC’s ownership to Fortune and said deed updates take “very long” to process, along with the Suffolk County Clerk’s office.

Press accounts, though not the paperwork, identify the buyer as LaLota donor Len Blavatnik: Behind the Hedges, citing a source, and The Real Deal. Blavatnik owns Warner Music and holds a stake in A24, the studio behind Lady Bird (2017), Queer (2024), the gay BDSM romance Pillion (2026) and Backrooms (2026).

The tabloid framing of the race borrowed from Eyes Wide Shut (1999), but the sex and the masks were bait. Kubrick’s real horror was a gated order where wealth and power circulate in a closed circle, insulated from consequences.

In his year, the guest list was paper: electronic filing stayed voluntary for most committees until 2000, so a donor was a scanned page, not a spreadsheet. In NY-1, the circle is no secret.

In an age of metadata, AI-scanned social feeds and Flock cameras, nobody wears a mask for long. The leather shoot was archived, authenticated by an attorney and sold back to voters as merchandise. Every FEC filing is a digital fossil Kubrick’s guests would never have left behind.

The economics were another matter. LaLota raised about 84 cents of every named dollar from outside the district; Gallant, nearly two-thirds. What stayed masked on Election Day was not Gallant’s leather photos but the money, and how much of it came from outside NY-1.

#5426. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5425. Seattle startup OneCourt brings tactile tablets for blind and low-vision fans to NHL games

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 2:01 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 7:00 am

Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams.

The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data.

The tablets debuted at the Heritage Classic on Oct. 25, and the Washington Capitals, Colorado Avalanche, Chicago Blackhawks and Detroit Red Wings are the first clubs to offer them at every home game.

“Our community has been asking us for hockey since day one, and launching it with Ticketmaster and the NHL is a milestone for OneCourt,” CEO Jerred Mace said in a news release.

The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks, along with Super Bowl LX.

Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand.

Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

#5424. 2 scandals, 1 destination—Why Nvidia can’t shake China smuggling allegations

For more than a year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeated the party line about covert smuggling of his highly coveted premium chips: There’s no evidence Nvidia AI chips are being diverted to China, Huang has asserted.

But now two bombshell scandals, both allegedly running through Southeast Asia, have blasted a data-center sized hole through Huang’s credibility. The first case, in which $2.5 billion in computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips are under scrutiny, involves Super Micro, a company led by a longtime friend of Jensen Huang’s and one of Nvidia’s closest partners. More recently, a separate string of reports has revealed that Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customer, Megaspeed, is under U.S. investigation for chip diversion.

There is no evidence so far that the two cases are directly connected, though some industry observers have pointed to potential areas of overlap. Whether the two cases are ultimately determined to be part of a larger scheme, or completely separate incidents, the dual scandals have left Nvidia, shareholders, and its famous CEO, reeling.

On Sunday, Huang told employees in an email he had betrayed his wife and family in an extramarital affair. His confession followed reports claiming that intelligence officials believe Huang’s affair partner, Alice Huang (no relation), was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to purportedly report on his doings to Beijing. Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, a Singapore company that reportedly became Nvidia’s largest chip buyer in Southeast Asia.

Alongside Huang’s admission, Nvidia’s board announced it has opened an independent investigation into whether Nvidia co-founder Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence operation but noted that board members maintain “confidence” in Huang. The board said it has no reason to believe that “either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Nvidia board members have retained acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run point on the investigation, Nvidia announced Tuesday.

Nvidia’s GPU chips are critical components for training and running advanced AI models such as those made by OpenAI and Anthropic. The U.S. government considers the chips to be dual-use technology with potential military applications, and requires specific export licenses to sell them to countries such as China—which haven’t been granted to Nvidia’s most high-powered chips.

How things will shake out for Nvidia is evolving in real time, but it’s likely that a terse letter Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) sent to Nvidia in June will turn into a subpoena. That’s thanks to midterm election results that saw Democrats regain the Senate with Warren poised to chair the powerful Senate Banking Committee in January. Warren and Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) called Monday for Nvidia to answer questions, and three House committee chairs have asked Huang to accede to a closed-door grilling before lawmakers November 18, the day after Nvidia is scheduled to report its third quarter financial results.

The June letter, which went to Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter and audit committee chair Brooke Seawell, sought answers from Nvidia regarding the state of its compliance program and noted that Nvidia continued to include Super Micro Computer (Supermicro) as a key partner in its network. The letter also cited Culper Research, a short seller who bet against Nvidia and published a report that alleges possible smuggling links between Supermicro, Nvidia, and Megaspeed, the company where Alice Huang was a top executive. U.S. authorities have investigated whether the billions in Nvidia hardware Megaspeed bought through Nvidia’s server partners went to Chinese firms barred from getting the chips. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

Alice Huang is now the link between the CEO infidelity and coverup scandal facing Jensen Huang, the poster CEO for the AI buildout, and a question that has persistently dogged Nvidia, which is where its chips actually wind up after they’re purchased. And as far as export control compliance goes, an alleged honey trap espionage case carries a lot more public-interest tailwind than the at times byzantine regulations involved in obtaining and complying with export restrictions and licensing. Meaning, this latest revelation is unlikely to blow over as a single rogue actor or administrative export record issue.

One export-control veteran, who asked to speak anonymously because of his clients, said if he were an independent director or general counsel, he’d be looking at whether the company they oversee has a Huang honeytrap problem—and not just at the CEO level. Executives who are supposed to inspect data centers or conduct due diligence have been the targets of these types of seduction schemes going back decades.

He also nodded to the March Supermicro indictment that pointed out that a compliance auditor was “off-site enjoying entertainment paid for by” another company. It’s a fairly common tactic, he said.

Until recently, the most high-profile case of contraband Nvidia chips involved one of Nvidia’s closest partners, a company run by Huang’s longtime friend, Supermicro CEO Charles Liang. Neither Liang nor Supermicro was charged and Supermicro has said it is cooperating with authorities. Liang and Huang, who both founded their respective companies in 1993, often took the stage together at an event called Computex in Taiwan and joked back and forth during their joint keynotes.

“When we’re together, sometimes we speak Taiwanese, sometimes we speak Mandarin, and then when we disagree, we speak English,” Huang joked before an adoring crowd at Computex in 2024. (Huang was photographed with Alice Huang, his affair partner, at a Taipei cocktail bar during Computex that year.)

In March, federal prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with routing about $2.5 billion in servers laden with Nvidia H200 and B200 GPUs to China via a Southeast Asian front company. Supermicro was not charged and has said it was a victim of the scheme. Liaw has pleaded not guilty, although one of the three who were charged pleaded guilty last month. Liaw cofounded Supermicro with Liang and Liang’s wife, Sara Liu the same year Huang co-founded Nvidia. Neither Liang nor Liu were named in the indictment.

According to Liaw’s indictment, the elaborate scheme involved staging thousands of nonworking dummy servers in three warehouses to trick auditors. Contractors used hair dryers to soften the adhesive on serial-number labels and peel them off. That alleged scheme followed a similar playbook as one that had ensnared Supermicro in 2006, when the company pleaded guilty to illegally exporting computer equipment to Iran through a distributor in Dubai. Both routes involved selling to a neighboring country to keep the real buyer hidden.

The Liaw indictment does not accuse Nvidia of wrongdoing, but it lays out how the front company’s orders for Supermicro hardware fed into Nvidia’s chip allocation. In December 2024, Liaw allegedly asked the front company for monthly forecasts, writing that the forecasts were “the only way” to get Nvidia to promise B200 chip allocations, according to the indictment. Bloomberg later reported and Culper agreed that the front company in the alleged scheme is OBON, a Bangkok AI infrastructure firm. OBON has not been charged.

Supermicro has since disclosed that it received a grand jury subpoena from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, subpoenas and inquiries from foreign authorities, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Bureau of Industry and Security. In Liaw’s case, his lawyer told the judge the documents Supermicro would give the government could be material to his defense, and his trial was pushed back from November 2026 to March 2027.

As details of the Megaspeed scandal emerge, Nvidia’s chips are now at the center of a second major smuggling case—this time involving one of its own customers. Megaspeed reportedly bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips during the past two years, with nearly $2 billion of the chips installed in data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia that are alleged to serve Chinese customers remotely, according to New York Times reporting.

Nvidia, in what could become a grave misstep, repeatedly assured the public that Megaspeed was credible. In October 2025, a spokesperson said Nvidia had visited Megaspeed operations and found no evidence of chip diversion. Last month, as reports about suspected Chinese spying emerged, Nvidia said the diversion allegations against Megaspeed had been “thoroughly investigated and debunked.” Jensen Huang, in a statement that has depreciated faster than an older-generation GPU, told Bloomberg his interactions with Alice Huang were “completely normal and not unusual.”

In May, Culper Research, which has shorted Nvidia, argued there were connections between the Supermicro indictment, alleged Nvidia chip smuggling, and Megaspeed. Culper wrote that Megaspeed’s website once listed Supermicro as a partner alongside Nvidia, Intel, and Gigabyte. The web entry was removed, but it still sits in the site code, Culper found. In addition, the report called the reported Supermicro-OBON smuggling route one of many that Nvidia chips travel before they get to China.

Huang next faces analysts on Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports third quarter earnings. The following day, House lawmakers have asked for a closed-door briefing. And in January, Warren is expected to wield the subpoena power of the Banking Committee and get the answers she originally sought back in June.

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5423. Larry Page Reportedly Gave This Two-Word Prediction About the Future of AI. Elon Musk Says It’s ‘Accurate.’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The Google co-founder’s prediction came secondhand via a popular investing podcast. But that didn’t stop Musk from weighing in.

Larry Page and Elon Musk don’t talk anymore, but that didn’t stop Musk from praising Page’s prediction about the future of AI — or at least something Page reportedly said to someone else.

It all started with a podcast last week. On the Nov. 4 episode of Invest Like the Best, host Patrick O’Shaughnessy recalls hearing that Page was asked how much of the world’s computing power, the servers that run AI and everything else online, would eventually be in space. Page’s reported answer was “five nines,” or 99.999%.

Musk shared the clip on X on Sunday. “Larry Page has made many accurate predictions and this is one of them,” he wrote.

Larry Page has made many accurate predictions and this is one of them https://t.co/HE2ro6Z2ey

The endorsement fits Musk’s own pitch. SpaceX, which absorbed his AI company xAI this year, wants to build AI data centers in space. Earlier this month, Musk argued that AI hardware could be easier to cool in orbit than on Earth. Google is testing the idea too, and its Project Suncatcher chips recently generated their first AI response in orbit.

The two billionaires fell out in 2015 after Musk recruited a top Google AI researcher to co-found OpenAI, according to Yahoo! Finance.
